verifiedBugs.title: crawl_ids_for_range generates non-existent Common Crawl IDs (odd-week snapping), so most WET/CDX/FineWeb fetches 404 and silently emit zero docs
verifiedBugs.description: crawl_ids_for_range() maps every ISO week in [start,end] to the nearest ODD week: `anchor_week = week if week % 2 == 1 else week - 1`. Real Common Crawl crawl IDs do NOT follow an odd-week pattern; they are spaced ~4-5 weeks apart at arbitrary week numbers. Verified against the live https://index.commoncrawl.org/collinfo.json: the real recent crawls are CC-MAIN-2026-21, -17, -12, -08, -04, CC-MAIN-2025-51, -47, -43. Several of these (04, 08, 12) are EVEN weeks the code can never produce, and the code instead emits dense odd-week IDs (CC-MAIN-2026-01,-03,-05,...) that do not exist. Reproduced: for the range 2025-10-01..2026-06-01 the function generates 19 IDs but only 5 correspond to real crawls; it entirely misses CC-MAIN-2026-04/-08/-12.
verifiedBugs.impact: This is the root cause of 'the app has no idea how to scrape the internet.' Every phantom crawl_id flows into: (a) WET discovery — wet.paths.gz returns 404, logged WARNING, run_partition returns yielding nothing; (b) CC-Index — the CDX `<crawl>-index` endpoint 404s, returns nothing; (c) FineWeb — the crawl_id is passed as the HF dataset config `name`/dump, which raises and is swallowed. The bulk-corpus path (WET) — the primary backfill source — therefore emits almost no documents and the user gets no error, only buried WARNING/INFO logs. Even when a generated ID happens to match a real crawl it is luck, not design.
verifiedBugs.repro: PYTHONPATH=src python -c "from awareness.sources.commoncrawl_wet import crawl_ids_for_range; from datetime import datetime,timezone; print(crawl_ids_for_range(datetime(2026,1,1,tzinfo=timezone.utc), datetime(2026,6,1,tzinfo=timezone.utc)))" → prints CC-MAIN-2026-01,-03,-05,...,-23; compare to real crawls 2026-04,-08,-12,-17,-21.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Do not synthesize crawl IDs from a parity heuristic. Fetch the authoritative crawl list once from https://index.commoncrawl.org/collinfo.json (cache it), parse each crawl's id and its from/to timestamps, and select the crawls whose time window overlaps [start,end]. Fall back to a small bundled snapshot of known crawl IDs if the network is unavailable. This single fix makes WET, CC-Index, and FineWeb target real crawls.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED. The claim is genuinely real and user-affecting. Verified end to end.

1) Repro is accurate. I reproduced crawl_ids_for_range's logic in isolation (the real module won't import due to a missing structlog dep, but the function is pure date math so I extracted it verbatim). For 2026-01-01..2026-06-01 it emits dense consecutive odd weeks: CC-MAIN-2026-01,-03,-05,...,-23. The anchor logic at line 87 (`anchor_week = week if week % 2 == 1 else week - 1`) snaps every ISO week to the nearest ODD week.

2) The central factual premise is correct. I fetched the authoritative https://index.commoncrawl.org/collinfo.json. Real recent crawls do NOT follow an odd-week pattern: 2026-21,-17,-12,-08,-04; 2025-51,-47,-43,-38,-33,-30,-26,-21,-18,-13,-08,-05; 2024-51,-46,-42,-38,-33,-30,-26,-22,-18,-10. 16 of these 27 are EVEN week numbers the parity heuristic can NEVER produce.

3) Quantified impact for 2025-10-01..2026-06-01: 19 IDs generated, only 5 are real crawls (CC-MAIN-2025-43/-47/-51, 2026-17/-21); 14 are phantom (will 404). The three real in-window crawls 2026-04/-08/-12 are entirely missed — exactly as claimed.

4) Impact chain confirmed in code: all three adapters consume crawl_ids_for_range and feed the IDs straight into network identifiers — commoncrawl_wet.py builds CC_BASE/crawl-data/<crawl_id>/wet.paths.gz; cc_index.py builds CDX_BASE/<crawl_id>-index (cc_index.py:67); fineweb.py passes crawl_id as load_dataset(..., name=dump) (fineweb.py:111).

5) Silent failure confirmed: phantom WET/CDX URLs return non-200 -> logger.warning + bare return yielding nothing (commoncrawl_wet.py:164-166, cc_index.py:76-82); fineweb load_dataset raises -> caught -> logger.warning + return (fineweb.py:112-114). No error reaches the user; only buried WARNING logs. The primary bulk backfill source (WET) thus drops the majority of its target crawls and ~74% of partitions are wasted 404s.

6) No mitigation exists: grep found no collinfo.json fetch and no bundled fallback crawl list anywhere in src/ or tests/. The parity heuristic is the sole source of IDs. The only unit test (tests/unit/test_planner.py:16) asserts merely count (12<=n<=30) and the 'CC-MAIN-2024-' prefix — it never validates the IDs are real, so the bug passes CI.

Corroborating signal: the docstring at line 83 says 'coalesce to even-week starts' while the code snaps to ODD weeks, and the module docstring (lines 19-23) assumes a ~2-week regular cadence — the heuristic was clearly never validated against the real, irregular ~4-5-week crawl schedule.

Not a style nit, not handled elsewhere. Genuine correctness bug in the Sources/Scraping layer.
verdict.correction: Real as described; root cause is exactly the parity heuristic at commoncrawl_wet.py:87-88 with no authoritative crawl list. Two refinements to the claim's wording: (a) Severity is better rated HIGH than CRITICAL. It is not a total zero-doc outage — the heuristic accidentally hits real ODD-week crawls (e.g. 2025-43/-47/-51, 2026-17/-21), so ~26% of generated IDs coincidentally work and some documents are still ingested. The defect silently DROPS the majority of crawls (all even-week ones, ~74% of generated IDs are 404 phantoms) and wastes most partitions, rather than producing literally zero docs. (b) The fix should also fix the existing unit test (tests/unit/test_planner.py:16), which currently only checks count/prefix and would still pass with phantom IDs; it should assert generated IDs intersect a known real-crawl set. Suggested fix (fetch+cache collinfo.json, select crawls whose from/to window overlaps [start,end], with a bundled fallback snapshot) is correct and addresses WET, CC-Index, and FineWeb in one place since all three share crawl_ids_for_range.

verifiedBugs.title: WET (and FineWeb) domain filter compares eTLD+1 against raw user domains, silently dropping all docs when user passes a subdomain
verifiedBugs.description: The shard parser builds `domains_filter = set(partition.payload['domains'])` from the user's request.domains verbatim, then keeps a record only if `domain_of(canonical_url(url)) in domains_filter`. But domain_of() returns the registered eTLD+1 (verified: domain_of('http://news.bbc.co.uk/a') == 'bbc.co.uk', domain_of('http://www.example.com') == 'example.com'). If the user passes a subdomain-qualified domain such as 'news.bbc.co.uk' or 'www.example.com' or 'blog.example.com', it will never equal the eTLD+1 produced by domain_of, so EVERY record is filtered out.
verifiedBugs.impact: A domain-narrowed WET/FineWeb backfill for any subdomain (very common: news.bbc.co.uk, www.cnn.com, en.wikipedia.org) yields zero documents with no error — the parser logs captures_emitted=0 and moves on. Contributes directly to 'no idea how to scrape the internet' for targeted backfills.
verifiedBugs.repro: Plan a backfill with domains=['www.example.com']; in _parse_wet_to_captures every url whose domain_of is 'example.com' fails the `dom not in domains_filter` check and is skipped, emitting 0 captures.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Normalize both sides through domain_of() before comparing: build `domains_filter = {domain_of(d) for d in request.domains}` (or match by suffix), so 'www.example.com' and 'example.com' both reduce to the same registered domain. Apply the same fix in fineweb.py:104/133-135.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED REAL. Verified every link in the chain:

1. domain_of() returns eTLD+1, stripping subdomains (empirically: domain_of('http://www.example.com/')=='example.com', domain_of('http://news.bbc.co.uk/a')=='bbc.co.uk'; also asserted in tests/unit/test_urls.py:36).

2. The WET filter (src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py:204 build, 302-304 check) compares domain_of(canonical_url(url)) for exact membership in a set built VERBATIM from request.domains. plan() at line 119 passes request.domains through with NO normalization (confirmed domain_of absent from plan source). fineweb.py:104,133-135 is identical.

3. No upstream normalization exists: CLI (main.py:1113), API (server.py:163), web UI (app.js:584) all pass domains verbatim; BackfillRequest.domains (jobs.py:54) has no validator.

4. Exact repro succeeds: filter {'www.example.com'} or {'news.bbc.co.uk'} returns False for EVERY URL on that domain (all docs dropped); {'example.com'} works. So a subdomain-qualified domain filter silently yields zero captures with only an info-level captures_emitted=0 log and no error.

5. Both adapters are default-active sources (planner.py:58-59), so this is on the default backfill path.

Strong corroborating evidence the claim omitted: the sibling Common Crawl Index adapter (cc_index.py:51) builds its filter as f"*.{dom}/*" — a wildcard/suffix match that correctly accepts BOTH eTLD+1 and subdomain inputs from the SAME request.domains. Since a domain-narrowed backfill also activates CC index (planner.py:65-66), the user would get results from CC index but zero from WET/FineWeb for a subdomain input — proving the exact-eTLD+1 equality is an inconsistent bug, not an intended contract, and producing a confusing silent partial failure.

This is not a style nit and is not handled elsewhere. It is genuinely user-affecting for the common case of www.-prefixed or multi-level subdomain inputs.
verdict.correction: Claim is accurate. Two refinements: (1) The bug manifests ONLY when the user passes a subdomain-qualified domain (www.cnn.com, news.bbc.co.uk); bare eTLD+1 inputs (cnn.com) work correctly, and the web UI placeholder nudges toward eTLD+1. This limits but does not eliminate impact, since www./multi-level inputs are extremely common and nothing documents or enforces the eTLD+1 requirement. (2) Root-cause framing is strengthened by the sibling cc_index.py:51 which uses wildcard suffix matching (*.{dom}/*) on the same request.domains — demonstrating the WET/FineWeb exact-equality is an inconsistency rather than a deliberate eTLD+1-only contract, and that a domain-narrowed backfill produces a silent partial failure (CC index returns docs, WET/FineWeb return zero). The suggested fix (domains_filter = {domain_of(d) for d in request.domains}) is correct; consider matching cc_index's suffix semantics for parity if subdomain-precision filtering is ever desired. Severity adjusted from the claimed 'high' and I concur with high (silent, default path, common trigger), not critical (does not corrupt data or break the eTLD+1 happy path).

verifiedBugs.title: Feeds cursor stores last 5000 of an unordered set, re-emitting thousands of already-seen URLs on every poll
verifiedBugs.description: The seen-URL cursor is updated via `merged = last_seen | {canonical_url(u) ...}` (a set) then `context.checkpoint['seen_urls'] = list(list(merged)[-5000:])`. A Python set has arbitrary, non-insertion order, so slicing `[-5000:]` keeps an essentially random 5000 elements and discards the rest. On the next poll the dropped URLs are no longer in last_seen and are re-classified as 'new'. Reproduced: with 7000 URLs, after one run only 5000 are retained; a second identical poll re-discovers 2000 URLs as new every time.
verifiedBugs.impact: For any feed/sitemap exposing more than ~5000 URLs, each poll re-enqueues thousands of TAIL_RECRAWL sub-partitions for pages already fetched, causing repeated re-fetching of the same pages, wasted bandwidth, rate-limit pressure on publishers, and dedup churn. The cursor never converges.
verifiedBugs.repro: PYTHONPATH=src python: build 7000 urls, run the cursor-update logic once (keeps 5000), reload as last_seen, re-filter the same 7000 → 2000 reported as new.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Use an order-preserving structure for the cursor (e.g. keep a list and dedup with dict.fromkeys to preserve order, then slice the most-recent N), or bound by an LRU/OrderedDict. Also call canonical_url(u) once per URL and reuse the value instead of computing it 2-3x.

verdict.reasoning:
The code-level defect is real and I reproduced it. At src/awareness/sources/feeds.py:73-75 the cursor is built as `merged = last_seen | {canonical_url(u) ...}` (a set) and persisted via `context.checkpoint['seen_urls'] = list(list(merged)[-5000:])`. A Python set has no insertion order, so `[-5000:]` keeps an arbitrary 5000 elements and silently drops the rest. The checkpoint genuinely persists across polls (verified end-to-end: tail/engine.py re-emits a task with the same partition_key `rss:<url>` each poll → workers/engine.py:309-311 restores the cursor via state.py:479 `get_last_task_checkpoint`, which is keyed on partition_key only, not job_id, so it even survives restarts → state.py:399-405 writes it back on completion). Empirical repro with 7000 distinct URLs: run 1 retains 5000, run 2 re-flags exactly 2000 as 'new'; the cursor never converges. So this is a true correctness defect, not a style nit or a non-persisted no-op.

However, the claimed PRIMARY impact — repeated network re-fetching of the same pages, wasted bandwidth, and publisher rate-limit pressure — is largely prevented by a second dedup guard the report missed. The feeds adapter emits recrawl sub-partitions with key `tail:{canonical_url(u)}` (feeds.py:82). When those reach storage/state.py add_tasks (lines 354-358), a TAIL_RECRAWL row that is already COMPLETED for the same (job_id, partition_key) is explicitly NOT re-armed (`continue`) — the comment there names this exact scenario: avoiding a 'redundant network re-fetch before dedup can fold it.' Within a running tail session all polls share one job_id, so each unique URL is fetched at most once regardless of how many times the buggy cursor re-emits it. tail_recrawl.py also has no other gate, but it never runs for these suppressed tasks.

What actually survives as harm: (1) per-poll enqueue/DB churn — thousands of no-op add_tasks lookups every poll for feeds >5000 URLs; (2) the feeds cursor never converging, so its own filter and the `feeds.urls_discovered`/new-URL accounting are permanently wrong/inflated; (3) the per-URL guard only protects COMPLETED rows — a recrawl that previously FAILED/dead-lettered (or any future code that drops that guard) would be re-armed and genuinely re-fetched, and the broken cursor removes the upstream defense. These are real but low-cost relative to the claimed bandwidth/rate-limit blowup. Hence real, but severity is low rather than medium. The suggested fix (order-preserving dedup via dict.fromkeys + slice most-recent N, and computing canonical_url once per URL instead of 2-3x at feeds.py:72/74/82) is correct and worthwhile.
verdict.correction: Real bug, correct root cause (set has no order, so [-5000:] keeps arbitrary elements and the cursor never converges for feeds/sitemaps exposing >5000 URLs; reproduced 7000→2000). But the impact is overstated: the headline 'repeated re-fetching / wasted bandwidth / publisher rate-limit pressure' is prevented within a tail job by the TAIL_RECRAWL re-fetch guard at src/awareness/storage/state.py:354-358, which drops already-COMPLETED per-URL fetch tasks before any HTTP GET. The true surviving cost is per-poll enqueue/DB churn, a permanently non-converging cursor with wrong 'new URL' metrics, and loss of the upstream defense in the non-COMPLETED (FAILED/dead-lettered) recrawl case. Severity downgraded from medium to low.

verifiedBugs.title: is_public_http_url performs blocking socket.getaddrinfo inside the async tail fetch path, stalling the event loop
verifiedBugs.description: tail_recrawl.run_partition calls `is_public_http_url(url)` synchronously at line 59 and again per-redirect at line 162 inside `_get_public_url`. is_public_http_url (util/urls.py:142) performs a blocking `socket.getaddrinfo(...)` DNS resolution. These calls are not wrapped in run_in_executor/to_thread, so they block the asyncio event loop for the full DNS round-trip on every tail fetch and every redirect hop.
verifiedBugs.impact: All concurrent tail recrawls are effectively serialized behind blocking DNS lookups; one slow/hanging DNS resolution stalls every other coroutine in the worker (fetching, flushing, progress). Under real-world tail/feed discovery with many domains this drastically reduces throughput and can make ingestion appear hung — reinforcing the 'janky / can't scrape' perception.
verifiedBugs.repro: Any tail_recrawl task: line 59 calls is_public_http_url → util/urls.py:142 socket.getaddrinfo executes on the event loop thread; with N concurrent tasks they cannot overlap their DNS resolution.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Wrap SSRF/DNS validation in `await asyncio.to_thread(is_public_http_url, url)` (or use an async resolver), both at the initial check and inside the redirect loop. Alternatively resolve once and reuse.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified against the code. The mechanism is real: `is_public_http_url` (src/awareness/util/urls.py:112) calls blocking `socket.getaddrinfo` at line 142 with no executor/to_thread wrapper and no timeout argument. It is invoked synchronously from the async path at src/awareness/sources/tail_recrawl.py:59 (initial check) and :162 (per-redirect inside `_get_public_url`). These coroutines run concurrently on a single event loop via `asyncio.gather(*(run_one(t) for t in tasks))` in the worker engine (src/awareness/workers/engine.py:217 in run_job and :292 in run_tail), with up to worker_concurrency tasks (default 8, config/settings.py:84). So the blocking DNS resolution does execute on the shared event-loop thread, freezing all other coroutines (fetches, flushes, progress, robots checks) for the duration of each getaddrinfo round-trip.

This is a genuine deviation from the codebase's own established convention: blocking work is offloaded via run_in_executor/to_thread throughout (gdelt.py:99, commoncrawl_wet.py:246/251, warc_repair.py:68, engine.py:445/459/491/519, storage/state.py). It is NOT handled elsewhere — there is no DNS cache and no executor wrapper anywhere in the call chain.

The real, user-affecting harm is head-of-line blocking / tail latency: because getaddrinfo takes no timeout, a single slow or hanging nameserver lookup freezes the entire worker event loop for the OS resolver timeout (seconds to tens of seconds), stalling every concurrent task — which matches the 'janky / appears hung' symptom.

Two corrections to the claim: (1) Impact is overstated. It does NOT 'effectively serialize all tail recrawls' or 'drastically reduce throughput' in the common case — with a healthy resolver (which itself caches), each stall is sub-millisecond to a few ms and merely additive; the actual HTTP fetches remain properly async. The defensible harm is the worst-case event-loop freeze on slow/hanging DNS, not steady-state serialization. This keeps severity at medium, not high. (2) Scope is understated. The same blocking call is also reached via src/awareness/util/robots.py:32 (`_get_public_robots_url`, called from robots.is_allowed at tail_recrawl.py:72 on the same loop), so the root cause is `is_public_http_url` itself being a blocking sync function with three event-loop call sites, not just the two cited lines.
verdict.correction: Real bug, severity medium confirmed. Root cause is `is_public_http_url` (util/urls.py:142 socket.getaddrinfo) being a blocking, untimed sync function called on the event loop. The cited lines (tail_recrawl.py:59, :162) are correct but incomplete — robots.py:32 hits the same blocking call on the same loop via robots.is_allowed (tail_recrawl.py:72). The claimed impact ('all concurrent recrawls effectively serialized / drastically reduced throughput') is overstated for healthy DNS; the genuine, user-affecting failure is worst-case head-of-line blocking — one slow/hanging getaddrinfo freezes the whole worker event loop for the OS resolver timeout (no timeout arg passed), stalling all coroutines and producing the 'appears hung' symptom. Suggested fix is sound: wrap validation in asyncio.to_thread (or use an async resolver) at all three call sites, and ideally add a short-TTL DNS cache; resolving once and reusing is harder here because each redirect hop must be re-validated.

verifiedBugs.title: WET shard fetch keeps no per-shard checkpoint; any retry re-parses the entire cached shard and re-emits all captures
verifiedBugs.description: _run_shard streams a 100-500MB WET file to disk then parses the whole file with _parse_wet_to_captures, which returns ALL captures as a single list (lines 251-264). It never writes context.checkpoint (grep for 'checkpoint' in commoncrawl_wet.py returns nothing). If the task fails partway through yielding (e.g. an exception during dedup/flush at doc 5000, or a transient error), engine.py marks the task for retry; on retry the entire shard is re-parsed from record 0 and every capture is re-emitted. The module docstring (lines 14, 197) promises 'Checkpoint stores last_offset/last_record_id so re-runs resume', but no such checkpoint exists.
verifiedBugs.impact: Wasted CPU/bandwidth on retries and a flood of duplicate captures that must be re-deduped; for large shards a single late failure forces a full re-parse. The advertised resume capability is missing.
verifiedBugs.repro: Trigger an exception during iteration of a WET shard task (e.g. storage flush error after N docs); on retry the shard is re-parsed entirely from the start because context.checkpoint was never populated.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Stream records lazily (generator instead of returning a full list) and write context.checkpoint['last_record_index'] (or WARC-Record-ID/offset) as captures are yielded, skipping already-processed records on resume — matching the documented behavior and the FineWeb adapter's row_index pattern.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED that the factual core of the claim is correct, but the claimed mechanism ("checkpoint lets other adapters resume mid-task on retry, WET is the odd one out") is wrong, which lowers severity.

Confirmed facts:
- src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py contains zero references to `checkpoint` (grep is empty). `_run_shard` (lines 197-267) streams the shard to disk and calls `_parse_wet_to_captures` (lines 274-368), which builds and returns ALL captures as a single `list[DocCapture]` (out.append at line 360, return at 368). No per-record cursor is written.
- The module docstring at line 14 does advertise "Checkpoint stores last_offset or last_record_id so re-runs resume," and the SourceRef even carries `source_offset_or_record_id=record_id` (line 340), so the resume capability is documented/implied but absent.
- On retry the whole shard is re-parsed from record 0 (the cached .gz on disk is reused at line 217, so bandwidth is NOT re-spent — only CPU/parse time is wasted; the claim's "wasted bandwidth" is inaccurate because the file is cached locally). Every capture is re-emitted.

WHY SEVERITY IS LOW, not medium:
1. The claim's framing that this is a WET-specific regression versus a working FineWeb pattern is misleading. The checkpoint subsystem does NOT provide mid-task crash recovery for ANY adapter. `context.checkpoint` lives only in memory; it is persisted exclusively by `complete_task` (state.py:438-458) on SUCCESS. The failure path in engine.py (lines 383-390) calls `fail_task`, which does not accept or write a checkpoint (state.py:460-477) and sets status back to PENDING. On retry, `init_checkpoint` is loaded via `get_last_task_checkpoint` (state.py:479-495), which only reads COMPLETED tasks for that partition_key — of which there are none for a task that has only ever failed. So FineWeb, given the exact repro scenario (exception at doc 5000 of an unfinished task), ALSO restarts from row_index 0. The checkpoint mechanism is designed for cross-run resume (a partition fully completes, then a later job with the same partition_key resumes) and for the feeds/tail incremental cursor — not for the intra-task retry the bug describes. So the suggested fix (write checkpoint as captures are yielded) would NOT actually fix the repro, because that in-memory checkpoint is discarded on failure before any retry sees it.
2. Impact is wasted CPU on re-parse, not correctness loss. Re-emitted captures hit the persistent content-hash dedup index (dedup/engine.py upsert_dedup on content_hash), so they are classified EXACT_DUP and do not corrupt the dataset — they create redundant provenance rows and burn CPU. No duplicate "unique" docs leak through.
3. `max_retries` bounds the blast radius (engine.py:385 dead-letters after attempts >= max_retries), so a shard cannot re-parse unboundedly.

Net: real documentation-vs-implementation gap and a genuine (if bounded) CPU-waste inefficiency on retries, but it is an efficiency/doc-accuracy issue, not a behavior/correctness break, and the proposed fix as written would not resolve the stated repro without also changing the engine to persist checkpoints on failure.
verdict.correction: Real but mischaracterized. (1) The cached shard is reused on retry (commoncrawl_wet.py:217), so NO bandwidth is wasted on re-download — only re-parse CPU. (2) The deeper root cause is engine-level, not WET-specific: checkpoints are only persisted by complete_task on success; fail_task (state.py:460-477) discards context.checkpoint, and get_last_task_checkpoint (state.py:479-495) reads only COMPLETED tasks. Therefore NO adapter — including the FineWeb "reference" pattern the claim cites — actually resumes mid-shard after a crash; all of them restart from index 0 on retry. (3) Consequently the suggested fix (lazily yield + write context.checkpoint['last_record_index'] as captures emit) is necessary but insufficient: it only helps if the engine is also changed to persist the running checkpoint on the failure path (fail_task) or to write checkpoints incrementally. (4) Re-emitted captures are caught by the persistent content_hash dedup (EXACT_DUP), so this is bounded wasted work and redundant provenance rows, not data corruption or duplicate unique docs. Severity downgraded medium -> low.

verifiedBugs.title: Discovery adapters swallow all HTTP/network failures and emit zero work with no error surfaced to the job
verifiedBugs.description: Across the discovery/fetch adapters, every network error or non-200 response is caught and turned into a bare `return` from an async generator (yielding nothing): CDX query failure (cc_index 82/93), wet.paths.gz 404/error (cc_wet 162/165), WET shard download failure (cc_wet 230/242), GDELT slot fetch (gdelt 92/96), FineWeb load_dataset (fineweb 113). The task is then marked COMPLETED with docs_emitted=0 (engine.py:399) — indistinguishable from 'this partition legitimately had no data'. No metric increments on most of these failure paths and no job-level error count.
verifiedBugs.impact: Transient network hiccups, rate-limiting (HTTP 429/503 from data.commoncrawl.org), or a wrong endpoint cause whole partitions to complete 'successfully' with zero documents. The job status shows tasks_completed rising and docs_emitted near zero, with the failure only visible in buried WARNING logs. This makes the scraping layer appear to 'work' (no failures) while producing no data — exactly the reported symptom, and it prevents retry since the task isn't marked failed.
verifiedBugs.repro: Point any adapter at an unreachable/404 endpoint (e.g. a phantom crawl_id from the odd-week bug): the discovery returns, the task is completed with 0 docs and no failure recorded.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Distinguish 'no data' from 'fetch failed': on network error or non-200 (other than a genuine 404-means-not-published), raise so the task is retried/dead-lettered, or at minimum increment a per-source failure metric and record a job-visible warning count. Treat repeated empty discovery as an alertable condition.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified end-to-end. All five cited adapter paths swallow non-200 responses and network errors with a bare `return` from the async generator: cc_index.py:82 (non-200) and :93 (httpx.HTTPError); commoncrawl_wet.py:163 (wet.paths.gz HTTPError), :166 (non-200), and :230/:243 (shard download non-200/HTTPError); gdelt.py:93 (non-200, logged only at INFO) and :97 (HTTPError); fineweb.py:114 (load_dataset failure). A bare return from these generators yields nothing.

The downstream handling makes this user-affecting. In workers/engine.py `_run_task` (lines 332-414), the try/except around `adapter.run_partition` only catches *raised* exceptions to call `fail_task` (which, per state.py:460-477, re-sets the task to PENDING for retry up to max_retries and then dead-letters it). Because the adapters return instead of raising, control reaches the success path: `context.extras['enqueue']` is empty, `complete_task(docs_emitted=0)` runs (engine.py:399), `increment_job_counters(..., completed=1)` runs (406), and the `tasks.completed` metric is incremented (413). The task is marked COMPLETED, never retried, never dead-lettered.

The observability claim also checks out: grep confirms NONE of the failure paths increment any metric — the only `get_metrics().inc(...)` calls (cc_index.matches, cc_wet.shards_*, gdelt.urls_discovered) are on the success path and simply don't execute on early return. There is no per-source failure counter and no job-level error count. I searched the entire source tree for any watchdog / stall detector / zero-doc alert and found none; status surfaces (planner.py:172-175, cli/main.py) display tasks_completed and docs_emitted verbatim. So a partition that hit a transient 429/503/timeout from data.commoncrawl.org is genuinely indistinguishable from 'this partition legitimately had no data', visible only in buried WARNING (or INFO for gdelt) logs. This precisely matches the reported symptom: scraping 'works' (tasks_completed rises, no failures) while producing ~0 documents, and retry is silently defeated.

Not a style nit and not handled elsewhere — the retry machinery exists but is bypassed by the swallow. Severity is medium rather than high: (1) it's a data-completeness/observability defect, not corruption — emitted records remain correct, and (2) for Common Crawl specifically a 404 on wet.paths.gz / a phantom crawl_id is partly intended 'not yet published' behavior (documented at commoncrawl_wet.py:22-23), and a 404 gdelt slot is legitimately 'no file'. The genuine defect is conflating *transient* failures (429/503/connection resets/timeouts) and outright network errors with that benign 'no data' case, with no retry and no distinct signal.

(1) Root cause is precise: the bare `return` from the async generators means workers/engine.py:333's try/except never fires, so the retry/dead-letter path in `fail_task` (state.py:460-477) is bypassed — the bug is the swallow defeating an otherwise-correct retry mechanism, not just 'no error surfaced'. The defensible, higher-impact framing is a transient HTTP 429/503/timeout or connection error from data.commoncrawl.org: those are caught identically to a 404, the partition completes with docs_emitted=0, no metric/error is recorded, and the task is never retried. Suggested fix stands: distinguish transient/network/5xx/429 failures (raise → retry/dead-letter, or at minimum increment a per-source failure metric and a job-visible error count) from a genuine 404 'not published', and treat repeated empty discovery as alertable.

verifiedBugs.title: Legacy near_dup_hash column is declared Integer (32-bit) but stores a 64-bit signed simhash value, overflowing on Postgres
verifiedBugs.description: add_near_dup_index computes legacy_hash = simhash_unsigned & 0xffffffffffffffff then sign-converts it into the signed 64-bit range (can be roughly -9.2e18 .. 9.2e18) and stores it in DedupNearRow.near_dup_hash, which is mapped_column(Integer). SQLAlchemy Integer maps to a 32-bit INTEGER on PostgreSQL (range ~ -2.1e9 .. 2.1e9). The default backend is SQLite (config/settings.py:135), where INTEGER is dynamically sized so it works, but the codebase explicitly targets Postgres (TailRow is documented 'Postgres-friendly'; StateDB accepts arbitrary URLs). On Postgres, writing a 64-bit value to a 32-bit INTEGER column raises NumericValueOutOfRange / DataError, crashing add_near_dup_index for essentially every document (the high bits of a simhash are almost always set), which then crashes the worker task exactly as in the merge bug.
verifiedBugs.impact: On a Postgres state DB, near-dup indexing fails for nearly all documents, breaking near-dup detection entirely and failing/dead-lettering tasks. Silent on SQLite, so it would only surface in a production Postgres deployment.
verifiedBugs.repro: Configure state_db_url to a Postgres DSN, run any ingestion that reaches add_near_dup_index. The INSERT into dedup_near.near_dup_hash with a value like 8446744073709551616-range fails with psycopg integer out of range.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Declare near_dup_hash as sqlalchemy BigInteger (with_variant for SQLite if needed): near_dup_hash: Mapped[int | None] = mapped_column(BigInteger().with_variant(Integer, 'sqlite'), nullable=True). BigInteger is 64-bit on Postgres and round-trips the signed legacy value correctly.

Verified against /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/storage/state.py and corroborating files.

FACTS CONFIRMED:
1. Column def (state.py:124): `near_dup_hash: Mapped[int | None] = mapped_column(Integer, nullable=True)  # legacy 64-bit signed`. Only `Integer` is imported (state.py:18-27); `BigInteger` is NOT imported and there is no `with_variant`/dialect override.
2. Value written (state.py:645-647, 656): `legacy_hash = simhash_unsigned & 0xffffffffffffffff` then sign-folded into signed 64-bit range, written unconditionally for every band row (16 rows/doc) of every document with non-empty text. Caller dedup/engine.py:82,95,104 passes `simhash128(cap.text)` (a 128-bit value), so the low-64-bit fold is a full signed 64-bit value.
3. Schema is created via `Base.metadata.create_all` (state.py:198); the only migration (state.py:200-209) just ADDs `sig_hex`, never altering `near_dup_hash`'s type. So Postgres DDL is generated directly from the model.
4. Empirically verified with SQLAlchemy 2.0.49: `Integer` compiles to `INTEGER` on the postgresql dialect (32-bit, range ±2.147e9), while `BigInteger` compiles to `BIGINT`. A representative low-64-bit simhash fold (-7.3e18) is far outside int32 range, so the INSERT raises NumericValueOutOfRange/DataError on Postgres.
5. Postgres is an explicitly documented production target: state.py:7 ("point this at Postgres in production without code changes"), state.py:166 (TailRow "Postgres-friendly"), and StateDB accepts arbitrary URLs (settings.py:60; default is SQLite at settings.py:135, where INTEGER is dynamically sized so the bug is silent).

verifiedBugs.title: Fixed near_threshold=24 over 128 bits is highly sensitive to document length, making near-dup merge decisions inconsistent for short docs
verifiedBugs.description: simhash128 is computed over k=3 shingles of the doc; for short documents there are very few shingles, so a single token edit flips a large, variable fraction of bits. Empirically a one-word substitution ('fast'->'slow') yields Hamming distance 21 in a 19-word document (BELOW the 24 threshold -> merged as NEAR_DUP) but 29 in a 16-word document (ABOVE threshold -> kept as NEW). The distance variance for a 'same magnitude' edit is large and length-dependent, so the binary threshold of 24 produces inconsistent grouping for short/medium documents: some genuinely-different short docs get merged into one dup_group, while some genuine near-dups are split. For long documents (40+ words) the calibration is good (verified: unrelated docs sit at Hamming 44+, no false-merges <=36). This is a correctness/quality issue for the short-document regime, not a crash. Note dedup never drops rows (all captures are persisted; only parent_doc_or_dup_group is set), so the user-visible effect is mis-grouped dup-groups in get_dup_group / sibling queries, not lost search rows.
verifiedBugs.impact: Inconsistent / occasionally-wrong near-dup grouping for short documents (titles, snippets, short articles): distinct short docs may be folded into one dup_group while true near-dups of short docs may be missed. Degrades dedup quality and any UI that folds by dup_group.
verifiedBugs.repro: simhash128 / hamming128 of 'the quick brown fox ... runs fast today extra words here for length' vs the same with fast->slow gives 21 (merged) for the 19-word variant and 29 (not merged) for a 16-word variant -- same single-word edit, opposite decision.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Either gate near-dup detection on a minimum shingle/token count (skip simhash near-dup for very short docs, where exact content_hash is the reliable signal), or scale the threshold with document length / number of distinct shingles, or use a relative threshold. At minimum document the short-doc limitation; consider raising the shingle count requirement before trusting simhash128.

The fixed near_threshold=24 over 128-bit simhash128 is strongly document-length-dependent. A single-word substitution — the canonical near-duplicate edit — yields a Hamming distance that scales with doc length:

Realistic-prose sweep (1-word edit, truncated to length L): L=8 -> ham=34 (NEW/split), L=16 -> ham=26 (split), L=20 -> ham=19 (NEAR_DUP/merge), L=30 -> 14, L=57 -> 20 (merge). Crossover at ~16-20 words exactly as claimed.

Systematic random-doc sweep (40 trials/length): fraction of genuine single-word-edit near-dups that merge (ham<=24) is only 0.23-0.47 at lengths 6-16 vs 1.00 at lengths 40-60. The repro reproduces: ~18-word doc 'fast'->'slow' = ham 22 (merged), ~15-word = ham 32 (split). My numbers differ slightly from the claimed 21/29 only because the claim's exact strings weren't provided; direction and magnitude match.

Code confirms the threshold is the deciding gate, not candidate retrieval: LSH banding is 16 bands x 8 bits (state.py:135-136), which is generous enough that the comparison reaches the engine's hamming128(sig,other)<=self._near_threshold check (engine.py:93). _shingles (hashing.py:52-55) collapses sub-k-token docs to a single shingle, making very short docs maximally unstable. No minimum-shingle/length gate exists anywhere. The project's tests/benchmarks only exercise long docs (50x-repeated bodies), and test_dedup.py:80 even hedges its near-dup assertion to (NEAR_DUP, EXACT_DUP, NEW), so short-doc behavior is neither tested nor guaranteed.

It is real and user-affecting: short genuine near-dups (titles, snippets) are systematically NOT folded into the same dup_group, degrading get_dup_group/sibling queries (duckdb_index.py:649). Severity low is correct: dedup never drops rows (engine.py only sets parent_doc_or_dup_group; all captures persist), so there is no data loss, no crash — only missed grouping.

REFUTED half: 'distinct short docs may be folded into one dup_group' / 'genuinely-different short docs get merged' is FALSE. verifiedBugs.title: Schema migration for legacy sig_hex column swallows all exceptions; a failed ALTER leaves later sig_hex writes broken with only a warning
verifiedBugs.description: init() attempts ALTER TABLE dedup_near ADD COLUMN sig_hex on legacy DBs inside a broad `try/except Exception` that only logs logger.warning('migration_failed', ...) and then sets _initialized=True and proceeds. If the ALTER fails for any reason (locked DB, partial migration, permissions, prior partial run), the dedup_near table lacks the sig_hex column but the ORM model (DedupNearRow.sig_hex) still tries to INSERT/SELECT it. Every subsequent add_near_dup_index() and find_near_dup_candidates() then fails with 'no such column: sig_hex' (or the Postgres equivalent), breaking near-dup detection entirely, and that failure is NOT swallowed at the call site -- it crashes the worker task. The migration error is hidden behind a single warning line, making this hard to diagnose.
verifiedBugs.impact: On a legacy DB where the one-shot column migration fails, all near-dup index reads/writes raise 'no such column: sig_hex', breaking dedup and crashing tasks, with only a single easily-missed warning explaining why.
verifiedBugs.repro: Pre-create a dedup_near table without sig_hex, then make the ALTER fail (e.g. hold a write lock or revoke DDL) and call init(); init() logs migration_failed and continues; the next add_near_dup_index raises OperationalError: no such column: sig_hex.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Narrow the except to the expected 'already exists'/no-op cases and re-raise (or refuse to mark _initialized) when the column is genuinely missing after the attempt. After the try block, re-inspect columns and raise a clear RuntimeError if sig_hex is still absent, so the failure is loud rather than deferred to every dedup write.

The ALTER only runs on a LEGACY dedup_near table lacking sig_hex, and it sits inside a broad `try/except Exception` that only does logger.warning("migration_failed", ...) and then unconditionally sets _initialized=True.

I empirically reproduced the failure: created a legacy dedup_near table without sig_hex, forced the ALTER to fail, and observed init() swallow the error, set _initialized=True, leave sig_hex absent, and then both add_near_dup_index() and find_near_dup_candidates() raise sqlite3.OperationalError: "no such column: dedup_near.sig_hex". Because _initialized=True short-circuits any later init(), the column stays missing for the whole process lifetime, so near-dup detection is broken for the entire run (the exact-dup path via upsert_dedup still works; only near-dup is affected). The single warning line makes it hard to diagnose, exactly as described.

The failure mode is realistically reachable, not purely theoretical: workers/main.py, tail/daemon.py, api/server.py and cli/main.py each construct their own StateDB over the same shared sqlite:///awareness.sqlite and call init(); during an upgrade, a concurrent writer holding a write lock can make the one-shot ALTER raise "database is locked," which is then swallowed.

The CLI diagnostic path (cli/main.py:3039 find_near_dup_candidates) would surface the error directly to the user. So the user-visible effect is "every dedup-touching task fails/retries/dead-letters and near-dup detection is silently disabled," not "the worker process crashes."

verifiedBugs.title: CLI `search` defaults to a 30-day fetch_ts window, silently hiding older matches (root cause of "bitcoin returned 2 results")
verifiedBugs.description: The CLI `search` command defines `start: str = typer.Option("30 days ago", ...)` and `end = "now"`. The user explicitly hit this 'in the terminal', and the FastAPI `/search` endpoint (server.py:429-430) defaults start/end to None (no window) — confirming this is a CLI-only default that produces exactly the reported 'bitcoin returns only 2 results' symptom when older bitcoin articles exist.

For any corpus older than a month, search appears 'broken' and returns far fewer results than exist. There is no on-screen indication that a date filter is being applied, so the user cannot tell why results are missing.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Change the default `--start` for the `search` command to an all-time default (e.g. None / no lower bound, or a very old date), or make the search command not apply a `fetch_ts` lower bound unless the user explicitly passes `--start`. At minimum, print the active date window in the results header (e.g. 'Searching captures fetched 2026-05-09 .. now') so the restriction is visible. The `inspect`/`captures` commands legitimately want a recent window; full-text `search` should default to the whole corpus.
verifiedBugs.repro: awareness search bitcoin   # implicitly --start '30 days ago'; misses any bitcoin doc fetched >30 days ago. Compare: awareness search bitcoin --start '2000-01-01'  (returns the full count).

verifiedBugs.title: FTS index only rebuilt when row COUNT changes, so in-place edits / capture_id churn serve stale full-text results
verifiedBugs.description: `_ensure_fts` decides whether to rebuild the materialized `captures_idx` table + FTS index using `if count == self._fts_built_for_count: ... return True` (line 330). Concretely: when `_views_signature` differs from `_fts_built_signature`, always rebuild `captures_idx`+index (drop the `count == self._fts_built_for_count` early-return), or incorporate a cheap content fingerprint (e.g. SUM(length(text)) + MAX(fetch_ts) + COUNT) into the rebuild trigger.

(2) The bug is masked on the primary HTTP /search surface because server.py builds a fresh DuckDbIndex per request (resetting _fts_built_for_count=-1, forcing a rebuild each request); it manifests on long-lived in-process reuse of one index while the corpus mutates (CLI interactive search loop, live-TAIL embeddings). Suggested fix is correct: key the FTS rebuild on _source_signature() (drop the count==_fts_built_for_count early return) or fold a cheap content fingerprint (SUM(length(text)) + MAX(fetch_ts) + COUNT) into the trigger. Severity downgraded high->medium because the main stateless API path self-heals per request, narrowing the real blast radius to long-lived reuse, though it is a genuine silent search-correctness defect (including a confidently-ranked phantom hit in the default 'auto' mode).

verifiedBugs.title: Compressed JSONL chunks (.jsonl.gz) are never read by the index: rglob('*.jsonl') misses them, so search returns nothing
verifiedBugs.description: When `jsonl_compress=True` (settings.jsonl_compress / `--compress`), `JsonlStagingWriter` writes chunks named `captures-...jsonl.gz` (jsonl.py:83-84, verified by running the writer). But `_refresh_views` discovers chunks with `captures_root.rglob('*.jsonl')` (line 151) and `_source_signature` uses the same `rglob('*.jsonl')` (line 122). `Path.rglob('*.jsonl')` does NOT match `*.jsonl.gz` (verified). So the entire compressed corpus is invisible: `staging_captures_raw` is built from an empty file list (the WHERE 1=0 all-NULL branch), and the signature never changes when new .gz chunks land. I verified DuckDB's `read_json_auto([...], union_by_name=true)` transparently reads .jsonl.gz, so the only thing missing is the glob match.
verifiedBugs.impact: If JSONL compression is enabled and Iceberg is off (or also affected), search/inspect/counts over the staging corpus return 0 results for everything, with no error — the data is on disk but never indexed. Total silent search failure for compressed deployments.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Match both extensions in both places, e.g. discover via `list(captures_root.rglob('*.jsonl')) + list(captures_root.rglob('*.jsonl.gz'))` for the file list at line 151 and for the signature loop at line 122 (or glob `*.jsonl*`). The dead `_staging_glob()` helper (line 107-109, never called) should also be updated or removed.
verifiedBugs.repro: Set jsonl_compress=True, ingest some docs (writes captures-*.jsonl.gz), then `awareness search <anything>` -> 0 results even though the .gz chunk contains matches.

verdict.reasoning: Verified end to end. (1) When jsonl_compress=True, JsonlStagingWriter writes final chunks named captures-<ts>-<hex>.jsonl.gz (jsonl.py:83-84,87; rename strips only the .tmp suffix, leaving .jsonl.gz — confirmed by replicating _commit_current logic). The setting is real (config/settings.py:109, default False), exposed via --compress, and wired to the writer at workers/engine.py:79 (compress=settings.jsonl_compress). (2) Empirically proved Path.rglob('*.jsonl') and Path.match('*.jsonl') do NOT match *.jsonl.gz, while *.jsonl* / *.jsonl.gz do. Both the corpus-discovery site (_refresh_views, line 151) and the signature site (_source_signature, line 122) use rglob('*.jsonl'), so compressed chunks are entirely invisible. (3) Grep confirms duckdb_index.py is the ONLY code path that discovers/reads JSONL staging chunks; there is no compensating reader for compressed files and the writer does not also emit a plain .jsonl. (4) Downstream consequences are exactly as claimed: with no matching files, _refresh_views falls into the else branch (lines 164-189) building staging_captures_raw as an empty WHERE 1=0 all-NULL view; and _source_signature returns an empty jsonl tuple, so _refresh_views_if_stale never detects new .gz chunks. search() (sole search entrypoint, via DuckDbIndex used by cli/main.py and api/server.py) then returns 0 results with no error. DuckDB's read_json_auto does transparently decompress .jsonl.gz by extension (couldn't run live — duckdb not installed in sandbox — but this is standard documented behavior), so the data is readable; the only defect is the glob never selecting it. The fix (glob *.jsonl* or union both patterns at lines 122 and 151) is correct, and _staging_glob() at 107-109 is indeed dead code (never called).
verdict.correction: Real and correctly root-caused (rglob('*.jsonl') excludes .jsonl.gz at duckdb_index.py:122 and :151). Two refinements to the claim: (a) Iceberg is NOT affected by this bug — the Iceberg view uses a separate metadata glob (lines 132/136, *.json on the metadata dir) and unions independently, so when Iceberg is enabled and populated those rows remain searchable. The claim's "Iceberg ... or also affected" is imprecise: only the JSONL *staging* corpus goes invisible. Therefore total silent search failure occurs specifically when jsonl_compress=True AND Iceberg is off (or Iceberg is enabled but lagging compaction, in which case only the recent not-yet-compacted compressed writes are missing from search/counts/inspect). (b) Because default jsonl_compress=False, this affects only opt-in compressed deployments — hence high rather than critical, but for those deployments it is a genuine silent data-visibility failure.

verifiedBugs.title: Multi-word queries return different result sets depending on FTS availability: FTS is OR, prefix fallback is AND
verifiedBugs.description: For a multi-token query like 'bitcoin price', the FTS path uses DuckDB `match_bm25(capture_id, $q)` whose default is OR/disjunctive matching (any term) — I reproduced FTS returning all 3 docs that match EITHER term. The prefix fallback ANDs every stem-root (`where.insert(...)` per root at 507-510), so it returns only docs matching ALL terms — reproduced returning 2 docs. In `auto` mode the user therefore gets a broad OR result when FTS is available and a narrow AND result when FTS is empty/unavailable, for the identical query. Result counts and membership change based on internal index state, not the query.
verifiedBugs.impact: Inconsistent, surprising search results for multi-word queries; the same query yields different totals/rows depending on whether FTS happens to be built/available. Contributes directly to 'search is janky in many places'.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Pick one semantics and apply it on both paths. If conjunctive (AND) is desired, pass `conjunctive := 1` to `match_bm25` (e.g. `fts_main_captures_idx.match_bm25(capture_id, $q, conjunctive := 1)`). If disjunctive is desired, OR the prefix roots instead of ANDing them. Document the chosen semantics.
verifiedBugs.repro: Index 3 docs: one with only 'bitcoin', one with only 'price', one with both. search('bitcoin price', mode='fts') -> 3 results; search('bitcoin price', mode='prefix') -> 2 results.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed and empirically reproduced against the project's pinned DuckDB 1.5.3.

CODE: In /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py the FTS path (lines 458-488) calls `fts_main_captures_idx.match_bm25(capture_id, $q)` with NO `conjunctive` argument. The prefix-fallback path (lines 503-511) builds one ILIKE clause per stem-root and joins them with " AND " (line 516, via repeated `where.insert(...)`), so it requires ALL terms.

REPRODUCTION (DuckDB 1.5.3, same PRAGMA create_fts_index call the code uses): with 3 docs — one containing only "bitcoin", one with "bitcoin"+"price", one with "cheap bitcoin price" — query "bitcoin price":
- default match_bm25 -> 3 rows (OR/disjunctive: any term matches)
- match_bm25(..., conjunctive := 1) -> 1 row
- prefix-style (title/text ILIKE %bitcoin% AND ILIKE %price%) -> 2 rows
This exactly matches the claim's stated FTS=3 vs prefix=2.

REACHABILITY (the part that makes it user-affecting): The default search mode is "auto" for BOTH entry points — CLI (cli/main.py:2623) and HTTP API (api/server.py:453), backed by settings.search_default_mode = "auto" (config/settings.py:116). In control flow (search(), lines 458/495): for default fields, "auto" enters the FTS branch; if `_ensure_fts` returns True and finds hits, it returns OR results and the prefix branch is skipped (`if not rows and ... total==0`). If the FTS extension is unavailable, the prefix AND branch runs instead. FTS is explicitly optional — `INSTALL fts`/`LOAD fts` is wrapped in try/except (lines 95-101) and sets `_fts_available=False` on failure (offline/sandboxed/extension-repo unreachable), and `_ensure_fts` flips it to False if index build fails (lines 355-357). So the SAME multi-word query returns a broad OR set when FTS is available and a narrow AND set when it is not — result totals and membership change based on internal index/extension state, not the query. This is genuine, not a style nit, and nothing downstream normalizes the two paths (the returned `mode` field merely reports which path ran).

Severity medium is correct: it is a real default-path consistency/correctness defect, but it surfaces only in the degraded state where FTS is unavailable or returns zero hits (a functional-but-degraded fallback), not on every query, and no data is lost or corrupted.
verdict.correction: Real, root cause as described, with two precision corrections: (1) The exact prefix count depends on the corpus, not a fixed "2" — the claim's specific 3-doc example yields prefix=1, but a different 3-doc set yields prefix=2; the OR-vs-AND asymmetry holds regardless. The repro example wording should make the corpus explicit (docs that contain BOTH terms determine the AND count). (2) The fallback trigger is not literally "FTS empty/unavailable" alone. In auto mode the prefix path runs when EITHER the FTS extension is unavailable/build-fails OR when FTS finds zero hits (total==0). The OR-vs-AND inconsistency is observable across the extension-availability boundary; the "FTS returns 0 hits -> prefix with stem-root broadening" branch is a deliberate recall feature, but it inherits the same conjunctiveness mismatch. Suggested fix is appropriate: pass `conjunctive := 1` to match_bm25 to make FTS conjunctive (verified it reduces the repro to 1 row, matching prefix-AND), or OR the prefix roots; then document the chosen semantics.

verifiedBugs.title: `auto` mode silently drops BM25 ranking when --fields is title,text in a different order (e.g. text,title)
verifiedBugs.description: `fts_eligible = list(cols) == list(DEFAULT_SEARCH_FIELDS)` compares the cleaned field list to the default by exact ordered equality. `_clean_fields` preserves the caller's order, so passing `--fields text,title` (the same two fields, swapped) yields `cols == ['text','title']`, which is `!= ['title','text']`, so `fts_eligible` is False and `auto` mode skips the ranked FTS path entirely and routes to the unranked prefix path (AND semantics, no scores). Verified: ['title','text']->eligible True; ['text','title']->eligible False; ['title']->False; ['text']->False.
verifiedBugs.impact: A user who specifies the exact default search fields in a non-canonical order (or just 'title' or 'text' alone) unexpectedly loses BM25 ranking and gets the narrower AND-based prefix matching — different, worse results with no scores and no indication why. Janky and non-obvious.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Compare as sets and only require that the requested fields are a subset of the FTS-indexed fields (title+text), e.g. `fts_eligible = set(cols).issubset({'title','text'}) and bool(cols)`. Order should not matter, and a subset like just 'title' can still legitimately use FTS (it indexes title+text together, accepting that text matches may also surface).
verifiedBugs.repro: awareness search bitcoin --fields text,title  -> used_mode becomes 'prefix' (unranked, AND) instead of ranked 'fts'; awareness search bitcoin --fields title,text -> ranked 'fts'.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED at the code level, but the claim is partially misdiagnosed and overstated.

The order-sensitivity is real. At duckdb_index.py:455, `fts_eligible = list(cols) == list(DEFAULT_SEARCH_FIELDS)` is an exact ORDERED list comparison. `_clean_fields` (lines 46-60) whitelists+dedups but preserves caller order. I reproduced the logic standalone (duckdb isn't installed): ['title','text']->True, ['text','title']->False. With mode=auto and fts_eligible=False, the FTS block (line 458) is skipped entirely and execution falls through to the prefix path (lines 493-535), which I confirmed joins each token root with AND (where.insert per root), returns score=NULL::DOUBLE, and orders by fetch_ts DESC (recency, not relevance). So `--fields text,title` genuinely yields used_mode='prefix', ranked=False, different/worse results than `--fields title,text`. Data flow is confirmed end-to-end with NO canonicalization: CLI main.py:2625 (`[f.strip().lower() for f in raw_fields.split(',')]`) and API server.py:440-444 both preserve user field order straight into search(). For the SAME set {title,text}, order is semantically irrelevant (FTS indexes both as one blob), so treating the swap differently is an unjustified defect with no test coverage.

HOWEVER, the claim is wrong about two-thirds of its scope and its suggested fix. The claim asserts `--fields title` and `--fields text` alone also 'unexpectedly lose BM25 ranking' and proposes subset-based eligibility (`set(cols).issubset({'title','text'})`). That is intended, documented, and explicitly tested behavior — NOT a bug. The code comment at lines 451-454 states FTS indexes title+text as one blob and cannot honor a narrowed fields request, and tests/unit/test_search_matching.py:98-105 (test_auto_mode_honors_narrowed_fields) asserts that mode='auto', fields=['title'] MUST route to mode=='prefix' so it doesn't silently match body text via the field-agnostic FTS path. The claim's proposed `issubset` fix would make ['title'] FTS-eligible, reintroduce body matches for a title-restricted query, and BREAK that test. So the suggested fix is incorrect.

Severity is low, not medium: triggering requires a user to explicitly pass the two default fields in a non-canonical order (text,title) — an uncommon, contrived invocation; the default and any natural title,text ordering already work correctly. Impact is degraded ranking/recall, not data loss, crash, or incorrect security behavior, and an explicit `--mode fts` escape hatch exists to force ranked search.
verdict.correction: Real but narrower than claimed, and the suggested fix is wrong. (1) The genuine bug is ONLY the order-sensitivity for the same default field SET (e.g. text,title vs title,text), caused by ordered list equality at duckdb_index.py:455. (2) The claim's inclusion of single-field cases (--fields title / --fields text) as bugs is a MISDIAGNOSIS — that non-eligibility is intentional, documented (lines 451-454), and guarded by tests/unit/test_search_matching.py:98-105. (3) The claim's suggested fix (`set(cols).issubset({'title','text'}) and bool(cols)`) is incorrect: it would make a title-only or text-only request ride the field-agnostic FTS path and match the other field, breaking test_auto_mode_honors_narrowed_fields. The correct minimal fix is order-insensitive equality on the SAME set, not subset: `fts_eligible = set(cols) == set(DEFAULT_SEARCH_FIELDS)`. I verified this fixes the swap (text,title->eligible) while keeping single-field requests ineligible (title/text alone stay False), preserving the existing test. Suggested severity: low.

verifiedBugs.title: Stem-root substring fallback misses valid matches because some stems are not substrings of their surface forms (e.g. mining→mine)
verifiedBugs.description: The prefix/`auto`-fallback path reduces each token to its Snowball stem and then does `ILIKE %stem%` (lines 505-510). This only works when the stem is a literal substring of the inflected surface form. For many words the Snowball stem is NOT a substring of common inflections: 'mining' stems to 'mine' (verified), and `%mine%` does not occur in 'mining', so a query 'mining' in the fallback path matches documents containing 'mine'/'mined' but MISSES documents that say 'mining'. Similarly 'financial' stems to 'financi' while 'finance' stems to 'financ' — the docstring's promised cross-match is only partial. So when FTS is unavailable or returns zero (the exact situation the fallback exists for), the fallback can return zero or wrong results for perfectly common terms.
verifiedBugs.impact: The 'auto' fallback — meant to broaden recall when FTS finds nothing — can instead MISS documents that plainly contain the query word, producing empty or wrong results for ordinary inflected queries. Reinforces 'search broken in many places' when FTS is degraded.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Do not substring-match on the Snowball stem. Either (a) match the raw token prefix/substring (`%token%`) rather than `%stem%`, or (b) match on a true prefix common to the inflections (strip only trailing characters), or (c) fix the FTS rebuild reliability (see other bugs) so the fallback is rarely needed. At minimum, also OR-in the raw token alongside the stem root.
verifiedBugs.repro: Disable/empty FTS so the prefix path runs; search('mining') builds ILIKE '%mine%' and returns 0 rows for a doc whose text is 'bitcoin mining operations'.

verdict.reasoning:
The underlying defect is real and I reproduced it end-to-end against the actual DuckDbIndex, but the claim's repro, trigger, and supporting examples are materially wrong.

REAL part (confirmed): _stem_roots (duckdb_index.py:372) computes the Snowball stem and the prefix path then does ILIKE '%stem%' (lines 509-510). For words where Snowball maps -ing/-ed to an -e root (mining->mine, hoping->hope, making->make), the stem is NOT a substring of the surface form. I verified stem('mining','english')='mine' and 'mine' not in 'mining'. Running the real code: idx.search('mining', fields=['text']) against a doc whose text is 'bitcoin mining operations' returns total=0 (mode=prefix) — a genuine miss of a document that plainly contains the query word.

WRONG part 1 (the claim's repro is false): The claim says 'Disable/empty FTS so the prefix path runs; search(mining) builds ILIKE %mine% and returns 0 rows.' That is incorrect. _stem_roots gates the stem() call on self._fts_available (line 370). When FTS is unavailable, it returns the RAW token ['mining'], builds ILIKE '%mining%', and returns total=1 (I observed this directly). So the exact situation the claim names — FTS down — does NOT exhibit the bug.

WRONG part 2 (real trigger is the opposite): The bug only fires when the FTS extension IS available (normal production state) AND the request leaves the default path — either fields are narrowed away from the default title,text (auto then routes to the prefix path via fts_eligible at line 455 / the total==0 branch at line 495) or mode='prefix' is explicitly requested. Both are user-reachable via the CLI --fields/--mode flags (cli/main.py:2641-2642) and the API fields/mode params (api/server.py:444-454). The default search (fields=title,text, mode=auto) is UNAFFECTED: BM25 stems both query and document, so search('mining') hits the FTS path and returns total=1 (confirmed). The fallback never even runs on the default path.

WRONG part 3 (bad examples): The claim's 'financial' and 'study' examples do not demonstrate a miss. stem('financial')='financi' and stem('studies')='studi', and both ARE substrings of their surface forms, so they match (I confirmed total=1 for both). The claim conflated cross-inflection recall with self-match. Only the non-substring-stem class (mine/mining etc.) actually misses.

Net: real correctness gap on a non-default path, narrow word subset, default behavior correct — hence low severity rather than the claimed medium, and the description/repro need correcting.
verdict.correction: Real, but root cause and trigger are mischaracterized. (1) The bug does NOT occur when FTS is disabled — _stem_roots is gated on self._fts_available (line 370) and uses the RAW token there, so ILIKE '%mining%' correctly matches (observed total=1). (2) The actual trigger is FTS AVAILABLE (normal production) plus a non-default request: narrowed fields (anything != title,text, which makes auto route to the prefix path at line 455/495) or explicit mode='prefix'. Reproduced: search('mining', fields=['text']) -> total=0 against text 'bitcoin mining operations'. (3) Default search (title,text + auto) is unaffected because BM25 stems both sides (search('mining') -> FTS path, total=1). (4) The 'financial'/'study' examples are wrong: financi/studi ARE substrings of financial/studies and match fine; only stems like mine (from mining) that are not substrings of the surface form miss. Fix: in the prefix path OR-in the raw token alongside the stem root (params: '%root%' OR '%token%'), or strip only trailing chars to a true common prefix; do not rely on the stem being a substring.

verifiedBugs.title: A single JSONL chunk missing a column breaks the entire `captures` view, making ALL search/inspect/counts queries fail
verifiedBugs.description: `_refresh_views` reads JSONL via `read_json_auto([...], union_by_name=true)` (line 161), producing `staging_captures_raw` whose columns are the UNION of keys actually present across the chunk files. The `captures` view then SELECTs an explicit fixed column list including `parent_doc_or_dup_group`, `source_locator`, `near_dup_hash`, etc. (lines 268-282). If those keys are absent from the JSONL (any chunk written by an older/alternate code path, a truncated last line, or hand-edited data), DuckDB raises a Binder Error ('Referenced column "parent_doc_or_dup_group" not found'), which is caught at line 287 and only logged as `duckdb_view_setup_failed`. The `captures` view is then never (re)created, and EVERY subsequent query — search(), /captures, /counts, /inspect — throws 'Catalog Error: Table with name captures does not exist'. I reproduced both the Binder Error and the cascading 'captures does not exist' failure by writing rows lacking some of the 29 fields. The engine currently always writes all 29 fields via as_iceberg_row(), but the view is fragile: one malformed file takes down all search.
verifiedBugs.impact: A single malformed/partial/legacy JSONL chunk silently disables the entire search subsystem (and inspect/counts) for the whole corpus — not just that file. Hard to diagnose because the only signal is a single warning log line; the user sees every query error out or (via callers that swallow) return nothing.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Make the `captures` view resilient to missing source columns: instead of selecting fixed column names from `staging_captures_raw`, coalesce missing columns to typed NULLs (e.g. build the SELECT defensively using `COLUMNS(...)`/`TRY` or reference columns via a normalized projection that supplies NULL for any absent field). Alternatively validate/skip unparseable chunks in `_refresh_views` and continue. Also surface the failure loudly (raise or at least WARN with the offending file) rather than leaving `captures` undefined.
verifiedBugs.repro: Place a JSONL chunk whose rows omit 'parent_doc_or_dup_group' (and other fields) under data/jsonl/captures/YYYY/MM/DD/; connect DuckDbIndex; any `SELECT ... FROM captures` raises 'Table with name captures does not exist' (preceded by a logged duckdb_view_setup_failed Binder Error).

verdict.reasoning: The core mechanism is real and I reproduced it with the project's own DuckDB 1.5.3. A JSONL chunk that structurally omits keys makes `staging_captures_raw` (built via `read_json_auto([...], union_by_name=true)`, line 161) contain only the present columns. The `captures` view then SELECTs a fixed 29-column list (lines 269-282); the missing column yields `BinderException: Referenced column "parent_doc_or_dup_group" not found`, which is caught at line 287 and only logged as `duckdb_view_setup_failed`. Because `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW captures` never succeeds, every subsequent `SELECT ... FROM captures` raises `CatalogException: Table with name captures does not exist`. I confirmed this cascade end to end. Callers reference `captures` pervasively (search() lines 518/530, /counts main.py 1694-1717, /inspect 2510, /captures 1658, dedup 3064), so a single bad chunk takes down the whole search/counts/inspect subsystem for the entire corpus, and the only diagnostic signal is one warning line with no offending filename. The maintainers are explicitly aware of this fragility: tests/unit/test_search_matching.py:19-29 documents "a partial JSONL row makes view setup fail" and the test helper deliberately builds `{k: None for k in _FULL_KEYS}` to avoid it. So the fragility and its blast radius are genuine.\n\nHowever, two of the claim's stated triggers are wrong, and the active impact is overstated. (1) An all-null column does NOT trigger it: I verified that a key present-but-null in every row still produces the column (29 cols intact); the trigger requires the key to be structurally absent from the JSON object, not merely null. (2) A truncated last line does NOT produce the claimed Binder cascade: it raises `InvalidInputException: Malformed JSON` at the `staging_captures_raw` CREATE (lines 157-163), which is OUTSIDE the try/except at 219-288, so it fails as a different, uncaught error path (it would propagate out of _refresh_views/connect). The claim conflates these distinct failure modes. (3) No current production code path writes partial rows: `as_iceberg_row()` (doc.py 137-169) always emits all 29 keys, `_row_to_jsonl` serializes them all (nulls included), and the atomic `.tmp`->`.jsonl` rename plus the `*.jsonl`-only glob prevent reading in-progress/partial files. Thus it only fires on hand-edited, legacy, or alternate-tool data — a latent robustness gap, not an actively-firing bug for normal users. The CLI /counts path also wraps queries in try/except and prints "Query failed: <error>", so the user sees a (cryptic) error rather than silent nothing as the claim implies. Given the genuine but large-only-if-triggered blast radius, the requirement of externally-malformed data, and that maintainers already guard it in tests, medium is the right severity rather than high.
verdict.correction: Real but latent, and the severity/triggers in the claim are partly wrong. Root cause is correct: the `captures` view's fixed explicit column list over a union_by_name JSONL staging view is non-defensive, and the swallowed BinderException at line 287 leaves `captures` undefined, cascading to CatalogException across all callers. Corrections: (a) the trigger is a STRUCTURALLY MISSING key, not an all-null column (a present-but-null key still yields the column, verified). (b) A truncated last line does NOT cause this cascade — it raises InvalidInputException at the staging_captures_raw CREATE (lines 157-163), outside the try/except, a different and uncaught failure path. (c) No current code path produces partial rows (as_iceberg_row always writes all 29 fields; atomic .tmp->.jsonl rename + *.jsonl-only glob prevent partial reads), so this requires legacy/hand-edited/alternate-tool data and is not actively user-affecting today; maintainers already document and work around it (test_search_matching.py:19-29). Suggested fix is sound: build the captures view defensively (coalesce absent source columns to typed NULLs, e.g. via COLUMNS()/a normalized projection), and/or validate/skip unparseable chunks in _refresh_views, and log the offending file loudly instead of leaving `captures` undefined.

verifiedBugs.title: Google Drive upload uses read_text() (fails on .jsonl.gz) and sends JSONL as Content-Type application/json
verifiedBugs.description: `upload_file` reads the chunk with `file_path.read_text(encoding='utf-8')` (line 148). When `jsonl_compress=True` the chunk is binary gzip (.jsonl.gz) and `read_text` raises UnicodeDecodeError, which is caught at 149-151 and returns None → the upload silently fails (the engine then retains the chunk but never uploads it). Separately, the multipart body embeds the file content under `Content-Type: application/json` (line 171) even though JSONL (newline-delimited) is not a single JSON document, and the raw content is interpolated into the multipart string without guarding against the boundary token appearing in the data (lines 166-174). For a GDrive-only deployment with compression on, every upload fails.
verifiedBugs.impact: With compression enabled, Google Drive uploads always fail (silent data non-delivery; chunk retained but accumulating). Even uncompressed, mislabeling JSONL as application/json and unescaped multipart assembly can corrupt or reject uploads.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Read the file as bytes (`file_path.read_bytes()`) and build the multipart body as bytes; set Content-Type to `application/octet-stream` (or `application/x-ndjson` / `application/gzip` for .gz). Use a robust multipart encoder (or httpx files=) and a boundary that cannot collide with content, instead of f-string interpolation.
verifiedBugs.repro: Enable gdrive + jsonl_compress; flush a batch; gdrive.upload_file(<chunk>.jsonl.gz) -> read_text raises, function returns None, 'gdrive_upload_read_failed' logged, chunk never uploaded.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED real for the primary defect. Verified the full chain: (1) jsonl_compress=True makes JsonlStagingWriter emit .jsonl.gz gzip-binary files via gzip.open (src/awareness/storage/jsonl.py:83-87). (2) The engine passes that chunk directly to gdrive.upload_file(chunk) (src/awareness/workers/engine.py:487). (3) upload_file reads it with file_path.read_text(encoding='utf-8') at src/awareness/storage/gdrive.py:148. I empirically reproduced that read_text on a real gzip .jsonl.gz file raises UnicodeDecodeError ("'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x8b in position 1" — the gzip magic byte). (4) That exception is caught at gdrive.py:149-151, logs gdrive_upload_read_failed, and returns None. (5) Back in engine.py, file_id is None -> gdrive_ok=False -> for a gdrive-only deployment the chunk is retained (engine.py:508-514), but there is NO recovery/re-upload path anywhere (list_pending_manifests at cli/main.py:2785 feeds only Iceberg compaction, not Drive). So with compression on, every Drive upload fails permanently and the data never reaches Drive while local chunks accumulate. The fix is demonstrably known elsewhere in the codebase: the Iceberg compaction reader at cli/main.py:2823-2824 correctly does `open_func = gzip.open if str(p).endswith('.gz') else open` — gdrive.upload_file simply fails to do the same. The existing test (tests/unit/test_gdrive.py:116-117) only covers the uncompressed .jsonl case, so the compressed path is untested. This is a genuine correctness/data-delivery bug, not a style nit and not handled elsewhere. The secondary claims are weaker: mislabeling JSONL as Content-Type application/json (gdrive.py:171) is cosmetically wrong but Google Drive's multipart media part is accepted regardless of declared subtype, so it does not by itself break or corrupt uploads; the fixed-string boundary (gdrive.py:154) is a real but extremely-low-probability collision risk for capture data. Those do not independently break behavior. Severity medium is correct: it is a deterministic 100% failure but only for users who opt into the (non-default, jsonl_compress defaults to False) compression option combined with Drive, and the chunk is retained on disk so it is recoverable rather than silently lost.
