The breaking defect is exactly ONE thing: gdrive.upload_file uses read_text(encoding='utf-8') (gdrive.py:148), which raises UnicodeDecodeError on .jsonl.gz chunks produced when jsonl_compress=True, causing a deterministic, total, unrecoverable-by-automation upload failure for gdrive+compression deployments. The claim's framing of this is accurate. The two secondary issues the report bundles in (Content-Type application/json mislabel, and unescaped multipart f-string/boundary assembly) are NOT independently breaking — Drive accepts the media part regardless of declared subtype, and the boundary collision is a theoretical low-probability hardening gap. They should be treated as code-quality follow-ups, not as causes of upload failure. Also worth noting: this only affects users who explicitly enable jsonl_compress (default False), so it is not 'every GDrive deployment' as a reader might infer — it is every GDrive deployment WITH compression enabled. Suggested fix is correct: read the file as bytes (read_bytes) and build the multipart body as bytes (mirroring the gzip-aware reader already at cli/main.py:2823-2824), and set Content-Type to application/octet-stream (or application/gzip for .gz / application/x-ndjson otherwise).

verifiedBugs.title: CLI search hard-defaults to a 30-day window, silently hiding most captures (API is unbounded)
verifiedBugs.description: The `search` command declares `start: str = typer.Option("30 days ago", ...)` and `end: str = typer.Option("now", ...)`. These are converted to `start_dt`/`end_dt` and passed to `idx.search(start=..., end=...)`, where they become `fetch_ts >= $start AND fetch_ts <= $end` filters (duckdb_index.py:439-444). So by default the terminal `search` only ever looks at documents captured in the last 30 days. The HTTP `/search` endpoint in api/server.py:429-430 defaults `start`/`end` to `None` (no date filter at all), so the SAME query returns very different counts in the terminal vs the API/dashboard. Any corpus captured (or backfilled) more than 30 days ago, or whose `fetch_ts` parses to a value outside the window, is invisible from the terminal unless the user knows to pass `--start`.
verifiedBugs.impact: Searching e.g. `bitcoin` in the terminal can return only a handful of rows (the user reported 2) while the real corpus contains many more — the documents exist and are returned by the API/dashboard, but the CLI silently scopes them out. Looks like 'search is broken' even though it is a hidden default-range filter.
verifiedBugs.repro: Backfill/ingest documents, wait (or set fetch_ts) so most are older than 30 days, then run `awareness search bitcoin`. Compare to `curl 'localhost:8085/search?q=bitcoin'` (unbounded) or `awareness search bitcoin --start '3650 days ago'` — the latter two return many more rows.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Make the CLI default range unbounded to match the API (default `--start` to empty/None and only apply a lower bound when the user supplies one), or at minimum print a visible banner like 'Showing captures from <start> to <end> — pass --start to widen' so the scoping is never silent. Also surface the active range in the results header.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified against the actual code; every load-bearing claim holds.

1. CLI default window is real and bounded. `search` declares `start: str = typer.Option("30 days ago", ...)` and `end: str = typer.Option("now", ...)` (src/awareness/cli/main.py:2595-2596). These are converted unconditionally at lines 2629-2630 via `start_dt = to_utc(start)` / `end_dt = coerce_relative_end(end)`. `to_utc("30 days ago")` genuinely returns `utcnow() - timedelta(days=30)` (src/awareness/util/timeutil.py:23-27); `coerce_relative_end("now")` returns `utcnow()` (timeutil.py:73-74). Both CLI paths — non-interactive (main.py:2639-2640) and interactive (main.py:2679-2680) — pass these into `idx.search(start=..., end=...)`. There is no branch that nulls them; the only way to widen is an explicit `--start`.

2. The filter is applied. In `DuckDbIndex.search`, `base_filters()` adds `fetch_ts >= $start` when start is not None and `fetch_ts <= $end` when end is not None (src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py:439-444), used by the FTS, prefix, and substring paths.

3. API/dashboard divergence is real. The HTTP `/search` route defaults `start: datetime | None = Query(None)` and `end: datetime | None = Query(None)` (src/awareness/api/server.py:429-430) and passes `start=to_utc(start) if start else None`, `end=... if end else None` (server.py:451-452), i.e. no date filter when unset. The web dashboard only sends start/end when the date inputs are non-empty (src/awareness/api/web/app.js:283-298, 304), so its default search is also unbounded. Both call the same `idx.search` backend, so an identical query returns different counts in CLI vs API/dashboard.

4. The repro is plausible, not just theoretical. `fetch_ts` is set from the source's own (historical) date for backfill sources: `fetch_ts = to_utc(row_date) or utcnow()` (src/awareness/sources/fineweb.py:145) and `fetch_ts = to_utc(fetched_at) or utcnow()` (src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py:327). So Common Crawl / FineWeb backfilled corpus carries old fetch_ts values that fall outside the 30-day window and become invisible to terminal search while remaining visible via the API/dashboard — exactly matching the reported "search returns only 2 rows" symptom.

5. The scoping is silent. Neither the non-interactive header (main.py:2651-2655) nor the interactive table title (main.py:2700) prints the active date range; they show query/total/mode/fields/ranked only. So a user gets no signal that a 30-day filter is in effect.

This is a genuine, user-affecting default-behavior/correctness divergence, not a style nit and not handled elsewhere. It is recoverable via --start (so not data-corrupting/critical), but the primary search UX silently hides most of a backfilled corpus by default.
verdict.correction: Claim is accurate. Minor note on line citations: api/server.py:429-430 are the `/search` route's `start`/`end` Query(None) parameter declarations (correct), and the actual `None`-passthrough conversion is at server.py:451-452. Note also there are other endpoints with required start (e.g. `/inspect` at server.py:282 uses `Query(...)`) and `/captures` (server.py:338-339) also defaults to None — but the relevant comparison endpoint, the BM25 `/search` at server.py:422-456, does default both to None as the claim states. Root cause is exactly as described: CLI Typer defaults bound the window to 30 days while the API/dashboard default to an unbounded (None) window, both feeding the same idx.search.

verifiedBugs.title: Non-'N days ago' relative start dates silently parse to None and drop the date filter (wrong, unsignaled results)
verifiedBugs.description: `start_dt = to_utc(start)` is the only validation of `--start`. `to_utc` only understands `now`/`today` and the exact suffix `'days ago'` (it does `int(s.split()[0])`). Anything else — `'1 week ago'`, `'last month'`, `'yesterday'`, a typo'd date — falls through to `dateutil.parser.parse`, and on failure returns `None` (timeutil.py:32-33). In `search`, `start_dt=None` means the `fetch_ts >= $start` filter is omitted entirely (duckdb_index.py:439). So a user who types `--start '1 week ago'` expecting a 7-day window instead gets an ALL-TIME search with no error and no indication the bound was ignored.
verifiedBugs.impact: Date filtering is silently wrong: a narrowing intent (`--start '1 week ago'`) becomes a widening (all time), and an invalid date is swallowed rather than rejected. Users cannot trust `--start`, reinforcing the 'janky / broken' perception.
verifiedBugs.repro: `python3 -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'src'); from awareness.util.timeutil import to_utc; print(to_utc('1 week ago'))"` prints `None`. Then `awareness search bitcoin --start '1 week ago'` searches all time instead of 7 days.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: In `search`, detect when `to_utc(start)` returns None for a non-empty `--start` and raise `typer.BadParameter(f"could not parse --start {start!r}")`. Better, extend `to_utc`/`coerce_relative` to handle common relative forms (weeks/months/'yesterday') consistently, and never silently drop a user-supplied bound.

verdict.reasoning: Verified end-to-end. (1) Root cause confirmed at src/awareness/util/timeutil.py:15-38: to_utc only handles 'now'/'today' and the exact 'N days ago' suffix; '1 week ago', 'yesterday', 'last month', and typos fall through to dateutil.parser.parse, whose failure is swallowed by `except (ValueError, TypeError): return None` (line 32-33). Ran it directly: to_utc('1 week ago'), to_utc('yesterday'), to_utc('last month'), to_utc('asdf qwerty') all return None. (2) Silent filter drop confirmed: the cited path 'index/duckdb_index.py:439' is slightly off — the real file is src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py, but the logic is exactly as described. In base_filters() lines 439-441, `if start is not None: w.append('fetch_ts >= $start')` means a None start omits the lower-bound clause entirely, so the query becomes unbounded (all-time) rather than the user's intended window. (3) Call site confirmed at src/awareness/cli/main.py:2629: `start_dt = to_utc(start)` with zero validation, passed straight into idx.search(start=start_dt). So `awareness search bitcoin --start '1 week ago'` silently searches all time with no error and no signal. Two facts strengthen the claim: (a) the very next line (2630) uses coerce_relative_end(end) for --end, which RAISES ParserError on the same inputs — confirmed by execution — so --end '1 week ago' crashes loudly while --start '1 week ago' silently widens; a clear, surprising asymmetry. (b) The suggested fix already exists in the same module: cli/main.py:1104-1106 does `start_dt = to_utc(start); if start_dt is None: raise typer.BadParameter('Invalid start date format')`. The search command simply omits this guard, proving it's an oversight/deviation, not intended. This is a genuine, user-affecting correctness bug (narrowing intent silently becomes widening; invalid dates swallowed), not a style nit and not handled elsewhere on this code path.
verdict.correction: Real bug. Minor correction to the report: the duckdb filter file is src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py (not src/awareness/index/duckdb_index.py), though the cited line numbers (439-441) and logic are correct. Severity adjusted from 'high' to 'medium': the bug only manifests for --start values outside the supported vocabulary ('now'/'today'/'N days ago'); the default '30 days ago' and any 'N days ago' input work correctly, so the blast radius is limited to users who guess unsupported relative syntax (weeks/months/'yesterday') or typo a date. Additional supporting evidence not in the original report: (1) --end has no such bug because coerce_relative_end raises on bad input — a loud-vs-silent asymmetry between the two adjacent lines; (2) the exact suggested fix is already the established pattern at cli/main.py:1104-1106, so the recommended remediation has direct in-codebase precedent.

verifiedBugs.title: Malformed --end raises an unhandled ParserError that crashes the search command with a traceback
verifiedBugs.description: `end_dt = coerce_relative_end(end)` is not wrapped in try/except. `coerce_relative_end` only special-cases `now`/`today`; for any other string it calls `dateutil.parser.parse(end)` directly, which raises `dateutil.parser.ParserError` (a subclass of ValueError) on unparseable input. Unlike `to_utc`, this function does NOT catch that error, so it propagates out of the `search` command as an uncaught exception and dumps a Python traceback to the terminal.
verifiedBugs.impact: A simple typo like `awareness search bitcoin --end lastweek` crashes with a stack trace instead of a friendly 'invalid date' message — poor UX and looks broken.
verifiedBugs.repro: `python3 -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'src'); from awareness.util.timeutil import coerce_relative_end; coerce_relative_end('lastweek')"` raises `ParserError: Unknown string format: lastweek`. Equivalent to `awareness search bitcoin --end lastweek`.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Wrap the `to_utc(start)` / `coerce_relative_end(end)` calls in the search/browse commands in try/except and convert failures to `typer.BadParameter`. Also have `coerce_relative_end` catch ParserError and raise a clear ValueError like `to_utc` does.

verdict.reasoning:

Empirically reproduced: `coerce_relative_end('lastweek')` raises `dateutil.parser.ParserError` (a ValueError subclass) at /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/util/timeutil.py:75, where it calls `_dateutil_parser.parse(end)` with no try/except — unlike `to_utc` (lines 30-33) and `parse_http_date` (lines 45-51) which both catch `(ValueError, TypeError)` and return None.

The Typer app (main.py:53) does not disable pretty exceptions, so an uncaught exception dumps a (Rich-formatted) traceback to the terminal rather than a clean error. So `awareness search bitcoin --end lastweek` crashes with a stack trace.

The inconsistency is real: `to_utc('lastweek')` returns None silently, so a malformed `--start` does NOT crash search (it's just ignored), whereas a malformed `--end` does crash. That asymmetry confirms this is an oversight, not intended behavior.

I could not run the full CLI end-to-end because the environment is missing the `structlog` dependency (import-time failure unrelated to this bug), but the crash mechanism is fully proven at the function level and by code inspection of the unguarded call site.

Not a style nit and not handled elsewhere: the try/except blocks in the sibling `query` (line 1663) and `counts` (line 1693) commands wrap only the later `idx.execute()` calls, which run AFTER `coerce_relative_end`, so they do not protect against this. The `search` command has no try/except at all around the date coercion.
verdict.correction: The claim is correct on root cause (timeutil.py:67-77, specifically line 75) and on the search call site (main.py:2630). Two refinements: (1) The bug is broader than just `search` — the same unguarded `coerce_relative_end(end)` appears in the `query` command (main.py:1644) and `counts` command (main.py:1692) before their try/except blocks (which only cover idx.execute), and in `backfill` (main.py:1111). verifiedBugs.title: highlight_query/highlight_tokens fail to highlight substring matches that aren't at a word boundary, even though search matched them
verifiedBugs.description: `highlight_query` builds the highlight regex as `re.compile(r"\b(" + "|".join(terms) + r")\w*", re.IGNORECASE)`. The leading `\b` anchor means a query term is only highlighted when it begins at a word boundary. But the search layer matches terms MID-WORD: substring mode uses `ILIKE '%query%'` (duckdb_index.py:500-501) and prefix mode matches the stem ROOT anywhere via `%root%` (lines 507-510). So a query that legitimately returns a document (e.g. searching `coin`, which matches `bitcoin` via ILIKE) renders the matched title/snippet/body with NOTHING highlighted, because `\bcoin\w*` does not match inside `bitcoin`. The snippet finder (`_snippet_for`) has a substring fallback and still centers on the hit, so the user sees the right text but no visible highlight, making search look like it returned an irrelevant or non-matching row.
verifiedBugs.impact: Matched documents render with no highlight whenever the match is a mid-word substring (any non-prefix substring query), so users can't see WHY a row matched — a core 'janky search' symptom. The highlight and the matcher disagree about what counts as a hit.
verifiedBugs.repro: `python3` reproduction: highlight_query('I love bitcoin today','coin') returns the text unchanged (no [bold yellow]). Yet `awareness search coin --mode substring` returns the bitcoin doc as a match.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Drop the leading `\b` so highlighting matches the same substring semantics the search uses (e.g. `re.compile('(' + '|'.join(re.escape(t)) + ')', re.IGNORECASE)`), or highlight per matched root with `\w*` on both sides. Keep the longest-first ordering to avoid partial overlaps.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED. I reproduced and traced the full path.

1. Highlight behavior (main.py:2418): `re.compile(r"\b(" + "|".join(...) + r")\w*", re.IGNORECASE)`. The leading `\b` anchors each term to a word START, and `\w*` only extends FORWARD. So a term is highlighted only when it is a literal PREFIX of a word. I verified: `highlight_query('I love bitcoin today','coin')` returns the text unchanged (no `[bold yellow]`), exactly as the claim states.

2. Search matcher disagrees:
   - substring mode (duckdb_index.py:499-502): `ILIKE '%query%'` on the raw query — `%coin%` matches `bitcoin`. Verified the row IS returned.
   - prefix mode / default `auto` fallback (duckdb_index.py:504-511): matches each Snowball STEM ROOT anywhere via `%root%`. `finance` stems to `financ` and matches `financial`. But highlight uses the RAW query `finance`, and `\bfinance\w*` does NOT match `financial` (diverges at financ|e vs financ|ial). So even the documented headline feature ("`finance` still surfaces `financial`", _stem_roots docstring) renders with zero highlight. Default mode is `auto` (config/settings.py:116, duckdb_index.py:41), so this hits the DEFAULT search path, not only explicit `--mode substring`.

3. Rendering path matches the claim: the search command calls `highlight_tokens(title, query)` and `highlight_tokens(snippet, query)` (main.py:2543/2660/2664/2712/2715) with the RAW user query — never the stem roots that the matcher actually used (`snippet_terms`/roots are computed but the CLI ignores them for highlighting; `snippet_hits` from `_snippet_for` is computed but unused by the CLI renderer). So the matcher and highlighter use different term semantics.

4. User impact: `_snippet_for` has a substring fallback (duckdb_index.py:599-605) that still centers the snippet on the hit, so the correct text is shown — but with NOTHING highlighted. The user sees a returned row where they cannot tell why it matched: a real "janky search" symptom.

5. Not already-handled: existing tests (tests/unit/test_cli_highlight.py:47, test_search_highlight_and_shell.py:103) only assert literal-prefix cases and crucially pass the ALREADY-STEMMED root `"financ"` directly to `highlight_tokens`, which masks the bug because production passes the raw query `finance`. No test covers mid-word substrings or stem-divergent surface forms, so this is an untested gap, not an intended contract.

Severity is medium (not higher): search RESULTS are still correct and the snippet TEXT is still displayed correctly; only the visual highlight is missing. It is a cosmetic/UX correctness mismatch, not a data or result-correctness bug. The claim's medium rating is appropriate.
verdict.correction: Claim is accurate. Two refinements: (a) The impact is broader than "any non-prefix substring query" — it also hits the DEFAULT `auto`/prefix path whenever the Snowball stem root diverges from the surface form (e.g. `finance`→`financial`, `studies`→`studied`), because highlight uses the raw query while the matcher uses stem roots. (b) Root cause is precisely that `highlight_tokens` is always called with the RAW `query` rather than the `snippet_terms`/stem-roots that search actually matched on; the `\b...\w*` regex then only catches literal-prefix matches. The suggested fix (drop `\b`, escape terms, longest-first) addresses the substring case; to also fix the stem-divergence case the highlighter should highlight on the same roots the matcher used (e.g. pass `res['terms']`/`snippet_terms` or use `snippet_hits` positions) rather than the raw query.

verifiedBugs.title: Piped/non-interactive search returns only one page (limit, default 10) with no pagination and no 'more results' signal
verifiedBugs.description: When stdout is piped or `--no-interactive` is used (`not interactive or not sys.stdin.isatty()`), the command calls `idx.search(limit=limit, offset=0, ...)` exactly once. `limit` defaults to `settings.search_default_limit` = 10 (schema.py:246). There is no pagination in this branch, so a query that matches hundreds of documents prints only the first 10 (or whatever the per-page default is) and returns. The header does say 'Found {total} documents, showing top {len(rows)}', but there is no way to get the rest in non-interactive mode, and the per-page default (10) is far smaller than `search_max_results` (200).
verifiedBugs.impact: `echo bitcoin | awareness search` or `awareness search bitcoin --no-interactive` shows only ~10 rows regardless of corpus size, looking like 'search only finds a few results'. Directly matches the reported symptom of too few results.
verifiedBugs.repro: With >10 matching docs: `awareness search bitcoin --no-interactive` prints only 10 rows even though the header reports a larger 'Found N'.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: In the non-interactive branch, default `limit` to `max_results` (or stream all rows up to the cap) rather than the per-page default, or add a `--limit`/`--all` that the piped path honors. At minimum, when `total > len(rows)`, print an explicit 'showing N of M; pass --limit to see more' line.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified against the source. In the non-interactive/piped branch (src/awareness/cli/main.py:2632-2667), search() is called exactly once with limit=limit, offset=0 and then the function returns — there is no pagination loop (the while-loop with n/p navigation only exists in the interactive branch at 2669+). The `limit` value resolves to settings.search_default_limit (=10, confirmed at config/schema.py:246, documented as "Default number of results shown per page"), while search_max_results defaults to 200 (schema.py:251). In DuckDbIndex.search (storage/duckdb_index.py:381-535) the `limit` argument maps directly to the SQL `LIMIT {int(limit)}` clause on both the FTS path (line 485) and the prefix/substring path (line 533), so only 10 rows are materialized regardless of corpus size. Thus `echo bitcoin | awareness search` (or `--no-interactive`) prints at most ~10 rows even when hundreds match. The claim's "no 'more results' signal" is also substantiated: the `(capped)` marker at line 2649 is gated on `total > len(rows) AND len(rows) >= max_results`; at the default per-page limit (10) and max_results (200), `10 >= 200` is False, so the marker never appears in the common case — it is effectively dead at defaults. No test asserts non-interactive result counts or the capped signal (tests/unit/test_cli_commands.py, test_cli_highlight.py, test_search_highlight_and_shell.py only check highlighting/invocation), so nothing pins the intended behavior to refute this.

Why this is NOT a style nit: a piped consumer silently receives a truncated result set with no pagination affordance, which genuinely under-reports matches — a real output-correctness/UX defect that matches a "search finds too few results" symptom.

Why I am downgrading severity from medium to low (refutation of the claim's framing, not the bug itself): (1) The claim says "there is no way to get the rest in non-interactive mode" — that is inaccurate. The `--limit/-l` option (main.py:2601) IS honored in this exact branch (resolved at 2626), so `awareness search bitcoin --no-interactive --limit 200` returns up to the 200 cap. A documented workaround exists. (2) The header DOES print the true total ("Found {total} documents, showing top {len(rows)}"), so the truncation is not fully silent — a user can see Found 500 vs showing top 10, even though no guidance/pagination is offered. (3) No crash, data loss, or incorrect ranking; the returned rows are the correct top-N by score. So this is a real but mild UX/defaults defect, best classified low.
verdict.correction: Real, but two parts of the claim are overstated. (a) "No way to get the rest" is false: the `--limit/-l` flag is honored in the non-interactive branch (main.py:2601, resolved at 2626), so `--no-interactive --limit 200` returns up to search_max_results (200) rows — the issue is a misleading per-page default plus missing 'more results' guidance and missing auto-pagination, not impossibility. (b) The header is not fully silent: it prints the true `total`, so the discrepancy is observable (just unguided). Root cause precision: the more concrete latent defect is that the `(capped)` indicator at main.py:2649 is effectively dead code at default settings because its condition `len(rows) >= max_results` can never be true when len(rows) is bounded by the per-page `limit` (10) and max_results is 200; a piped user therefore gets no truncation/pagination hint. Suggested fix is reasonable: in the non-interactive branch default `limit` to `max_results` (or stream up to the cap), and/or when `total > len(rows)` always print an explicit 'showing N of M; pass --limit to see more' line rather than the currently-unreachable (capped) marker. Severity: low, not medium.

verifiedBugs.title: The '(capped)' indicator in non-interactive search can never be shown due to a wrong comparison
verifiedBugs.description: `capped = ' (capped)' if total > len(rows) and len(rows) >= max_results else ''`. In this branch `len(rows)` is bounded by the per-page `limit` (default 10), while `max_results` is the overall ceiling (default 200). The condition `len(rows) >= max_results` is therefore essentially always False (10 >= 200 is False), so the 'capped' hint never appears even when results were truncated by `max_results`. The intended signal — telling the user the hard ceiling clipped their results — is dead code.
verifiedBugs.impact: Users are never told when `max_results` truncated their result set, hiding the fact that there are more matches than shown. Contributes to the 'where did my results go' confusion.
verifiedBugs.repro: With `limit=10`, `max_results=200`, `total=200`, `len(rows)=10`: `total > len(rows)` is True but `len(rows) >= max_results` is False, so capped == ''. Verified in Python.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Compare against the cap correctly: e.g. signal capping when `total >= max_results` (the ceiling was hit) rather than `len(rows) >= max_results`. Better, have idx.search return an explicit `capped`/`truncated` flag and render that.

verdict.reasoning: Verified the claim against the code. The condition at line 2649, `total > len(rows) and len(rows) >= max_results`, requires len(rows) >= max_results, which can only hold when limit >= max_results. By design limit is the per-page knob (default search_default_limit=10, settings.py:118) and max_results is the larger overall ceiling (default search_max_results=200, settings.py:119). So `len(rows) >= max_results` evaluates 10 >= 200 = False under defaults, and is False for any sane config where limit <= max_results. verifiedBugs.title: Pressing 'n' past the last page silently re-renders the final page while the page counter keeps incrementing
verifiedBugs.description: The interactive loop advances with `offset += limit` on 'n' and never bounds-checks `offset` against `total`. When `offset` exceeds the corpus, `idx.search` clamps it: if `offset >= max_results` it resets `offset = max(0, max_results - limit)` (duckdb_index.py:413-416), so the SAME last page of rows is returned. Because the rows are non-empty, the `if not rows` end-of-results branch (2691) is never hit, and the loop keeps prompting. Meanwhile the table title computes the page number from the CLI-side, unclamped offset: `Page {offset // limit + 1}` (2700). So the displayed page number climbs (Page 21, 22, 23…) while the rows shown are stuck on the real last page, and there is no 'end of results' message.
verifiedBugs.impact: Paging forward at the end of results spins in place: the page label keeps increasing but the content does not change, with no signal that the user has reached the end. Confusing, janky navigation. (Note: the clamp only engages once offset crosses max_results=200; below that, an over-range offset returns empty and the existing back-off branch handles it — the broken case is specifically near/at the max_results ceiling.)
verifiedBugs.repro: With max_results=200 and a corpus around that size, press 'n' repeatedly past the last real page: the page number in the title increments (e.g. 'Page 21') but the listed rows are identical to the previous page, and no end-of-results notice appears.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Bound-check before advancing: only increment offset if `offset + limit < total`, otherwise show 'End of results.' Use the offset actually returned by idx.search (it returns the clamped offset) to compute the page label so the title and rows stay consistent.

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the actual code. In the interactive search loop (src/awareness/cli/main.py:2669-2742), 'n' does `offset += limit` (line 2740) with no bound check against `total`. Inside idx.search (duckdb_index.py:413-416), `offset >= max_results` (200 >= 200) clamps it back to `max(0, 200-10) = 190`, so the SAME last page of rows is returned. Those rows are non-empty, so the `if not rows` end-of-results / back-off branch (main.py:2691-2698) is never hit and the loop keeps prompting. The table title (main.py:2700) computes the page number from the CLI-side UNCLAMPED offset: `offset // limit + 1`, so it prints Page 21, 22, 23... while the displayed rows never change. Crucially, `total` returned by search is the full real corpus count (duckdb_index.py:472-473 / 517-521), not clamped, so the title's "Found N total" stays correct while the page label lies. The dict does return the clamped `offset` (line 554), but the CLI ignores it and keeps its own diverging value — so the suggested fix (resync from res["offset"] and/or bound-check before advancing) is correct. I also confirmed the claim's own caveat: when total < max_results, an over-range offset returns empty rows and the existing back-off branch (lines 2696-2698) handles it with a visible "No more pages" message, so the broken case is specifically at/above the 200-row ceiling. The bug is genuine and user-affecting (misleading climbing page counter, frozen content, no end-of-results signal), not a style nit and not handled elsewhere. Severity medium is fair: no data loss or crash, rows shown are the genuine last page, but the UI actively misleads (incrementing page numbers imply new content) and requires a >=200-row matching corpus to trigger.
verdict.correction: Confirmed real and root cause is exactly as described. Two refinements: (1) the broken/loops-forever case requires the matching corpus to have at least max_results (default 200) rows so the offset>=max_results clamp engages and returns non-empty rows; below that ceiling the over-range offset yields empty rows and the existing back-off branch (main.py:2696-2698) shows "No more pages" — so it is not unbounded there. (2) search already returns the clamped offset in its result dict (duckdb_index.py:554); the CLI bug is that it discards this and uses its own unclamped local `offset` for both the page label (2700) and advancement (2740). Fix: bound-check before `offset += limit` (only advance if more rows exist) and/or compute the page label from res["offset"].

verifiedBugs.title: FTS index is fully rebuilt on every /search request because DuckDbIndex is instantiated per-request
verifiedBugs.description: Every query endpoint constructs a brand-new DuckDbIndex object per request (server.py:289,316,345,393,413,435). The FTS build-state lives on the instance: _fts_built_for_count is initialized to -1 in DuckDbIndex.__init__ (duckdb_index.py:73). In _ensure_fts the only skip conditions are `_fts_built_signature == _views_signature` (None on a fresh instance) and `count == _fts_built_for_count` (-1 on a fresh instance), so neither is ever satisfied. As a result EVERY /search call executes `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE captures_idx AS SELECT ... FROM captures` (a full corpus materialization) followed by `PRAGMA create_fts_index(...)` (a full trie/BM25 rebuild over the whole corpus). The signature/count caching the code was written to provide is dead because the object is thrown away after each request.
verifiedBugs.impact: Search latency grows linearly with corpus size on EVERY keystroke-debounced search (SPA fires /search 300ms after typing). On a non-trivial corpus this makes search feel 'broken/janky' and can take seconds per query. The CLI hides this because it is single-shot, but the API + the SPA's repeated searches make it pathological.
verifiedBugs.repro: Add a few thousand captures, then issue two consecutive GET /search?q=bitcoin requests and observe the log line `duckdb_fts_index_built rows=N` emitted on BOTH (it should only build once). Time scales with corpus size each call.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Make DuckDbIndex a process-wide singleton (build it once in lifespan and store on _State, or use an lru_cache/module-level cache keyed by db_path) so the FTS materialization and view-signature caching actually persist across requests. Alternatively persist captures_idx + the FTS index in the on-disk DB and gate rebuilds on the source signature rather than per-instance state.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED via code reading + empirical reproduction. The claim's mechanism is correct, only the cited file path is slightly off (real file: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py, not .../api/...; line numbers and code match exactly).

Code evidence: server.py `_State` (lines 80-84) holds state/planner/tail but NO DuckDbIndex. All six query endpoints (/inspect 289, /counts 316, /captures 345, /captures/{id} 393, /related 413, /search 435) construct a brand-new `DuckDbIndex(...)` per request. There is no module-level cache, no lru_cache, no singleton anywhere in the API (grep confirmed). `DuckDbIndex.__init__` (duckdb_index.py:66-79) resets `_fts_built_for_count=-1`, `_fts_built_signature=None`, `_views_signature=None` on every instance. In `_ensure_fts` (307-358) the only two skip conditions are `_fts_built_signature == _views_signature` (None vs a real signature on a fresh instance → never equal) and `count == _fts_built_for_count` (count vs -1 → never equal), so on every fresh instance it always runs `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE captures_idx AS SELECT ... FROM captures` (full corpus materialization) followed by `PRAGMA create_fts_index(...)` (full BM25/trie rebuild). The in-instance caching the code was written to provide is dead because the object is discarded after each request.

Empirical proof (duckdb 1.5.3, project .venv, real DuckDbIndex code): 3 identical GET /search?q=bitcoin requests over an unchanged 3000-row corpus emitted `duckdb_fts_index_built rows=3000` THREE times; the same 3 searches against a single reused instance emitted it ONCE. This exactly matches the claim's stated repro and proves the root cause is the per-request instantiation (the caching logic itself is correct when the instance persists). Latency measured: per-request /search = 291 ms @ 2k rows and 764 ms @ 8k rows, vs cached 18 ms / 32 ms — i.e. 16-24x slower and scaling linearly with corpus size, while the cached path stays roughly flat. On the SPA's 300ms-debounced search this is pathological exactly as described.

This is a genuine, user-affecting performance/correctness-of-design defect, not a style nit and not handled elsewhere. Severity high (not critical): functionality still returns correct results and small corpora are tolerable, but search latency degrades unboundedly with corpus size on every keystroke search.
verdict.correction: Real bug; root cause exactly as stated (per-request DuckDbIndex instantiation makes the signature/count FTS caching dead across requests). Two corrections/refinements: (1) The cited file path is wrong — the file is /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py (the claim wrote .../api/duckdb_index.py), though the cited line numbers 73 and 307-358 are accurate. (2) The FTS rebuild is the worst offender but not the only per-request cost: `connect()` opens a fresh on-disk DuckDB connection and runs `_refresh_views()` (rebuilds all views) on every request, and `execute()`/`search()` additionally run `_refresh_views_if_stale()` — so the non-/search endpoints (/inspect,/counts,/captures,...) also pay a per-request connection-open + view-rebuild, just without the FTS materialization. Suggested fix is sound: build one DuckDbIndex in lifespan and store it on _State (or lru_cache keyed by db_path) so connection, views, and FTS state persist across requests. The shared-instance contrast test confirms this collapses 3 rebuilds to 1 and search latency from ~291ms to ~18ms at 2k rows.

verifiedBugs.title: Concurrent /search requests crash with DuckDB 'Catalog write-write conflict' on captures_idx
verifiedBugs.lines: 333-354 (CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE captures_idx) reached from server.py:445
verifiedBugs.description: Because _ensure_fts always rebuilds (see fts-index-rebuilt-every-request), each /search runs `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE captures_idx`. FastAPI executes the synchronous /search endpoint in its threadpool, so two browser searches that overlap run in two threads, each with its own DuckDbIndex and its own DuckDB connection to the SAME on-disk file. The per-instance threading.RLock does NOT serialize them (different instances → different locks). I reproduced this: 6 threads each doing CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE captures_idx + create_fts_index against one shared DuckDB file produced 5 failures with `TransactionException: Catalog write-write conflict on create with ... Table ... captures_idx`. The surviving thread succeeds; the rest raise.
verifiedBugs.impact: Overlapping searches (e.g. fast typing with 300ms debounce, or multiple browser tabs/users) cause /search to return HTTP 500. The SPA surfaces this as 'query failed: 500 ...' in #caps-meta. This is a direct, concrete cause of 'search is broken/janky in many places.'
verifiedBugs.repro: Open the captures view in two tabs (or type quickly) so two /search calls overlap; one or more return 500 with a catalog write-write conflict. Verified standalone with 6 concurrent threads doing the same CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE captures_idx on a shared .duckdb file: 5/6 raised TransactionException.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Build captures_idx + the FTS index exactly once behind a single shared lock on a single shared connection (singleton DuckDbIndex), not per request. If kept per-request, serialize the rebuild with a global lock and/or check for an existing captures_idx before CREATE OR REPLACE, and treat the write-write conflict as a 'someone else is building it' retry rather than a 500.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed and reproduced. Root cause chain is exactly as claimed: (1) every /search builds a fresh DuckDbIndex (server.py:435-439) with its own DuckDB connection to the same on-disk file data/duckdb/metadata.duckdb (settings.py:170-172); (2) the /search handler is synchronous `def search` (server.py:423), so FastAPI runs overlapping requests on separate threadpool threads; (3) the per-instance threading.RLock (duckdb_index.py:70) is created in __init__, so different instances hold different locks and DO NOT serialize each other; (4) the FTS fast-path early-returns at duckdb_index.py:318 and :330 rely on per-instance state (_fts_built_signature/_fts_built_for_count) that is always reset on a fresh instance, so CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE captures_idx + create_fts_index (lines 335-350) runs on every auto/fts-mode search with default fields; (5) /search has no try/except, so duckdb TransactionException propagates as HTTP 500, and the SPA renders it as 'query failed: 500 ...' in #caps-meta (app.js:127 throws `500 <detail>`, app.js:326 prints 'query failed: ' + err.message). The SPA uses no AbortController, so its 300ms debounce (app.js:984) does not prevent overlap across tabs, multiple users, or with the 5s dashboard/feed pollers.

I reproduced it two ways on the project's pinned DuckDB 1.5.3: (a) standalone 6-thread CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE captures_idx + create_fts_index on one shared .duckdb file -> 5/6 raised 'TransactionException: Catalog write-write conflict on create ... captures_idx'; (b) end-to-end through the real DuckDbIndex.search() with realistic 8ms-staggered overlapping requests (mimicking debounced typing / two tabs) -> 5/6 searches raised the same write-write conflict and would surface as HTTP 500.

This is a genuine, user-affecting correctness/availability bug, not a style nit and not handled elsewhere. High severity is appropriate: it intermittently breaks a core feature (search) for any concurrent usage, but it is a transient per-request failure (one thread still succeeds; retry usually works) rather than permanent data corruption, so not critical.
verdict.correction: Real, root cause is correct, but the blast radius is broader than the claim states. The write-write conflict is not limited to CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE captures_idx in the FTS path. In the real code path it fires even earlier on CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW staging_captures_raw inside _refresh_views (duckdb_index.py:149+), which is invoked via connect()/_refresh_views_if_stale (lines 102, 142-147, 300-301, 426-427) on EVERY request regardless of search mode. So overlapping non-FTS searches (mode=prefix/substring) and other endpoints that share this code (/captures, /counts, /inspect, /captures/{id}/related) can also 500 with the same Catalog write-write conflict. The suggested fix is correct in direction: use a single shared DuckDbIndex (singleton, e.g. on app.state) with a single connection and its single RLock so all view/table/FTS rebuilds are serialized, instead of constructing a new per-request instance. Alternatively serialize all writes behind a process-wide lock and/or treat the write-write conflict as a 'someone else is rebuilding' condition (retry/skip) rather than letting it become a 500. Note the per-instance fast-path caching (_fts_built_signature) only becomes effective once the index is a long-lived singleton.

verifiedBugs.title: 'To' date filter excludes the entire selected end day (midnight boundary, off-by-one)
verifiedBugs.description: The SPA's date inputs (#caps-start/#caps-end) are <input type=date>, which yield 'YYYY-MM-DD' strings. The server parses end with to_utc('YYYY-MM-DD') which resolves to that day at 00:00:00 UTC (verified: to_utc('2026-06-08') -> 2026-06-08 00:00:00+00:00). The filter is then `fetch_ts <= $end`. So selecting To=2026-06-08 only includes rows captured at or before 2026-06-08T00:00:00 and excludes everything captured DURING 2026-06-08. The start filter (`fetch_ts >= $start`, start-of-day) is correct/inclusive, but the end filter is effectively exclusive of the chosen day. Same pattern in /search (duckdb_index.py:443-444 `fetch_ts <= $end`) and /inspect (server.py:295 `fetch_ts <= $end`).
verifiedBugs.impact: Users who set a To date to bound a range silently lose all captures from that final day — the most recent and most likely-relevant data. Setting From=To=today returns zero results even when many captures exist today. This is a classic, user-visible date-filter correctness bug.
verifiedBugs.repro: In the Captures view set To = today and Apply; captures made today (any time after 00:00) disappear. Equivalent: GET /captures?end=2026-06-08 omits all rows with fetch_ts during 2026-06-08.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: When the end value is date-only (no time component), treat it as inclusive end-of-day: either add one day and use `fetch_ts < end+1day`, or coerce the bare date to 23:59:59.999999 of that day before binding. Apply consistently to /captures, /search, and /inspect.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed genuine and user-affecting. Trace verified end-to-end:

1. SPA sends a bare date. app.js lines 283-298: `end = $("#caps-end").value` (an `<input type="date">`, index.html:188) yields `YYYY-MM-DD` and is appended as-is via `params.set("end", end)` — no time component is added.

2. Server parses it to midnight. `/captures` (server.py:355-357), `/inspect` (294-296), `/counts` (321-323), and `/search` (451-453 → duckdb_index.py:442-444) all type the param as `datetime`. I verified via pydantic `TypeAdapter(datetime).validate_python('2026-06-08')` -> `datetime(2026, 6, 8, 0, 0)`, and `to_utc()` on that -> `2026-06-08 00:00:00+00:00` (start-of-day).

3. Filter excludes the day. The predicate is `fetch_ts <= $end`. I confirmed `fetch_ts` is a `TIMESTAMPTZ` (duckdb_index.py:230/245/275 `TRY_CAST(... AS TIMESTAMPTZ)`; iceberg_schema.py:44 `TimestamptzType`), so captures made during the day carry non-midnight times. A capture at 2026-06-08 14:00 fails `<= 2026-06-08 00:00:00+00:00` (verified False). Setting From=To=today yields the empty/degenerate range `[00:00, 00:00]`, returning ~zero rows. The start filter (`fetch_ts >= $start`, also midnight) is correctly inclusive; only the end bound is the off-by-one.

The bug is real, reproducible, and silently drops the most-recent full day of data — the data users most often want. Severity high is appropriate (correctness, silent data loss, default-likely user action). Not a style nit; not handled or compensated anywhere (no end-of-day coercion exists for date-only inputs; `coerce_relative_end`/`to_utc` do not bump bare dates to end-of-day).
verdict.correction: Claim is correct in substance, location, impact, and suggested fix. One technical nit in the repro's proof: the cited evidence `to_utc('2026-06-08') -> ... 00:00:00+00:00` exercises the STRING path of to_utc, but in the live request path FastAPI/Pydantic first coerces the query param (typed `datetime`) to `datetime(2026,6,8,0,0)` (naive midnight), and `to_utc` then only attaches UTC tzinfo. The end value bound is identical (2026-06-08 00:00:00+00:00), so the conclusion is unchanged — the string-vs-datetime detail does not affect the bug. Also worth noting the same defect additionally affects `/counts` (server.py:321-323, `fetch_ts BETWEEN $start AND $end`), which the claim did not list but is identically impacted; the suggested fix should be applied there too. Recommended fix unchanged: for date-only end inputs, treat as inclusive end-of-day (e.g., `fetch_ts < end + 1 day`, or coerce bare dates to 23:59:59.999999), applied consistently across /captures, /search, /inspect, and /counts.

verifiedBugs.title: Search pagination silently rewrites offset past max_results, corrupting page position and rows
verifiedBugs.description: search() clamps the page: `if offset >= max_results: offset = max(0, max_results - limit)` then `limit = max(1, min(limit, max_results - offset))`. With the SPA's caps.limit=30 and default max_results=200, paging to offset=210 is rewritten server-side to offset=170 (verified). The server returns rows for offset 170 but the response echoes the clamped offset, while the SPA keeps its own caps.offset (210) and computes the displayed range/next-button state from caps.offset and data.total (app.js:313-323). Additionally `total` reflects ALL matches (can exceed 200), so `caps.offset + caps.limit >= data.total` (app.js:323) stays false beyond offset 200, leaving the Next button enabled and letting the user page into the clamped dead zone.
verifiedBugs.impact: Past 200 results the Captures pager shows wrong 'from–to of N' labels and serves rows from offset 170 repeatedly while claiming to be on a later page — duplicated/stale results and a Next button that never disables. Pagination is effectively broken for any search with >200 matches.
verifiedBugs.repro: Search a common term with >200 matches; click Next repeatedly past page ~7 (offset 210). The position label keeps advancing but the same rows (offset 170) are returned, and Next never disables.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Cap pagination coherently: when offset >= max_results return an empty page (total capped to max_results) rather than rewriting offset to a different window, and have the API report an effective/capped total so the SPA disables Next correctly. Or surface the server's clamped offset back to the SPA and have loadCaptures honor it.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed real by tracing server and SPA code end-to-end.

SERVER (src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py:413-416): When offset >= max_results, the page is silently rewritten: `offset = max(0, max_results - limit)` then `limit = max(1, min(limit, max_results - offset))`. With max_results=200 (settings.py:119, actually passed via server.py:455) and limit=30, requesting offset=210 yields offset=170, limit=30. The row query uses this clamped offset (LIMIT/OFFSET at lines 485 and 533), so rows 170-199 are returned. Crucially `total` is an uncapped COUNT(*) over ALL matches (lines 472-473 for FTS, 517-521 for prefix) — it is never min()'d against max_results. The response echoes the clamped offset (line 554).

SPA (src/awareness/api/web/app.js): caps state is `{ limit: 30, offset: 0, total: 0 }` (line 275). Next does `caps.offset += caps.limit` (line 988) and the SPA NEVER reads data.offset back from the response (confirmed: only data.total and data.rows are consumed, lines 311-314). The displayed range is computed from the SPA's own caps.offset (lines 313-314), and the Next-disable check is `caps.offset + caps.limit >= data.total` (line 323). Because data.total is uncapped (>200 for the affected case), this stays false past offset 200, so Next never disables.

Walk-through for total>240: pages advance 0,30,...,180,210,240. At offset=210 the server clamps to 170 and returns rows 170-199 while the SPA shows '211-240 of N'. At offset=240 it clamps to 170 again — the same window is served indefinitely while the position label keeps climbing. This is exactly the claimed corruption: duplicated/stale rows, wrong 'from-to of N' labels, and a Next button that never disables.

Scope check: this is specific to /search. The /captures browse endpoint (server.py:334-369) has no offset clamp and honors offset directly, so browse mode is unaffected — consistent with the claim. No other guard caps total or syncs the SPA offset. Not a style nit and not handled elsewhere.

Severity medium is correct: it requires a single search with >200 matches, only corrupts the tail of pagination (past ~page 7/offset 210), and degrades a secondary UI feature without data loss, crashes, or security impact.
verdict.correction: Real, as described. One minor imprecision in the repro: it is not strictly 'offset 170 repeatedly' for every page past 200 — the first boundary page (offset=180) returns only 20 rows because limit is also clamped (min(30, 200-180)=20), giving rows 180-199. The duplicated/stale 'offset 170, 30 rows' window kicks in from offset>=210 onward (210→170, 240→170, etc.). The root cause and user impact are exactly as claimed. The suggested fix is sound: either return an empty page beyond max_results AND report a capped total so the SPA disables Next, or echo the clamped offset back and have loadCaptures honor data.offset (currently ignored at app.js:311-314).

verifiedBugs.title: Snippet term highlights never render in prefix/substring (fallback) search mode
verifiedBugs.description: In prefix mode the terms attached to each result row are stem ROOTS, not whole words: snippet_terms = roots (duckdb_index.py:506,549), e.g. 'financial' -> 'financ', and ILIKE matches via `%financ%`. But both the server's _snippet_for (regex `\b(term)\b`, lines 596 & 622-624) and the SPA's highlightedFragment (regex `\b(term)\b`, app.js:340) require a WORD-BOUNDARY match. A root like 'financ' has no word boundary inside 'financial', and a singular root 'bitcoin' won't match plural 'bitcoins'. I verified both: `\bfinanc\b` finds nothing in 'financial sector', `\bbitcoin\b` finds nothing in 'many bitcoins', and _snippet_for(...,['financ']) returns hits=[] while still centering the snippet correctly. So fallback-mode results show snippets with ZERO highlighted terms even though those rows genuinely matched.
verifiedBugs.impact: Whenever auto-mode falls back to prefix matching (the documented behavior for surfacing 'financial' from 'finance', or any morphological/partial match), the user sees result snippets with no <mark> highlights, making it look like the match is wrong or the search is broken. Contributes to the 'janky search' complaint.
verifiedBugs.repro: Search a term that only matches via stemming/partial (e.g. 'finance' where corpus has 'financial', or 'bitcoin' where text has 'bitcoins') and that misses FTS so it falls to prefix mode; the snippet renders but nothing is highlighted.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Drop the `\b...\b` word boundaries when terms are stem roots (use substring/prefix-aware matching), or return both the original tokens and the roots and highlight on a prefix pattern like `(root)\w*`. Keep server _snippet_for hits and SPA highlightedFragment consistent with how rows were actually matched (ILIKE %root%).

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED via the project's own code and DuckDB stemmer. The data flow: in prefix mode (duckdb_index.py:504-511) each query token is reduced to its Snowball stem root via _stem_roots (line 360-379, calls DuckDB `stem(t,'english')`), and rows are matched by ILIKE `%root%` (line 509-510). The roots are then stored as snippet_terms (line 506) and attached to every row as r["terms"] (line 549) and passed to _snippet_for (line 545). But _snippet_for highlights via `\b(term)\b` (line 596, 622-624) and the SPA's highlightedFragment uses the same `\b(term)\b` (app.js:340), rendering BOTH the title (app.js:377) and the snippet (app.js:385) through it with r.terms = the roots.

I ran the real DuckDB FTS stemmer in the project's .venv:
  finance   -> 'financ'  (\bfinanc\b does NOT match 'finance' or 'financial')
  financial -> 'financi'
  running   -> 'run'      (\brun\b does NOT match 'running')
  bitcoins  -> 'bitcoin'  (\bbitcoin\b does NOT match 'bitcoins')
The stemmer truncates the trailing characters, so the root is a strict prefix that NEVER has a word boundary inside the surface form it matched. The word-boundary regex therefore finds nothing for essentially every stemmed token (even the query word itself, e.g. 'finance').

I also ran the actual _snippet_for from the codebase with roots=['financ'] against text containing 'financial': it returns a correctly-centered snippet (via its substring fallback at lines 598-605) but hits=[]. So the row renders, the snippet is positioned over the real match, yet zero <mark> highlights are produced — on both the server payload (snippet_hits=[]) and the client (SPA recomputes with r.terms=roots and ignores snippet_hits entirely, app.js:385).

Default mode is "auto" (line 41), and auto falls back to this prefix path whenever FTS returns nothing (line 458/495) — the documented behavior for surfacing 'financial' from 'finance'. So in real fallback searches the user sees snippets with no highlighting, exactly as claimed. This is a genuine, user-visible correctness/UX defect, not a style nit, and it is not handled elsewhere (no original-token list is preserved; r["terms"] is overwritten with roots at line 506).

Not higher than medium: it does not break search correctness (rows are still returned and snippets are still centered on the true match); it only degrades highlighting in the fallback path. The ranked FTS path (the common case when FTS is available and matches) is unaffected because there snippet_terms stays as the raw tokens from _tokenize_query (line 494) which do have word boundaries. So impact is confined to the prefix/substring-fallback subset of searches.
verdict.correction: Real, and the claim's root cause and locations are accurate. One refinement: the failure is broader than "singular vs plural" / "partial" — the Snowball stemmer truncates virtually every token (even an exact-match query like 'finance' -> 'financ'), so in prefix/fallback mode highlighting is broken for almost all queries that reach that path, not just morphological edge cases. Also worth noting the title is highlighted through the same broken path (app.js:377), so titles lose marks too, not only snippets. The suggested fix is sound: either drop the `\b...\b` boundaries when terms are roots and use a prefix pattern like `(root)\w*`, or keep both the original tokens and the roots and highlight on a prefix-aware pattern, ensuring server _snippet_for and SPA highlightedFragment stay consistent with the ILIKE `%root%` matching that actually selected the rows.

verdict.reasoning:

Severity high (not critical) is appropriate: it breaks one specific entry path (resume/reuse) completely, but the default fresh-start path works, so tailing is not 100% dead for all users.

The cited line numbers map to this file revision as 29 (import) and 108 (faulty reference); the JSON's "lines: 28, 108" is off by one on the import line (the import is on line 29 here, line 28 is the SourceKind import), but this is cosmetic and does not change the finding.

verifiedBugs.title: claim_pending_tasks is not atomic — concurrent workers double-claim the same task
verifiedBugs.description: The stated invariant is 'PENDING → RUNNING transition is atomic: only one worker sees each task.' But claim_pending_tasks does a plain SELECT ... WHERE status='pending' followed by an in-Python loop that sets status='running', committed at the end — with no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / with_for_update(), no SKIP LOCKED, no BEGIN IMMEDIATE, and (notably) WITHOUT taking the instance-level self._lock RLock that exists on StateDB (it is only used in init()). Under SQLite's default deferred transactions, two concurrent sessions can both run the SELECT before either commits the UPDATE, so both claim the same rows.
verifiedBugs.impact: When two WorkerEngine instances run against the same job concurrently, the same task is processed twice: duplicate network fetches, duplicate captures written to JSONL/Iceberg, and corrupted job counters (tasks_completed can exceed tasks_total, docs double-counted). This is directly reachable because POST /backfill/{job_id}/run (api/server.py:175-190) spawns a fresh WorkerEngine with NO guard against the job already running, so two POSTs race. It also races the standalone `awareness-worker` process against an in-CLI run.
verifiedBugs.repro: Submit a backfill, then POST /backfill/{job_id}/run twice in quick succession (or run `awareness-worker` while the API/CLI is also draining the job). Observe duplicate captures and tasks_completed > tasks_total in `planner.status`.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Make the claim atomic: either wrap the SELECT+UPDATE under StateDB's self._lock and use a single UPDATE ... WHERE status='pending' ... RETURNING (DuckDB/Postgres) / an UPDATE limited by a subquery of ids for SQLite, or open the session with isolation_level='SERIALIZABLE'/BEGIN IMMEDIATE. Additionally, guard /backfill/{job_id}/run against starting a second runner for a job already RUNNING.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL. The code at /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/storage/state.py:420-436 matches the claim exactly: claim_pending_tasks runs `SELECT ... WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT n`, then an in-Python loop sets status='running'/started_at/attempts+=1, committed at the end. There is no with_for_update(), no SKIP LOCKED, no BEGIN IMMEDIATE, no SERIALIZABLE isolation, and self._lock (RLock at state.py:187) is taken only in init() (state.py:195), never in claim_pending_tasks. The docstring even falsely promises 'Atomically transition PENDING tasks to RUNNING.'

I empirically reproduced the double-claim. Using the project's own StateDB against a temp SQLite file with two separate StateDB instances (= two engines/connections, emulating the API process and the standalone awareness-worker process), two threads each looped claim_pending_tasks(JOB, limit=4) until drained. Across 3/3 runs the SAME task ids were claimed by BOTH connections (8, 8, and 20 duplicates out of 60 tasks; TOTAL claims 68, 68, 80 > 60). No OperationalError('database is locked') was raised — SQLite's default deferred read transactions let both sessions see the same PENDING rows and both commit their UPDATEs (last-writer-wins on the row).

Reachability is real cross-process: API server.py:93, CLI `backfill run`, and the standalone worker workers/main.py:28 ALL default to the same `sqlite:///awareness.sqlite` (settings.state_db_url). workers/main.py _drive() drains any job in pending/running/paused, so running `awareness-worker` while the API/CLI drains the same job double-processes tasks. There is also no guard in /backfill/{job_id}/run (server.py:175-190): it unconditionally builds a new WorkerEngine and asyncio.create_task(run_job) with no check that the job is already RUNNING.

Impact validated end-to-end: each duplicate _run_task (engine.py:300-414) appends captures to its own buffer and flushes them, so the same partition's captures get written twice to JSONL/Iceberg. And increment_job_counters (state.py:271-296) does an unconditional SQL `tasks_completed = tasks_completed + 1` (and docs_emitted/bytes_processed) with NO clamp against tasks_total, so the counters corrupt and tasks_completed can exceed tasks_total. This is a genuine correctness bug (duplicate network fetches, duplicate persisted captures, corrupted job metrics), not a style nit, and it is not handled elsewhere.
verdict.correction:
Bug is real, but the claim's LEADING repro (two quick POSTs to /backfill/{job_id}/run in the same API process) is largely a false path and overstates in-process reachability. claim_pending_tasks is called SYNCHRONOUSLY (blocking, NOT wrapped in asyncio.to_thread) inside the async run_job loop at engine.py:209. Two _runner coroutines in the same event loop cannot interleave inside one synchronous claim_pending_tasks call — the SELECT+UPDATE+commit runs to completion before the loop yields — so within a single process the claims are effectively serialized at that call boundary and will NOT double-claim via plain async interleaving. (The two POSTs are real waste — two engines both draining the same job, redundant fetches/flushes are still possible via separate engine buffers — but the core PENDING->RUNNING double-claim is not triggered purely in-process.)

The genuinely reachable trigger, which I reproduced, is the CROSS-PROCESS race the claim also lists: the standalone `awareness-worker` process running concurrently with the API/CLI against the same SQLite file. Separate processes = separate engines/connections, so their deferred read transactions overlap and both claim the same rows.

Suggested fix is sound but note self._lock alone is insufficient because it is per-process (it would not help the cross-process case that actually triggers this). The robust fix must be at the DB level: a single atomic UPDATE...WHERE status='pending' (with a LIMIT-by-subquery of ids for SQLite, or RETURNING on Postgres/DuckDB), and/or open the claim transaction with BEGIN IMMEDIATE / SERIALIZABLE; plus a job-already-RUNNING guard on /backfill/{job_id}/run. Counters should also be clamped (or made idempotent per task) so a future regression can't push tasks_completed past tasks_total.

verifiedBugs.title: run_job marks job COMPLETED on graceful stop even with PENDING/RUNNING tasks remaining (lost progress)
verifiedBugs.description: The main loop is `while not self.is_stopping():`. When request_stop() is called (e.g. SIGINT via workers/main.py:36-43, or any external stop), the loop exits immediately and falls into the finally block. Lines 224-229 then set the job to COMPLETED if its status is not already CANCELLED/COMPLETED/FAILED — regardless of whether PENDING tasks are still unprocessed or whether tasks were interrupted mid-flight. There is no check that all work actually finished.
verifiedBugs.impact: A Ctrl-C / SIGTERM during a backfill prematurely marks the job COMPLETED. Because workers/main.py:51 only resumes jobs in pending/running/paused state, a falsely-COMPLETED job is never resumed, so the remaining tasks (and their would-be documents) are permanently lost. This silently produces a near-empty corpus after any interrupted run.
verifiedBugs.repro: Start a long backfill with `awareness-worker run` (or CLI run), press Ctrl-C after the first batch. Job status becomes COMPLETED with tasks_completed < tasks_total. Re-running `awareness-worker run` does not pick the job back up.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Only set COMPLETED when the loop exited because work was genuinely drained (empty_polls threshold reached) AND not self.is_stopping(). On stop, leave the job in RUNNING/PAUSED (or a dedicated INTERRUPTED state) so it can be resumed.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed real and user-affecting. The defect is the conflation of two distinct loop-exit reasons in run_job's finally block.

EXIT PATHS into the finally (engine.py:219): (a) queue genuinely drained — loop exits because `empty_polls >= 3` (line 212-213) while `is_stopping()` is still False; (b) graceful stop — `request_stop()` sets `_stop_event`, so `while not self.is_stopping()` (line 198) is false at the next iteration boundary. Both fall into the SAME finally.

The finally (engine.py:223-229) re-reads the job and, if its status is not already CANCELLED/COMPLETED/FAILED, unconditionally calls `set_job_status(job_id, COMPLETED)`. There is NO `is_stopping()` guard and NO check that PENDING/RUNNING tasks are drained. So a stop with unprocessed tasks marks the job COMPLETED.

The stop is cooperative: on SIGINT/SIGTERM/ENTER/`/stop`, `_stop()` -> `request_stop()` fires (cli/main.py:1216-1221, 1236, 1271; workers/main.py:36-43). The in-flight `asyncio.gather` of claimed tasks finishes (or is short-circuited via `context.is_stopping`, engine.py:320), then the loop re-checks line 198 and exits. For any backfill with more partitions than one batch (claim limit = concurrency*2, line 209), this leaves rows still PENDING — and additionally leaves interrupted tasks in RUNNING (claim_pending_tasks set them RUNNING at state.py:432, and nothing ever resets stale RUNNING back to PENDING; no requeue path exists in state.py).

The job is then COMPLETED with tasks_completed < tasks_total. Resume is blocked: `awareness-worker run` only re-drives jobs whose status is in {pending, running, paused} (workers/main.py:51), and I found no other entry point that re-arms a COMPLETED job's leftover PENDING tasks. The CLI run path's post-run code (cli/main.py:1294) is read-only and does not correct the status. So the remaining work is silently abandoned under a falsely-successful COMPLETED status.

The cited file/lines are accurate (loop at 198; finally COMPLETED logic at 223-229, specifically the set at 229). The drained-queue path that also hits the same finally is correct behavior; the bug is purely that the stop path is not distinguished.

Skeptical checks that did NOT refute it: (1) No mid-flight or post-loop guard re-sets the status to a resumable state. (2) The PAUSED branch (203-207) and CANCELLED/FAILED short-circuits (201-202) are unrelated — a plain stop hits neither and reaches the COMPLETED set. (3) Data rows are not physically deleted, but no supported flow resumes them, so it is effectively lost progress with an incorrect terminal status.
verdict.correction: Real, root cause and lines as claimed. Two minor refinements to the report: (1) Interrupted tasks are left in RUNNING (not reset to PENDING) in addition to the still-PENDING tasks, because claim_pending_tasks marks claimed rows RUNNING (state.py:432) and there is no stale-RUNNING requeue; even if the COMPLETED bug were fixed, those RUNNING rows would also need re-arming on resume (claim_pending_tasks only selects PENDING, state.py:425). (2) The 'near-empty corpus' wording is an overstatement — documents from already-completed batches are persisted/flushed; the real harm is a falsely-COMPLETED job with tasks_completed < tasks_total whose remaining work is unresumable via any supported entry point. Suggested fix is correct: in the finally, only set COMPLETED when the loop drained the queue (empty_polls threshold) AND not self.is_stopping(); on stop, leave the job RUNNING/PAUSED (or a dedicated INTERRUPTED state) and reset interrupted RUNNING tasks to PENDING so resume picks them up.

verifiedBugs.title: Tasks stuck in RUNNING after a crash/stop are never reset to PENDING (permanent loss)
verifiedBugs.description: claim_pending_tasks moves tasks PENDING→RUNNING and increments attempts. If the process crashes or is stopped while a task is RUNNING, nothing ever transitions it back. I grepped the whole storage/workers/planner layer: there is no reaper, no stale-RUNNING reset, no heartbeat/lease timeout. claim_pending_tasks only selects status='pending', so orphaned RUNNING rows are never re-claimed.
verifiedBugs.impact: Any crash, OOM, or stop mid-task strands those tasks in RUNNING forever. On restart the job cannot make progress on them, so their documents are never ingested. Combined with the premature-COMPLETED bug, an interrupted ingest leaves a partially- or near-empty corpus that no resume can repair — matching the user's 'has no idea how to scrape the internet' and near-empty search results.
verifiedBugs.repro: Claim tasks, kill -9 the worker mid-batch, restart `awareness-worker run`. The previously-RUNNING tasks remain RUNNING and are never processed.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Add a recovery step (in init/run_job startup or a periodic reaper) that resets tasks in RUNNING with started_at older than a lease timeout back to PENDING, respecting max_retries. Use a lease/heartbeat column to distinguish live vs. orphaned RUNNING tasks.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed real after tracing the full task lifecycle and grepping the entire storage/workers/planner/tail/cli/api layer. claim_pending_tasks (state.py:420-436) is the ONLY RUNNING transition; it commits RUNNING + attempts++ before any work runs. The only exits from RUNNING are complete_task (state.py:438) and fail_task (state.py:460), both invoked in-process inside _run_task (engine.py:300-414). A kill -9 / OOM / hard stop between claim and completion leaves the row permanently RUNNING. On restart, workers/main.py:24-59 calls state.init() (only create_all + a dedup_near migration, state.py:194-211) and then run_job, whose poll loops (engine.py:198-217, 277-289) ONLY call claim_pending_tasks which selects status==PENDING. Exhaustive grep confirms the only RUNNING->PENDING transitions are fail_task retry (state.py:476) and add_tasks rearm-by-partition-key (state.py:362). There is no reaper, no lease/heartbeat, no started_at-based stale reset. The list_running_tasks query (state.py:506) is read-only (used only by api/server.py:274 for display). So orphaned RUNNING rows are genuinely never re-claimed.
verdict.correction: The core mechanism in the claim is correct, but the blast radius needs refinement so a fix targets the right cases. (1) BACKFILL jobs are the unambiguous, permanent-loss case: submit_backfill (planner.py:42) runs once with a fresh uuid job_id and adds tasks once; the planner is NOT re-run on restart, so nothing re-adds those partition keys and the add_tasks rearm never fires for them. RUNNING orphans are stranded forever, AND the poll loop terminates on empty_polls>=3 (engine.py:212) then marks the job COMPLETED (engine.py:223-229) even with RUNNING orphans remaining — silent partial-corpus loss that compounds with the premature-COMPLETED bug. (2) The claim's tail framing is partly wrong: tail SEED discovery rows (rss:/atom:/sitemap:/gdelt:gkg:slot) DO self-heal, because the reseed loop (tail/engine.py:123-198) re-adds those exact partition keys every tail_poll_seconds and add_tasks rearm resets a RUNNING orphan to PENDING. (3) Tail tail_recrawl per-URL sub-partition rows (enqueued via enqueue_subpartitions during discovery) are NOT re-added by the reseed loop and only recover if that exact URL is rediscovered (not guaranteed). Severity adjusted from the implied 'entire corpus lost forever' to high: per-crash orphan count is bounded by in-flight concurrency (claim limit = _concurrency*2, engine.py:209/288), not the whole job, and tail discovery self-heals — but for backfill the loss is real, silent, and unrepairable by resume. The suggested fix (startup/periodic reset of RUNNING rows older than a lease timeout back to PENDING, respecting max_retries, ideally via a started_at/lease check) is appropriate.

verifiedBugs.title: Discovery adapters yield nothing and all fetch/HTTP failures are swallowed — silent empty ingest
verifiedBugs.description: Discovery adapters (feeds.py:90, gdelt.py:118, cc_index.py, commoncrawl_wet.py) deliberately return without yielding any DocCapture; they only enqueue TAIL_RECRAWL sub-partitions via context.extras['enqueue']. The whole corpus therefore depends on the sub-partition fetch (tail_recrawl) succeeding. But tail_recrawl.run_partition returns early and silently on virtually every failure mode: non-public URL (line 60), no domain (line 64), robots disallow (line 78), HTTP error (line 95), status>=400 or empty body (line 100), non-text content-type (line 104), and text-too-short (line 110) — each just increments a metric and returns with zero captures. In the worker, _run_task treats a zero-yield run as success (complete_task, docs_emitted=0) with no warning. If discovery returns 0 URLs (e.g. feed fetch returned [] on any non-200, feeds.py:100-101) or every fetch is filtered, the job completes 'successfully' with an empty corpus and no surfaced error.
verifiedBugs.impact: The ingestion pipeline can run to COMPLETED while producing zero documents, with no error visible to the user — exactly the reported 'the app has no idea how to scrape the internet' / near-empty corpus. Network problems, wrong User-Agent, robots blocks, or an empty/misconfigured seed file all manifest as silent success rather than a diagnosable failure.
verifiedBugs.repro: Run a tail or backfill where the seed feeds 404 or the network is restricted: feeds._read_feed returns [] (line 101), no sub-partitions are enqueued, the discovery task completes with docs_emitted=0, the job reports COMPLETED, and search returns nothing. No error is logged at the task level.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Distinguish 'discovered N URLs / enqueued N sub-partitions' from 'yielded 0 captures' and log a warning when a discovery task enqueues 0 sub-partitions or when a job completes with 0 docs emitted. Surface fetch-failure metrics/counts to the CLI/API status so empty results are explainable, not silent.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL, but the claim overstates "no error visible" and one swallow site. The code structure is accurate:

1. Discovery adapters are pure enqueuers. feeds.py:90 and gdelt.py:118 both `return` with no yield; they only push TAIL_RECRAWL sub-partitions into context.extras['enqueue']. So all actual document yielding happens in tail_recrawl.

2. feeds._read_feed (feeds.py:100-101): `if r.status_code != 200 or not r.content: return []` — a 404/403/500 feed yields [] with NO log (only the httpx.HTTPError branch at 103-105 logs a warning). This is genuinely silent. With [] URLs, no sub-partitions are enqueued, and the discovery task completes with docs_emitted=0.

3. tail_recrawl.run_partition early-returns on: non-public URL (60-61, metric), no domain (63-64, NO metric/log at all), robots disallow (76-78, metric), HTTP error (92-95, warning log + metric), status>=400/empty body (98-100, metric), non-text content-type (102-104, NO metric/log), text-too-short (108-110, metric). Each returns zero captures.

4. workers/engine.py _run_task (332-414): a zero-yield async-for falls straight through to complete_task(docs_emitted=0)/increment_job_counters(completed=1) with NO warning. run_job (line 229) then sets job status COMPLETED unconditionally (only skipped if already CANCELLED/FAILED). So an empty corpus + empty seed/blocked network/wrong UA all manifest as a 'successful' COMPLETED job.

CORRECTIONS to the claim:
- "no error visible to the user" is overstated: docs_emitted (=0) IS rendered in the CLI status table ('Unique Documents Ingested', cli/main.py:1186) and in job listings. The user can see 0; it is just never flagged as anomalous. So the defect is 'no warning/no surfaced error', not 'completely invisible'.
- "No error is logged at the task level" is wrong for the HTTP-fetch-error case: tail_recrawl.py:93 logs tail_fetch_failed (warning) and increments tail.fetch_errors. The truly silent sites are feeds.py:101 (feed non-200), tail_recrawl.py:64 (no domain), and tail_recrawl.py:104 (content-type filter).
- This is an observability/diagnosability defect, not a correctness/data-integrity bug: the pipeline behaves as designed (it filtered/discovered nothing). Notably the same engine DOES warn on analogous silent conditions (workers/engine.py:435 all_destinations_disabled, :473 gdrive unauthorized), so the absence of any zero-discovery/zero-docs warning is a genuine inconsistency, supporting that this is an oversight rather than intentional.

User impact is real and matches the reported 'app has no idea how to scrape' / near-empty corpus symptom: empty/misconfigured seeds, restricted networks, wrong User-Agent, or robots blocks all complete 'successfully' with an unexplained empty result. The suggested fix (warn when a discovery task enqueues 0 sub-partitions, and when a job completes with docs_emitted==0; surface fetch-failure metric counts to status) is appropriate. Severity downgraded high→medium: no data corruption or crash, and the zero count is at least visible in status even though unflagged.
verdict.correction: Real, but root cause is an observability/no-warning gap rather than a correctness bug, and two sub-claims are inaccurate: (1) docs_emitted=0 IS shown in CLI status (cli/main.py:1186), so it is unflagged rather than invisible; (2) HTTP fetch errors ARE logged at the task level (tail_recrawl.py:93 tail_fetch_failed + tail.fetch_errors metric). The genuinely-silent paths are feeds.py:101 (feed non-200 returns [] with no log), tail_recrawl.py:64 (no-domain return, no metric/log), and tail_recrawl.py:104 (content-type filter, no metric/log), plus the worker/job layers never warning on 0 enqueued sub-partitions or 0 docs_emitted before setting COMPLETED (engine.py:229). Fix as suggested. Severity medium, not high.

verifiedBugs.title: Default search restricts results to the last 30 days, silently hiding most of the corpus
verifiedBugs.description: The search command defaults `--start` to '30 days ago' and `--end` to 'now' (lines 2595-2596). These are passed to idx.search(start=start_dt, end=end_dt), and DuckDbIndex.search applies them as hard WHERE filters `fetch_ts >= $start` and `fetch_ts <= $end` (duckdb_index.py:439-444) on BOTH the FTS and prefix paths. I confirmed to_utc('30 days ago') resolves to a real cutoff (~2026-05-09 for today). Any capture with fetch_ts older than 30 days — or with a NULL/unparseable fetch_ts (TRY_CAST yields NULL, and `NULL >= start` is false) — is excluded.
verifiedBugs.impact: `awareness search bitcoin` only returns documents fetched in the trailing 30 days; everything older is invisible, and any row whose fetch_ts failed to cast is dropped entirely. This directly explains 'searching bitcoin returned only 2 results' and 'search is broken/janky' — the corpus is silently date-windowed and NULL-timestamp rows vanish.
verifiedBugs.repro: Ingest documents, wait/backdate beyond 30 days (or have rows with non-castable fetch_ts), run `awareness search <term>`. Only recent, well-timestamped rows appear; total is far lower than the true corpus. Passing `--start '10 years ago'` recovers the missing results, proving the window is the cause.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Default `--start` to None (no lower bound) for search, or make the date filter opt-in. Also treat NULL fetch_ts rows as passing the range filter (e.g. `(fetch_ts IS NULL OR fetch_ts >= $start)`) so untimestamped captures remain searchable.
