verdict.reasoning: Confirmed against source. The CLI `search` command defaults `--start` to "30 days ago" and `--end` to "now" (src/awareness/cli/main.py:2595-2596). These flow into `to_utc(start)` / `coerce_relative_end(end)` (main.py:2629-2630); I executed the helpers and verified to_utc('30 days ago') resolves to a real ~30-day-back cutoff (e.g. 2026-05-09 for today 2026-06-08), and 'now' resolves to current time. Both values are passed as start=/end= to DuckDbIndex.search, where base_filters() appends hard WHERE clauses `fetch_ts >= $start` and `fetch_ts <= $end` (storage/duckdb_index.py:439-444). These filters are applied on BOTH the FTS/ranked path (where_sql injected at line 463/470) and the prefix/substring path (line 496/516), so no search mode escapes the window. Both the non-interactive (main.py:2632-2644) and interactive (main.py:2673-2684) branches use the same start_dt/end_dt. The decisive corroboration: the HTTP API search endpoint (api/server.py:429-430) defaults start/end to None (unbounded), passing None through to search so no date filter is built — proving the date window is meant to be opt-in and the CLI's "30 days ago" default is an inconsistent, almost-certainly-unintended anomaly, not a deliberate global design. Net effect: `awareness search bitcoin` silently returns only documents fetched in the trailing 30 days; everything older is invisible with no warning, which plausibly explains the user-reported 'only 2 results' / 'search is broken' symptom on a corpus containing older captures. This is a genuine correctness/usability defect in the primary user-facing search path, not a style nit and not handled elsewhere. The secondary NULL-fetch_ts claim is weaker and largely theoretical: DocCapture.fetch_ts is a required non-optional datetime (schemas/doc.py:96), the Iceberg schema marks it required=True/nullable=False (storage/iceberg_schema.py:44,87), and every ingest source falls back to utcnow() when the source date is missing (local_fixture.py:70, warc_repair.py:121, fineweb.py:145 all use `... or utcnow()`), so validly-ingested rows should not have NULL fetch_ts. TRY_CAST yielding NULL on a corrupt stored string is possible but an edge case, not the main driver; in SQL such a row (NULL >= start = unknown) would indeed be dropped, but that is secondary to the real root cause.
verdict.correction: Real bug, root cause is exactly the 30-day default window on the CLI `search` command (main.py:2595-2596) applied as a hard fetch_ts range filter in duckdb_index.py:439-444. Severity is high (not critical): it silently hides most of the corpus from the main CLI search with no user-visible indication, but data is not lost and the HTTP API search path is unaffected (it defaults start/end to None). Two corrections to the claim's secondary points: (1) The NULL/unparseable-fetch_ts angle is largely theoretical — fetch_ts is a required schema field with a utcnow() fallback at every ingest source and a non-nullable Iceberg column, so NULL rows should not arise in normal operation; the window default alone explains the symptom. (2) The suggested workaround `--start '10 years ago'` only 'works' by accident: to_utc() does not parse 'years ago' (only the 'days ago' branch), so it returns None and thereby drops the lower bound. A literal like '3650 days ago' would be the correct manual workaround; 'N years ago' silently degrades to no-lower-bound rather than computing a real date. Recommended fix: default the CLI --start to None (opt-in date filtering, matching the API), and optionally make the range filter treat NULL fetch_ts as passing via `(fetch_ts IS NULL OR fetch_ts >= $start)` for defense-in-depth.

verifiedBugs.title: tail/engine.py uses undefined JobStatus on the --job-id resume path (NameError crashes tail start)
verifiedBugs.description: In TailEngine.start(), when a job_id is supplied (the resume / reuse path), the else branch runs `self._state.set_job_status(job_id, JobStatus.RUNNING)` and `self._state.set_tail(...)`. But JobStatus is never imported in this module. AST and bytecode inspection confirm: the module's imported names are {Any, Path, Planner, SourceKind, StateDB, TaskState, WorkerEngine, ...} with NO JobStatus, and start.__code__.co_names references the global 'JobStatus' which is absent. Python resolves JobStatus as a module global at runtime and raises NameError. The CLI exposes `--job-id` (cli/main.py:1330 `job_id: str = typer.Option(None, '--job-id', ...)`) and passes it straight through (cli/main.py:1488 `job_id=job_id`). The job_id=None default path goes through planner.submit_tail() and works; only the explicit-job_id branch is broken.
verifiedBugs.impact: Running `awareness tail start --job-id <existing>` (the documented resume flow — the module docstring says 'on restart, start() is called again with the same seeds') crashes immediately with NameError before any seeding or scraping begins. The user trying to resume live capture gets a hard failure and zero ingestion, contributing to 'the app has no idea how to scrape the internet'.
verifiedBugs.repro: From the CLI: `awareness tail start --job-id tail-abc123` (any non-empty job id). start() takes the else branch at line 107 and raises `NameError: name 'JobStatus' is not defined`. Reproduced statically: `python -c "import awareness.tail.engine as te; print(hasattr(te,'JobStatus'))"` prints False, and `te.TailEngine.start.__code__.co_names` includes 'JobStatus'.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Import JobStatus in tail/engine.py: `from awareness.schemas.jobs import JobKind, JobStatus, TaskState` (JobStatus is defined in awareness/schemas/jobs.py). Also re-seed the initial feed/sitemap discovery tasks in this branch (submit_tail seeds them for the None path, but the resume branch only flips status and never enqueues feed tasks, so even after fixing the import the resumed job would have no initial seeds until the first reseed tick).

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed real and user-affecting via static and runtime evidence against the actual module.

ROOT CAUSE: /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/tail/engine.py line 108 in TailEngine.start() uses JobStatus.RUNNING, but the module never imports JobStatus. Line 29 imports only `from awareness.schemas.jobs import TaskState`. No module-level or function-local import of JobStatus exists anywhere in the file.

RUNTIME PROOF (ran the real module through the project's .venv with PYTHONPATH=src): `hasattr(te, 'JobStatus')` is False and `'JobStatus' in TailEngine.start.__code__.co_names` is True. So `JobStatus` is referenced as a module global that does not exist; Python raises `NameError: name 'JobStatus' is not defined` when the else-branch executes (also reproduced the literal statement in a matching namespace -> NameError).

USER REACHABILITY: CLI cli/main.py:1330 defines `--job-id` (typer.Option(None)); cli/main.py:1488 passes `job_id=job_id` straight to tail.start() with no intervening validation (lines 1334-1488 only validate --match-field and --gdelt-max-urls). When job_id is None (default) start() takes the `if` branch -> planner.submit_tail() (no JobStatus) and works; only an explicit non-empty --job-id takes the `else` branch and crashes. set_job_status's signature (state.py:256) does expect a JobStatus, so the call site is otherwise correct — only the import is missing.

NO COVERAGE: The only test touching tail + job_id (tests/smoke/test_tail_lifecycle.py) drives WorkerEngine directly and merely sets job_id on TaskState objects; it never calls TailEngine.start(job_id=<non-None>). The else branch is entirely untested, which explains why the NameError went unnoticed.

The claimed lines (107-109), file, repro, and suggested import fix are all accurate. The secondary observation in suggested_fix is also correct: the resume else-branch only flips status + set_tail and never enqueues the initial feed/sitemap/atom seed tasks (unlike submit_tail), so even after the import fix a resumed job would have no initial seeds until the first reseed_loop tick (tail_poll_seconds later) — a real but lesser latency issue, not a crash.

SEVERITY: high (not critical) — it is a deterministic hard crash on the documented resume/--job-id flow, but the default `awareness tail start` (job_id=None) path is unaffected and works, so it does not break the primary tail-start happy path.
verdict.correction: Claim is correct as written. Primary defect: missing `JobStatus` import in tail/engine.py causes NameError at line 108 on the explicit --job-id resume path. Fix: `from awareness.schemas.jobs import JobKind, JobStatus, TaskState` (verified JobStatus is defined in schemas/jobs.py:27 and imports cleanly). The default job_id=None path is unaffected. The claim's note that the resume branch also fails to re-seed initial discovery tasks is accurate and worth addressing alongside the import fix, but it is secondary to the crash.

verifiedBugs.title: Live tail (and WARC repair) call html_to_text without min_chars/max_chars, silently ignoring text_min_chars/text_max_chars config
verifiedBugs.description: tail_recrawl.py:107 calls `html_to_text(html, url=url)` and warc_repair.py:114 calls `html_to_text(html, url=target)` — neither passes min_chars/max_chars. So these paths use the hardcoded defaults in html_to_text (min_chars=200, max_chars=1_500_000) instead of settings.text_min_chars / settings.text_max_chars. The body adapters do it correctly: fineweb.py:138-139 and commoncrawl_wet.py:315-316 pass `min_chars=settings.text_min_chars, max_chars=settings.text_max_chars`. Because the tail recrawl is the PRIMARY live-scraping path (RSS/Atom/sitemap -> tail_recrawl), the user's main ingestion route does not honor the documented 'Corpus filters' knobs.
verifiedBugs.impact: A user who sets text_min_chars (e.g. raises it to keep only substantial articles, or lowers it to capture short posts) sees no effect on live tail capture — the setting is silently ignored. This is a 'config that silently does nothing' bug. With the default value (200 == 200) it is invisible, which makes it easy to ship and hard to notice, but any non-default value breaks the user's expectation and can over- or under-filter the live corpus.
verifiedBugs.repro: Set `text_min_chars: 1000` in configs/awareness.yaml, run tail capture; pages between 200 and 1000 chars are still ingested because html_to_text uses its 200 default. Grep confirms tail_recrawl/warc_repair omit the kwargs while fineweb/commoncrawl pass them.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: In tail_recrawl.run_partition and warc_repair, fetch settings (already done in tail_recrawl) and call `html_to_text(html, url=url, min_chars=settings.text_min_chars, max_chars=settings.text_max_chars)` to match the body adapters.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified the claim against source. tail_recrawl.py:107 (`html_to_text(html, url=url)`) and warc_repair.py:114 (`html_to_text(html, url=target)`) both omit min_chars/max_chars, so html_to_text uses its hardcoded defaults (min_chars=200, max_chars=1_500_000 at html.py:52-53) and forwards them to normalize_text (html.py:82). By contrast the body adapters explicitly pass the config: fineweb.py:138-139 and commoncrawl_wet.py:315-316 use min_chars=settings.text_min_chars, max_chars=settings.text_max_chars.

The config knobs are real and user-facing: settings.py:99-100 define text_min_chars=200 / text_max_chars=1_500_000; config/schema.py:161-170 documents them under the "Corpus filters" group ("Drop documents whose extracted text is shorter/longer than this"); configs/awareness.yaml:19-20 exposes them. So they are advertised as the corpus length filter.

I attempted to refute by looking for a downstream stage that re-applies the filter to captured docs: there is no filters/ directory, and grep shows no pipeline/writer/engine code re-applying text_min_chars/text_max_chars or char-length filtering to DocCapture. The length filter is enforced ONLY at each adapter's normalize_text call site. Therefore on the tail and WARC-repair paths the config genuinely has no effect — a true "config that silently does nothing" bug, not handled elsewhere.

Impact is real but bounded: with default values (200 == 200) it is invisible; only a non-default text_min_chars/text_max_chars is silently ignored. tail_recrawl IS the primary live path — feeds.py (RSS/Atom/Sitemap) emits TAIL_RECRAWL sub-partitions (feeds.py:9,12,81) that tail_recrawl fetches — so a user who raises text_min_chars to keep only substantial articles, or lowers it to capture short posts, sees no effect on live capture. No crash, no data corruption; failure mode is over/under-filtering of the live corpus, which is recoverable. Hence medium severity is correct (not high).
verdict.correction: Real bug, correctly located. One inaccuracy in the suggested fix: it claims settings are "already done in tail_recrawl" — true for tail_recrawl (settings = get_settings() at line 66, so the one-line fix at line 107 is straightforward). But warc_repair does the extraction inside _parse_warc_record, a synchronous helper executed via run_in_executor that does NOT fetch settings; the fix there requires fetching settings in run_partition and threading text_min_chars/text_max_chars through the already-long _parse_warc_record parameter list (or calling get_settings() inside it). The claim glosses over this, but the underlying bug at both sites is valid.

verifiedBugs.title: Feeds checkpoint dedup uses arbitrary set ordering when truncating to 5000, breaking cross-poll dedup
verifiedBugs.description: The seen_urls cursor is rebuilt as `merged = last_seen | {canonical_url(u) ...}` (a set), then stored as `list(list(merged)[-5000:])`. `merged` is a Python set, so `list(merged)` has arbitrary, non-insertion order. Taking the last 5000 of an unordered list does NOT keep the 5000 most-recently-seen URLs — it keeps an arbitrary 5000. Worse, the slice is non-deterministic across runs (set iteration order depends on hash seeding/insertion history). When a feed's distinct-URL count exceeds 5000, URLs that should remain remembered can be dropped arbitrarily and then re-emitted as 'new' on the next poll, causing re-fetch churn; and even under 5000 there is no correctness benefit because order is meaningless. The map's note that 'older URLs re-enter new_urls' is real, but the root cause is using a set (not an ordered structure) for an order-sensitive bound.
verifiedBugs.impact: Duplicate re-fetching of feed URLs across polling intervals (wasted fetches, duplicate captures flowing through dedup), and unstable resume behavior. On busy feeds/sitemaps this re-fetch churn wastes politeness budget and pollutes metrics, and makes the 'NEW vs DUP' terminal output noisy/incorrect.
verifiedBugs.repro: Feed with >5000 distinct URLs across two polls: after the first poll, `list(set(...))[-5000:]` retains an arbitrary subset; the second poll re-flags the dropped ones as new and re-enqueues tail_recrawl sub-partitions for them.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Preserve insertion order and bound by recency: keep seen_urls as an ordered list (e.g. dedup with dict.fromkeys to preserve order), append newly-seen canonical URLs in feed order, then keep the last N: `ordered = list(dict.fromkeys([*last_seen_list, *new_canon])); context.checkpoint['seen_urls'] = ordered[-5000:]`. Do not round-trip through an unordered set before slicing.

verdict.reasoning:
The mechanical defect is real and verified. In /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/sources/feeds.py:74-75 the cursor is rebuilt as `merged = last_seen | {canonical_url(u) ...}` (a set) then stored as `list(list(merged)[-5000:])`. `list(set)` yields arbitrary, hash-seed-dependent order, so `[-5000:]` keeps an ARBITRARY 5000, not the most-recently-seen 5000, and is non-deterministic across runs. The checkpoint is genuinely persisted/restored cross-poll: complete_task (engine.py:404 -> state.py:456) writes checkpoint_json, and each re-poll restores it via get_last_task_checkpoint(partition_key) (engine.py:309-311), with the reseed loop (tail/engine.py:134-190) re-emitting the same RSS/sitemap partition every tail_poll_seconds. I simulated the logic: a stable feed with 6000 distinct URLs re-flags ~1000 URLs as 'new' every poll; an UNCHANGED 5000-URL feed re-flags ~2463 as 'new' once the union exceeds 5000. So the cursor correctness, recency-retention, and determinism are all genuinely broken, and the claimed root cause (unordered set used for an order-sensitive bound) and suggested dict.fromkeys fix are both correct.

BUT the claimed user-facing IMPACT is substantially overstated and mostly mitigated downstream, which is why this is low, not medium. The feeds adapter emits each recrawl with a stable partition_key `tail:{canonical_url(u)}` (feeds.py:82). When a spuriously-'new' URL is re-enqueued, planner.enqueue_subpartitions -> state.add_tasks hits the guard at state.py:347-358, which EXPLICITLY skips (`continue`) a TAIL_RECRAWL task whose partition_key already exists and is COMPLETED, with a comment stating the purpose is to avoid 'a redundant network re-fetch before dedup can fold it.' A tail_recrawl that fetched nothing (HTTP error/robots/short text) still falls through to complete_task as COMPLETED (engine.py:333-405, no yield -> still completes), so it too is permanently suppressed. Net result: the headline impacts — duplicate re-fetching, wasted fetches/politeness budget, duplicate captures flowing through dedup, polluted tail.fetches metrics, and noisy/incorrect NEW-vs-DUP terminal output (which is driven only by tail_recrawl DocCaptures, engine.py:356-380) — do NOT actually occur for any URL already fetched to COMPLETED. The only residual real costs are: (1) a redundant PartitionSpec build + one DB (job_id, partition_key) lookup per re-emitted URL per poll, (2) genuine re-fetch only in the narrow case where the prior tail_recrawl ended FAILED/DEAD_LETTERED via the exception path (engine.py:383-389), and (3) a permanently churny, non-deterministic seen_urls cursor. Real correctness bug worth fixing, but the expensive consequences are defended at state.py.
verdict.correction: Real bug, but impact is overstated. The dedup-cursor logic at feeds.py:74-75 is genuinely incorrect (arbitrary, non-recency, non-deterministic truncation via list(set)[-5000:]) and the suggested ordered-dedup fix is right. However, the primary claimed impacts (re-fetch churn, wasted politeness budget, duplicate captures through dedup, noisy/incorrect NEW-vs-DUP terminal output, polluted tail.fetches metrics) are PREVENTED by the COMPLETED tail_recrawl skip guard at /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/storage/state.py:347-358 combined with the stable partition_key `tail:{canonical_url(u)}` at feeds.py:82. Spuriously re-flagged URLs that were already fetched are skipped before any network fetch or capture. Residual cost is limited to per-poll PartitionSpec/DB-lookup overhead, a non-deterministic cursor, and real re-fetches only in the narrow FAILED/DEAD_LETTERED prior-task case. Severity should be low, not medium.

verifiedBugs.title: coerce_relative_end does not accept 'N days ago' even though to_utc does, causing asymmetric date parsing failures
verifiedBugs.description: to_utc() accepts relative literals 'now', 'today', and 'N days ago' (lines 21-29). coerce_relative_end() — used to coerce CLI/API backfill end markers — only special-cases 'now'/'today' (lines 72-74) and otherwise hands the string to dateutil.parser.parse, which raises ParserError on '3 days ago'. So a backfill end of '3 days ago' (a natural value a user would try, given to_utc supports it) raises ValueError/ParserError instead of resolving. Confirmed: `coerce_relative_end('3 days ago')` raises `ParserError: Unknown string format: 3 days ago` while `to_utc('3 days ago')` returns a valid datetime.
verifiedBugs.impact: A backfill request using a human relative end like '3 days ago' (and likely the symmetric start) fails to plan with a confusing parser error, even though the codebase advertises relative-time support elsewhere. Inconsistent, surprising failure for a plausible CLI input.
verifiedBugs.repro: `python -c "from awareness.util.timeutil import coerce_relative_end as c; c('3 days ago')"` raises ParserError; `to_utc('3 days ago')` succeeds.
verifiedBugs.suggested_fix: Route coerce_relative_end through to_utc (which already handles 'now'/'today'/'N days ago' and naive/aware datetimes), or add the same 'days ago' branch. e.g. `dt = to_utc(end); if dt is None: raise ValueError(...); return dt`.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct execution against the actual module (PYTHONPATH=src, project .venv): `coerce_relative_end('3 days ago')` raises `dateutil.parser.ParserError: Unknown string format: 3 days ago`, while `to_utc('3 days ago')` returns a valid datetime (2026-06-05...). The asymmetry is genuine and not handled anywhere else: coerce_relative_end (timeutil.py:67-77) only special-cases 'now'/'today' (lines 73-74) then hands the raw string to _dateutil_parser.parse (line 75), which has no 'N days ago' branch and no fallback — unlike to_utc (lines 23-29) which explicitly handles `s.endswith('days ago')`.

The claim is real and, if anything, understated. The most compelling user-facing vector is not backfill but the `search`, `browse`, and `audit` CLI commands (main.py:2595, 2460, and the query command at ~1630). In `search` and `browse`, `--start` *defaults* to the literal string "30 days ago" and is parsed via `to_utc` (works), while the paired `--end` is parsed via `coerce_relative_end`. A user who mirrors the start syntax — e.g. `awareness search "x" --start "30 days ago" --end "3 days ago"` — triggers an UNCAUGHT ParserError. These CLI call sites wrap nothing in try/except around coerce_relative_end (main.py:1644, 2476, 2630), so the failure surfaces as a raw Python traceback, not a clean BadParameter/error message. So it is a real correctness + UX defect on plausible, by-example-advertised input.

Not a style nit, not already-handled-elsewhere: verified the only relative-handling branch is now/today; no caller normalizes 'days ago' before calling coerce_relative_end (CLI passes raw typer option strings; API server.py:149 passes body.end_str which is user-supplied). Suggested fix (route through to_utc, raising ValueError when it returns None) is correct.
verdict.correction: Real bug; root cause as described (coerce_relative_end lacks the 'days ago' branch that to_utc has). Correction to emphasis/severity: the claim frames the impact mainly on `backfill` end, but `backfill submit --end` help text only advertises "(ISO, yyyy-mm-dd, or 'now')" so a user is less likely to try 'days ago' there. The stronger, more user-affecting vector the claim misses is the `search`/`browse`/`audit` commands whose `--start` option DEFAULTS to the literal "30 days ago" (parsed fine by to_utc), making a symmetric `--end "N days ago"` a very natural input that crashes with an uncaught ParserError traceback. Severity raised from 'low' to 'medium' because it produces an uncaught traceback (not a graceful error) on input the start-side syntax actively invites, across multiple commands — though it is not hit on default invocations (default --end is 'now', which works), which keeps it below high.

rejectedBugs.title: FineWeb (a default backfill source) is a complete silent no-op because the optional `datasets` package is not installed
rejectedBugs.description: plan() and run_partition() both `try: import datasets / from datasets import load_dataset` and on ImportError just log at INFO level and return [] / return (yielding nothing). I confirmed `datasets` is NOT importable in this project's venv (`.venv/bin/python -c 'import datasets'` → ModuleNotFoundError). FineWeb is one of the three DEFAULT backfill sources selected by the planner (planner.py:57-61: WET, FINEWEB, GDELT) when the user specifies no sources.
rejectedBugs.impact: In the default configuration, an entire one-third of the backfill sources (FineWeb/FineWeb2) silently contributes zero documents and zero tasks. The only signal is an INFO log line 'fineweb_skipped_missing_datasets_lib'. The user running a normal backfill has no idea a whole high-volume source produced nothing. Combined with the broken crawl-id bug above (which also breaks FineWeb's `name=dump`), FineWeb yields nothing even if `datasets` were installed.
rejectedBugs.repro: .venv/bin/python -c 'import datasets' → ModuleNotFoundError. Then a default `submit_backfill` plans WET+FINEWEB+GDELT; FineWeb.plan() returns [] with only an INFO log.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Make `datasets` a hard dependency for the FineWeb adapter (or fail registration loudly so registry.get returns None and produces a visible 'no_adapter' error). At minimum, surface a WARNING/metric counter when a default source is skipped due to a missing dependency so the user sees it. Also add `datasets` to pyproject dependencies if FineWeb is meant to be a default source.

verdict.reasoning:
The factual observations are correct but the "high-severity bug" framing is refuted. The no-op-when-datasets-absent behavior is intentional, documented design, not a missing/forgotten dependency.

Verified:
1. datasets is NOT importable in the venv (confirmed: ModuleNotFoundError).
2. FineWeb IS a default backfill source — planner/planner.py:55-61 sets defaults {COMMON_CRAWL_WET, FINEWEB, GDELT} when request.sources is empty. (Claim cited the wrong path "planner.py:57-61"; the real file is src/awareness/planner/planner.py.)
3. fineweb.py plan() (lines 57-61) and run_partition() (lines 94-98) both swallow ImportError and no-op with only an INFO log.

Why this is NOT a bug:
- datasets is an EXPLICIT optional dependency, not a missing hard dep: pyproject.toml:45-46 declares `[project.optional-dependencies] hf = ["datasets>=2.20", "huggingface-hub>=0.23"]`.
- The behavior is documented as intentional in the module docstring (fineweb.py:4-7): "The `datasets` package is optional; if it's not installed, plan() returns an empty list ... and the adapter becomes a no-op. This keeps the dependency surface lean for users who just want the WET + tail path."
- There is a dedicated troubleshooting entry: docs/troubleshooting.md:52-58 "FineWeb adapter is a no-op — It only activates when the `datasets` package is installed: uv pip install -e '.[hf]'".
- README.md:246-247 documents `uv pip install -e '.[hf]'` as the optional HuggingFace install.
- Registration is NOT broken: FineWebAdapter.__init__ does not import datasets, so base.py:104-126 registers it fine and registry.get(FINEWEB) returns a valid adapter. The suggested-fix idea of "fail registration loudly" does not match how the import is deliberately deferred to plan()/run_partition().

The only legitimate (minor) sub-point: the docstring says the no-op happens "with a warning," but the code logs at INFO level ("fineweb_skipped_missing_datasets_lib"), not WARNING. This is a doc/log-level inconsistency and a weak observability signal, not a correctness defect — the default WET + GDELT sources still produce documents, and the missing FineWeb data path is fully documented. The claim's cross-reference to a separate "broken crawl-id bug" is out of scope for this file and not substantiated here.

Net: real observation, false bug. At most a low-severity UX/observability nit (bump the skip log from INFO to WARNING and/or add a metric counter), not the claimed high-severity silent data-loss defect.
verdict.correction: False as framed. The datasets dependency is intentionally optional (pyproject.toml:46 `hf` extra), the no-op is documented intended behavior (fineweb.py:4-7 docstring; docs/troubleshooting.md:52-58; README.md:246-247), and the adapter still registers correctly. The only valid, minor improvement is observability: the skip is logged at INFO ("fineweb_skipped_missing_datasets_lib") while the docstring promises "a warning" — bump it to WARNING and/or emit a metric so users notice the default source is inactive. Also note the claim's file path for the planner is wrong: it is src/awareness/planner/planner.py:55-61, not planner.py:57-61. Downgrade from high to low.

rejectedBugs.title: CC-Index CDX url filter uses '*.{domain}/*' which is not valid CDX wildcard syntax and likely returns zero matches
rejectedBugs.description: plan() builds `url_filter = f'*.{dom}/*'` and run_partition queries the CDX server with params {url: '*.example.com/*', output: 'json'} and no matchType. The Common Crawl/pywb CDX API supports a leading host wildcard via matchType=domain (or url=*.example.com) OR a trailing path wildcard (url=example.com/*), but a combined leading-and-trailing wildcard '*.example.com/*' is not a documented/supported pattern and the CDX server typically interprets it as an exact (non-matching) literal, returning an empty result set. The adapter then logs nothing useful, increments cc_index.matches by 0, and enqueues no WARC sub-partitions.
rejectedBugs.impact: If the pattern is rejected/empty, domain-narrowed CDX discovery yields zero URLs and zero WARC-repair sub-partitions, so the targeted full-fidelity (WARC/HTML) path discovers nothing — silently. Marked low confidence because I could not run a live CDX query to confirm the server's exact handling of this pattern.
rejectedBugs.repro: Query https://index.commoncrawl.org/CC-MAIN-2025-43-index?url=*.example.com/*&output=json and observe whether any rows return; the combined wildcard is non-standard.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Use the documented form: pass `url=example.com` with `matchType=domain` (covers domain + all subdomains), or `url=*.example.com`. Validate against a known-good domain and assert a non-empty result in tests. Also emit a metric/warning when a CDX query returns 0 rows so silent empties are visible.

verdict.reasoning:
The claim's central technical assertion is empirically false. I ran the exact query the adapter constructs against the live Common Crawl CDX server and it works correctly.

Adapter behavior (src/awareness/sources/cc_index.py):
- plan() line 51 builds url_filter = f"*.{dom}/*" (e.g. "*.example.com/*")
- run_partition() lines 67-68 issue GET https://index.commoncrawl.org/<crawl_id>-index with params {"url": "*.example.com/*", "output": "json", "limit": ...} and no matchType.

Live verification against CC-MAIN-2025-43-index:
- url="*.example.com/*" -> HTTP 200, returned valid JSON rows (not empty, not an error literal).
- Each returned row contains url, filename, offset, and length — exactly the fields the adapter reads at lines 100-118 to enqueue COMMON_CRAWL_WARC sub-partitions. So the WARC-repair enqueue path works.
- Results cover example.com, www.example.com, http and https — i.e. the leading host wildcard DOES expand to subdomains as intended.
- I also confirmed "*.example.com", "example.com", and "example.com/*" all return 200 with rows; the combined "*.example.com/*" form is handled identically by the pywb CDX server, which strips the leading/trailing wildcards and applies a host+path wildcard match.

The claim states the server "typically interprets it as an exact (non-matching) literal, returning an empty result set." That is directly contradicted by the live 200/non-empty response. The claim itself is marked low confidence precisely because the author "could not run a live CDX query to confirm" — and the live query disproves the hypothesis.

The only fragment of the claim with any merit is the observability aside: line 95 increments cc_index.matches by len(records) and nothing logs a warning when a query legitimately returns 0 rows. That is a minor logging/observability nit, not the asserted bug, and does not affect correctness of the wildcard query. The suggested_fix (switch to matchType=domain) would change behavior only marginally and is unnecessary; the current pattern is functional.

Verdict: the alleged bug (invalid wildcard syntax causing silent zero-result domain-narrowed discovery) does not exist. The code discovers URLs and enqueues WARC partitions correctly.
verdict.correction: False. The pattern "*.example.com/*" is accepted by the Common Crawl pywb CDX server and returns valid, non-empty JSON results with filename/offset/length fields, which the adapter correctly uses to enqueue WARC sub-partitions (cc_index.py lines 95-118). Verified live against CC-MAIN-2025-43-index: HTTP 200, 10 rows, covering example.com + www subdomain, http + https. The claimed "non-standard combined wildcard returns zero matches" premise is empirically wrong (the claim was self-described as low-confidence because it was never tested against a live server). The only residual, much weaker point is purely observability: there is no warning emitted when a CDX query genuinely returns 0 rows (line 95 only bumps the metric). That is a minor enhancement, not a correctness bug, and the suggested matchType=domain rewrite is not required.

rejectedBugs.title: add_near_dup_index uses s.merge() which cannot dedup on the (doc_id, seg) unique constraint, raising IntegrityError that crashes the worker task and loses its buffered captures
rejectedBugs.lines: 639-661 (write); UniqueConstraint at 127; consumed via dedup/engine.py:95,104 and workers/engine.py:340-390
rejectedBugs.description: DedupNearRow has an autoincrement integer PRIMARY KEY (id) plus a separate UniqueConstraint('doc_id','seg'). SQLAlchemy Session.merge() matches existing rows ONLY by PRIMARY KEY. Because add_near_dup_index() never sets `id`, every merged DedupNearRow is treated as a brand-new transient row and SQLAlchemy issues an INSERT. If the same doc_id is indexed a second time, the 16 INSERTs collide with the (doc_id, seg) UNIQUE index and SQLite/Postgres raise IntegrityError (verified empirically: re-calling add_near_dup_index('docA', sig) raises `sqlite3.IntegrityError: UNIQUE constraint failed: dedup_near.doc_id, dedup_near.seg`). The function's own docstring/usage implies it should be idempotent (it is also called on the NEAR_DUP path at engine.py:95), but merge() gives upsert semantics ONLY when matching on the PK, which it never does here. In the common single-pass engine flow a given doc_id reaches add_near_dup_index at most once (a re-seen URL+content short-circuits to REVISION at engine.py:64 before re-indexing), but the bug is reachable when: (a) a task is retried/re-yields the same doc_id after a partial run, (b) two partitions in the same job discover the same canonical URL+content (same doc_id) and the content_hash commit interleaves, or (c) any future index-rebuild re-invokes the method. Because evaluate() is called inside the worker's try block (workers/engine.py:340), the IntegrityError propagates to the except at engine.py:383, marks the whole task failed/dead-lettered, and the captures already appended to _batch_buffer for that task are not flushed (data loss for the partition).
rejectedBugs.impact: A worker task can crash with IntegrityError instead of completing; the task is failed/dead-lettered and its in-flight captures are dropped from durable storage. Manifests as intermittently missing documents (contributes to 'few search results') and DLQ entries, with no recovery because the same retry hits the same collision.
rejectedBugs.repro: from awareness.storage.state import StateDB; from awareness.util.hashing import simhash128; db=StateDB('sqlite:///tmp.db'); db.init(); s=simhash128('a b c d e f g h i j k l'); db.add_near_dup_index('docA', s); db.add_near_dup_index('docA', s)  # -> raises sqlite3.IntegrityError: UNIQUE constraint failed: dedup_near.doc_id, dedup_near.seg
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Make the write a true upsert keyed on (doc_id, seg). Either (1) delete existing rows for the doc_id first within the same session (DELETE FROM dedup_near WHERE doc_id=:doc_id) before inserting the 16 band rows, or (2) use a dialect upsert (sqlite/postgres INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(doc_id, seg) DO UPDATE SET sig_hex=..., seg_value=..., near_dup_hash=...), or (3) guard the whole block in a try/except IntegrityError that rolls back and treats it as a no-op (already indexed). Do not rely on Session.merge() for a non-PK unique key.

verdict.reasoning:
The MECHANISM is verified true: DedupNearRow has an autoincrement integer PK (state.py:121) plus a separate UniqueConstraint('doc_id','seg') (state.py:127). add_near_dup_index (state.py:639-661) uses s.merge() without ever setting `id`, so SQLAlchemy treats each row as a new transient object and issues INSERT. I reproduced the claimed error exactly: calling db.add_near_dup_index('docA', sig) twice raises `sqlite3.IntegrityError: UNIQUE constraint failed: dedup_near.doc_id, dedup_near.seg`. merge() does not give upsert semantics for a non-PK unique key. That part of the claim is correct.

However, the bug is NOT reachable in the current architecture, so it is not user-affecting today:

1. Gated callers only. add_near_dup_index has exactly two callers, both in dedup/engine.py (lines 95 and 104), and BOTH sit inside the `was_new` branch. evaluate() step 1 calls upsert_dedup(content_hash, doc_id); if the content_hash was seen before it returns was_new=False and short-circuits to REVISION/EXACT_DUP (engine.py:64-77) WITHOUT re-indexing. doc_id is deterministic from canonical_url+content_hash (doc.py:8), so any second occurrence of the same doc_id necessarily has the same content_hash, which upsert_dedup (committed durably in its own session at state.py:633/636) reports as was_new=False. Therefore the same doc_id can reach add_near_dup_index at most once. The claim itself concedes this for the single-pass flow.

2. Scenario (a) retry does NOT trigger it. On non-dead-letter failure, fail_task sets the task back to PENDING (state.py:476); the retry re-yields docs, but the DedupRow rows committed before the failure are durable, so each re-seen doc short-circuits before add_near_dup_index. No collision.

3. Scenario (b) intra-process race is impossible. evaluate() is fully synchronous — dedup/engine.py contains zero await/async/yield — and is called un-awaited at workers/engine.py:340 inside an asyncio worker pool. With a single event loop, no other coroutine can interleave between upsert_dedup's commit and add_near_dup_index. A cross-connection TOCTOU race would require multiple worker PROCESSES on a shared Postgres, but docs/architecture.md:156 marks multi-process workers as a 'future' capability; the current topology is one process / pool of asyncio workers.

4. Scenario (c) index-rebuild caller does not exist in the codebase (grep confirms only the two engine.py callers).

5. Impact is overstated. _batch_buffer (workers/engine.py:95) is a SHARED worker-wide buffer, not per-task. On the except/return at engine.py:383 the buffer is NOT cleared, and is flushed by the next _flush(force=False) in the outer run loop (engine.py:218/293) and the final _flush(force=True) (engine.py:297). So even if the IntegrityError fired, already-buffered captures would not be lost.

Conclusion: real latent code smell (merge() misused for a non-PK unique key; not idempotent as the docstring implies), worth fixing defensively, but no present code path reaches it and the stated user impact (DLQ entries, dropped captures, 'few search results') does not occur in the shipped single-process architecture. Downgrading from high to low.
verdict.correction: Real mechanism, but FALSE as a high-severity user-affecting bug. The empirical repro is genuine (second add_near_dup_index for the same doc_id raises UNIQUE constraint IntegrityError because s.merge() matches only the autoincrement PK, never the (doc_id,seg) unique key). But it is unreachable in the current codebase: add_near_dup_index is only invoked when upsert_dedup returns was_new=True (engine.py:95,104), and since doc_id is deterministic from content_hash and upsert_dedup commits the DedupRow durably first, any re-seen doc_id short-circuits to REVISION/EXACT_DUP before re-indexing. The intra-process concurrency race (scenario b) cannot happen because evaluate() is fully synchronous (no await/yield) under a single asyncio event loop; multi-process workers are explicitly 'future' (docs/architecture.md:156). Scenario (c) index-rebuild caller does not exist. The data-loss impact is also wrong: _batch_buffer is a shared worker-wide buffer flushed by the outer run loop (engine.py:218/293/297), not a per-task buffer dropped on failure. Recommend keeping the suggested fix (true upsert keyed on (doc_id,seg), or DELETE-then-insert, or ON CONFLICT) as low-priority hardening before any multi-process worker or index-rebuild feature lands, not as a high-severity bug.

rejectedBugs.title: Iceberg view read sets unsafe_enable_version_guessing=true, can read inconsistent/stale snapshots
rejectedBugs.description: Before creating `iceberg_captures_raw` via `iceberg_scan('{table_path}')`, the code runs `SET unsafe_enable_version_guessing = true;` (line 207). This tells DuckDB's Iceberg reader to guess the latest metadata version rather than resolving it strictly via the catalog's `version-hint`/metadata pointer. If the warehouse has multiple metadata.json files or a stale/partial one, version guessing can pick a different snapshot than the catalog's current pointer, so search may read an inconsistent or stale view of the Iceberg corpus (different from what writers committed). This is a deliberate safety bypass to avoid setup friction, but it trades correctness for convenience.
rejectedBugs.impact: Search results over the Iceberg-backed corpus may reflect a stale or inconsistent snapshot (missing the latest committed captures, or reading data from a superseded metadata version), contributing to 'search seems to miss things'. Low likelihood in the single-writer local default, higher with concurrent writers or after failed commits.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Prefer resolving the current metadata file from the SqlCatalog (load_table().metadata_location) and point `iceberg_scan` at that exact metadata.json, rather than enabling version guessing. If guessing must stay for compatibility, gate it behind config and log the resolved snapshot id so drift is observable.
rejectedBugs.repro: With >1 metadata.json in data/iceberg/awareness/captures/metadata (e.g. after several appends or a failed commit), iceberg_scan under version guessing may bind to a non-current snapshot; the captures count via DuckDbIndex can differ from the catalog's current snapshot count.

verdict.reasoning:
Empirically refuted as a behavior/correctness bug. The cited line at /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py:207 (`SET unsafe_enable_version_guessing = true`) is load-bearing, not a removable convenience bypass.

Verified facts:
1. The writer (src/awareness/storage/iceberg.py:121) uses PyIceberg's SqlCatalog, which does NOT emit a `version-hint.text` file. The real on-disk warehouse confirms this: data/iceberg/awareness/captures/metadata/ contains only one `00000-...metadata.json` and NO `version-hint.text`. The authoritative current pointer lives in data/iceberg/catalog.sqlite (iceberg_tables.metadata_location).
2. I ran DuckDB 1.5.3 iceberg_scan against the actual warehouse path. With guessing OFF (the state the claim implies is safer), iceberg_scan FAILS with "No version was provided and no version-hint could be found ... globbing ... is disabled by default" and returns zero rows. With guessing ON (the code path), it succeeds. So the flagged SET is REQUIRED for Iceberg search to function at all with this catalog; removing it breaks Iceberg-backed search entirely rather than making it safer.
3. The claim's stale/inconsistent-snapshot risk does not hold under this codebase's documented mode. PyIceberg writes monotonically-prefixed metadata files (00000-, 00001-, ...); DuckDB guessing picks the lexicographically-latest, which equals the newest committed version. The repro (a higher-numbered-but-stale metadata.json from a failed commit fooling the guesser) isn't produced by PyIceberg's single-writer append path used here (JSONL-first, RLock-guarded append, single local writer per iceberg.py:8-9,157-162). No mechanism in this code creates an orphaned higher-numbered metadata file.

The suggested fix is technically valid and would be a strict improvement: I confirmed iceberg_scan accepts a direct metadata.json path with guessing off, and the catalog row exposes the exact metadata_location. So resolving via SqlCatalog.load_table().metadata_location and scanning that exact file would make reads deterministic and observable. But that is a hardening/determinism improvement, not a fix for a currently-broken behavior. Under the actual default deployment, guessing resolves to exactly the current snapshot, and the alleged 'search misses things' impact is speculative and unreproduced.

Verdict: false as a correctness bug. The mechanism described is accurate (globbing-based version resolution), but it is necessary given the chosen catalog, and the user-affecting harm is not reachable in the documented single-writer local mode. Best classified as a low-priority robustness/observability enhancement, not a bug.
verdict.correction: False as a bug: the SET is not a gratuitous safety bypass but a hard requirement. PyIceberg's SqlCatalog (iceberg.py:121) writes no version-hint.text, and the empirical test shows iceberg_scan(table_path) errors out and returns nothing without version guessing. Removing the flagged line would break Iceberg search, not protect it. The stale-snapshot scenario in the repro is not produced by this single-writer, JSONL-first, monotonically-numbered-metadata append flow. The real, accurate kernel of the claim is the suggested improvement: resolve the current metadata.json via the catalog's metadata_location (confirmed: iceberg_scan accepts a direct metadata.json path with guessing off) for deterministic, observable reads. That is a low-severity hardening item, not a behavioral/correctness defect.

rejectedBugs.title: Re-armed TAIL_RECRAWL task that is already COMPLETED is skipped with no log, silently dropping re-seen URLs
rejectedBugs.description: In `add_tasks`, when an existing task row matches (job_id, partition_key) and `existing.status == COMPLETED` and `t.source_type == TAIL_RECRAWL`, the code `continue`s — it neither re-arms nor inserts, and emits no log for that specific skip (only an aggregate 'tasks_rearmed' is logged later, which excludes these). This is intentional to avoid redundant re-fetch of an already-fetched URL, but because there is no per-skip signal, an operator cannot tell that a URL appearing again (e.g. the same article surfaced by a later GDELT/RSS poll) was deliberately dropped vs lost. Combined with the fact that dedup folding happens only after a fetch, a legitimately updated page at the same URL will never be re-fetched.
rejectedBugs.impact: Silently dropped re-crawl requests for URLs already fetched once: updated content at a previously-seen URL is never re-ingested, and there is no observability that this happened. Minor for static pages, but for changing pages it means the corpus goes stale without any signal.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Emit a debug/info log (or a counter) when a TAIL_RECRAWL row is skipped because it is already COMPLETED, including the partition_key, so the drop is observable. Optionally support an explicit force/refetch flag for updated content.
rejectedBugs.repro: add_tasks() a TAIL_RECRAWL task for URL X; let it complete; add_tasks() the same (job_id, 'tail:X') again -> the second add is silently skipped (returns 0 new, no per-URL log).

verdict.reasoning:
The cited code (state.py:354-358) does exactly what the claim describes: when an existing TaskRow matches (job_id, partition_key), its status is COMPLETED, and the new task's source_type is TAIL_RECRAWL, it `continue`s with no per-skip log or counter. The factual repro is accurate, and I confirmed there are no metrics counters anywhere in state.py and the only log in add_tasks is the aggregate `tasks_rearmed` (line 412), which by construction excludes these skips. So the description is technically correct.

However, this is NOT a bug — it is documented, intentional behavior with no correctness or behavioral breakage:

1. The code comment at lines 348-353 explicitly explains the design: one-shot per-URL tail_recrawl rows MUST NOT be re-armed once COMPLETED, precisely to avoid a redundant network re-fetch when overlapping GDELT/RSS slots re-surface the same URL. The claim's own text repeatedly concedes 'This is intentional.'

2. There is no correctness violation. Nothing is lost incorrectly: a URL already fetched is correctly suppressed, job counters stay consistent (the rollback logic at 395-409 only applies to genuinely re-armed rows), the `added` return value correctly reports 0 new rows, and no exception/corruption occurs. The de-dup is also content-aware: tail_recrawl.py:117 computes `doc_id_for(cu, ch)` where `ch` is a content hash, so the engine's identity model is content-based, not a promise of URL re-fetch.

3. The 'updated content at a same URL is never re-fetched' point is the documented design (reactive one-shot per-URL fetch), not a deviation from intended behavior, and the claim itself rates it 'Minor for static pages.'

4. The remaining substance — 'no per-skip log/counter' — is a pure observability/logging nicety. The suggested fix is literally 'emit a debug/info log.' That is a style/enhancement request, not a behavioral or correctness defect. An operator can already infer the skip from the aggregate (return value < input count).

This is a style/observability nit presented as a bug, with the author acknowledging the behavior is deliberate. It does not break behavior or correctness, so is_real is false.
verdict.correction: False positive (not a bug). The behavior at state.py:354-358 is intentional and documented (see the comment at lines 348-353): one-shot tail_recrawl rows are deliberately not re-armed once COMPLETED to avoid redundant network re-fetches of an already-fetched URL. There is no correctness break, no data loss, no state inconsistency, and no incorrect return value — only the absence of a per-skip log line, which is a minor observability/enhancement suggestion, not a defect. The 'stale corpus for changing pages' framing is the documented design intent (content-addressed via doc_id_for(cu, content_hash) in tail_recrawl.py:117), not a deviation from intended behavior. If anything, the suggested fix (add a debug log/counter on the skip path) is a reasonable nice-to-have, but it does not correct any broken behavior.

rejectedBugs.title: Empty-result search in non-interactive/piped mode is indistinguishable from success (no error, no nonzero exit)
rejectedBugs.description: In the non-interactive branch, a query that matches zero documents prints the 'Found 0 documents, showing top 0' header to stdout and returns normally (exit code 0). There is no message on stderr and no nonzero exit status. When `search` is used in a pipeline or script (`echo bitcoin | awareness search`), a zero-result run is byte-for-byte a 'successful but empty' run, so callers cannot detect 'no matches' programmatically, and the empty case is easy to miss visually.
rejectedBugs.impact: Scripts and pipelines cannot distinguish 'no matches' from 'matched but printed nothing', and a silent empty result reads as a broken search rather than a legitimate zero-hit. Compounds the perception that terminal search is unreliable.
rejectedBugs.repro: `echo zzzznotaword | awareness search --no-interactive; echo "exit=$?"` prints the empty header and `exit=0` with nothing on stderr.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: In the non-interactive branch, when `total == 0` print a clear 'No documents matched' line (to stderr) and exit nonzero (e.g. `raise typer.Exit(code=1)`), mirroring the interactive branch's explicit 'No documents matched' message.

verdict.reasoning:
The code description is factually accurate: in the non-interactive branch of `search` (src/awareness/cli/main.py:2632-2667), a zero-match query prints `Search Results for: '<q>' (Found 0 documents, showing top 0, Mode: ..., ...)` to stdout via rprint and returns with exit code 0, with nothing on stderr and no typer.Exit. I confirmed there is no stderr usage or Exit in that branch. But this is not a genuine bug:

1. Zero results is a legitimate SUCCESS outcome, not an error. Returning exit 0 with a clear count is standard, defensible CLI behavior. The existing test tests/unit/test_cli_commands.py:17-21 (test_search_non_interactive_empty_db) explicitly pins exit_code == 0 for an empty-DB search — so the suggested fix (raise typer.Exit(1)) would be a deliberate regression that breaks a codified expectation.

2. The claim's core impact ("byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a successful-but-empty run; callers can't detect no-matches") is FALSE: the header literally prints "Found 0 documents", and rows are only printed when present, so there is no "matched but printed nothing" ambiguity. A consumer can read the count.

3. The premise that `search` is a scripting/pipeline command is unsupported. It is a human-facing Rich TUI; --no-interactive emits colored Rich markup (bullets, decorative headers), not JSON/parseable output. There is no --json flag and no documented machine-readable contract anywhere in README/docs. The whole CLI deliberately routes all user output to stdout and reserves typer.Exit(1) for real error conditions only.

4. The repro is also broken: `query` is a REQUIRED positional argument, not read from stdin, so `echo bitcoin | awareness search` would error on a missing argument, not run a zero-result search.

This is at most a minor UX preference (a friendlier empty-result line could be nice), not a correctness or behavior defect.
verdict.correction: False / working-as-intended. The non-interactive empty-result behavior (exit 0, count printed to stdout) is intentional and is pinned by tests/unit/test_cli_commands.py:17-21. The output is NOT indistinguishable from a printed-nothing success — the header always shows the document count ("Found 0 documents"). `search` is a human-facing Rich TUI, not a documented scriptable/JSON command, and the entire CLI uses stdout-only output with typer.Exit(1) reserved for genuine errors. The repro is invalid because `query` is a required positional argument (cannot be piped via stdin). The suggested fix would regress an existing test and surprise users who correctly treat zero matches as success.

rejectedBugs.title: Every query endpoint opens a DuckDB connection that is never closed (resource leak)
rejectedBugs.description: All read endpoints (/inspect, /counts, /captures, /captures/{id}, /captures/{id}/related, /search) build a local DuckDbIndex and call .connect() (directly or via .execute()/.search()), but none of them call idx.close() and the object is not stored anywhere — it is dropped at end of request while still holding an open duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection (DuckDbIndex.close() at duckdb_index.py:568 is never invoked from the API). Each request therefore opens a new on-disk DuckDB connection and relies solely on GC/finalizer to release it.
rejectedBugs.impact: Under the SPA's continuous polling (refreshDashboard + refreshFeed every 5s, tail view every 2s, plus user searches) connections accumulate until GC runs. This leaks file handles/memory, multiplies the already-expensive view-refresh/FTS-rebuild work, and increases the window for the write-write conflict above. On constrained hosts this can exhaust file descriptors over a long session.
rejectedBugs.repro: Leave the dashboard open; observe a steady stream of new DuckDB connections opened (one per /captures poll) with no corresponding close, growing FD/memory until garbage collection.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Use a single shared DuckDbIndex (created in lifespan, closed on shutdown) instead of per-request instances, or wrap each per-request idx in try/finally that calls idx.close(). Sharing one instance also fixes the FTS-rebuild and write-write-conflict bugs.

verdict.reasoning:
The factual code observations are accurate: every read endpoint in /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/src/awareness/api/server.py (lines 289-293, 316-320, 345-349, 393-397, 413-419, 435-439) constructs a fresh per-request DuckDbIndex, calls .connect()/.execute()/.search() (which runs duckdb.connect at duckdb_index.py:86), and never calls idx.close(). I confirmed via grep that no idx.close() exists in server.py, DuckDbIndex has no __del__/weakref/finalize, and there is no process-level caching/sharing of the index in the API. The SPA does poll continuously (app.js: setInterval refreshDashboard/refreshFeed every 5000ms hitting /captures, tail view every 2000ms).

However, the claim's core thesis — a resource leak where connections "accumulate until GC runs," "leak file handles/memory," and can "exhaust file descriptors" — is empirically false. I reproduced the exact pattern against the project's own venv (duckdb 1.5.3, CPython 3.13):

1. No reliance on cyclic GC. The per-request idx is a plain local with no reference cycle, so CPython refcounting drops it to zero on endpoint return and the DuckDB connection's C++ destructor (__dealloc__) closes it synchronously. With gc.disable() entirely, 0 of 20 per-request connections survived after their function returned (weakref test confirmed the conn is dead immediately after `del`, no gc.collect needed). So "connections accumulate until GC runs" does not happen on CPython.

2. No FD growth / no FD-exhaustion risk. DuckDB shares a single OS file handle per database file per process. Holding 200 simultaneous open connections to the same db file showed exactly ONE lsof entry to the file. So even in an impossible worst case the per-request pattern cannot grow file descriptors.

Therefore the leak (file handles/memory until GC, FD exhaustion) is refuted. What remains real is a pure efficiency smell, not a leak: each request rebuilds the index and re-pays connect() setup (INSTALL/LOAD iceberg+fts, full _refresh_views), and the per-instance FTS-build cache state (_fts_built_for_count/_fts_built_signature) is thrown away every request, so /search can redo the COUNT/FTS-rebuild probe more than a shared instance would. That is a performance optimization opportunity (the suggested shared-lifespan-index fix is reasonable), but it does not break behavior or correctness and does not leak resources.
verdict.correction: False as a resource leak. The connections are NOT leaked: on CPython, refcounting closes each per-request DuckDB connection synchronously when the endpoint returns (no reference cycle, so cyclic GC is irrelevant — verified with gc.disable()). And DuckDB uses a single shared OS file handle per db-file per process (200 concurrent connections = 1 fd), so "leaks file handles" / "exhaust file descriptors" cannot occur for this pattern. The real, much smaller issue is efficiency: building a fresh DuckDbIndex per request re-pays connect() setup (extension install/load + _refresh_views) and discards the per-instance FTS-build cache, so the FTS rebuild/probe and view-refresh work is repeated more than necessary under polling. Recommend downgrading from a medium-severity resource leak to a low-severity per-request efficiency cleanup; the suggested shared-lifespan-index fix is still worthwhile, but as an optimization, not a leak fix.

rejectedBugs.title: auto search never falls back to broader matching once FTS returns any hit, and FTS only indexes title+text
rejectedBugs.description: In auto mode the prefix/substring fallback runs only `if not rows and (... or (mode=='auto' and total==0))` (line 495). So if FTS returns even a single hit (total>0), the broader stem-prefix path is skipped entirely. Compounding this, the FTS index is built over only title and text (PRAGMA create_fts_index('captures_idx','capture_id','title','text', ...) at line 349) and FTS is only taken when fields == the default ('title','text') (fts_eligible, line 455). Therefore documents whose only occurrence of the query is in the domain or url are invisible to auto search even though ALLOWED_SEARCH_FIELDS includes domain/url and prefix mode would find them. Also, BM25 will only ever return documents where the stemmed term appears in title/text, so a term present mostly in URLs/domains yields very few hits with no fallback.
rejectedBugs.impact: Searches return surprisingly few results (e.g. 'bitcoin returned only 2 results') when the term is sparse in title/text but common in URLs/domains, because auto stops at the small FTS result set and never broadens. The mode shown is 'BM25-ranked' so the user has no indication that a broader match was available.
rejectedBugs.repro: Index documents that mention 'bitcoin' only in the URL/domain (e.g. coindesk.com paths) plus a couple in body text; auto search for 'bitcoin' returns only the 2 body-text hits and never the URL/domain ones, with no fallback.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: In auto mode, when the default-field FTS result count is below the requested limit (or below a threshold), additionally run the prefix path over the full field set and merge/dedupe, or at least expose to the user that only title+text were ranked. Optionally include domain/url in the FTS corpus.

verdict.reasoning:
I read the cited code (src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py lines 320-560), the API caller (server.py:422-456), the SPA (web/app.js:285-328), config defaults, and the search tests, and ran the actual code against the venv duckdb to validate the repro.

The structural facts the claim cites are accurate: FTS is built over only title+text (line 349); auto's prefix fallback runs only `if not rows and (... or (mode=='auto' and total==0))` (line 495); and `fts_eligible` requires fields == DEFAULT_SEARCH_FIELDS (line 455). So once FTS returns ≥1 hit in default auto mode, the prefix path is skipped.

But the claim's headline impact — "documents whose only occurrence of the query is in domain or url are invisible to auto search ... even though prefix mode would find them" — is FALSE / mis-rooted. The reason domain/url-only docs aren't returned by default auto search is NOT the fallback-skip; it is that the default `fields` config is `title,text` (config/settings.py search_default_fields), which scopes BOTH the FTS path and the prefix path. I proved this empirically with the claim's own bitcoin repro (2 docs with bitcoin in body, 5 with bitcoin only in URL/domain):
  - default auto (fields=title,text): total=2, mode=fts
  - prefix with default fields=title,text: total=2  ← the prefix fallback ALSO misses the domain/url docs, directly refuting "prefix mode would find them"
  - auto with fields=title,text,domain,url: total=7, mode=prefix  ← domain/url docs ARE found when those fields are requested; auto routes straight to prefix because fts_eligible becomes False
So domain/url search already works via the documented `fields` parameter; the proposed fix (running the fallback over the full field set) would actually violate the documented field-scoping contract that test_auto_mode_honors_narrowed_fields / test_fields_restriction enforce.

The only genuinely real sub-behavior — that within title/text, stem-root substring matches BM25 misses (e.g. 'finance' query catching 'refinancing') aren't surfaced once FTS returns ≥1 hit — I also confirmed empirically (auto: total=1/mode=fts vs prefix: total=2). However this is explicitly documented intended design (module docstring line 39 and search() docstring lines 398-400: "FTS first; if it returns nothing, fall back to prefix") and is codified by a passing regression test, test_fts_still_ranks_when_term_present, which asserts mode=='fts' precisely when the term is present. It is an intentional precision-over-recall tradeoff for the FTS-first ranked path, with the prefix fallback existing only to recover zero-hit queries (the original 'finance returns nothing' regression), not to broaden non-empty result sets.

Net: structural facts correct, but the user-facing impact is misattributed (it's field-scoping config, not a fallback defect), the 'prefix would find them' premise is demonstrably false, and the remaining narrow behavior is documented-and-tested intended design. This is a recall/UX enhancement request framed as a bug, not a correctness defect.
verdict.correction: False as a bug. (1) Root cause mis-stated: domain/url-only documents are absent from default auto results because the default search field scope is title,text (config search_default_fields), which constrains BOTH FTS and the prefix fallback — NOT because the fallback is skipped. Empirically, prefix mode with default fields also returns only the 2 body-text hits, so the claim's "prefix mode would find them" is incorrect. (2) Domain/url matching is already supported: passing fields including domain/url makes fts_eligible False, routes auto to the field-aware prefix path, and returns all matches (7/7 in the repro). This is handled at duckdb_index.py:455,495-511 and asserted by tests test_auto_mode_honors_narrowed_fields and test_fields_restriction. (3) The one real behavior — auto not broadening to stem-root substring within title/text once FTS has any hit — is documented intended design (duckdb_index.py:39,398-400) and is locked in by the passing test test_fts_still_ranks_when_term_present (tests/unit/test_search_matching.py:81-86). At most this is a low-severity recall/UX enhancement (optionally surface that only title+text were BM25-ranked, or merge a capped prefix pass), not a correctness bug.

rejectedBugs.title: POST /backfill/{id}/run can launch concurrent workers for the same job (no in-flight guard)
rejectedBugs.description: run_backfill unconditionally creates a new WorkerEngine and asyncio.Task for the given job_id every time it is called; it never checks whether a task for that job_id is already running (the _State.background_tasks set is keyed by Task object, not job_id, and job status is not consulted). The SPA already auto-calls /run once after submit (app.js:590), but any second invocation (double-click, retry, command palette, a second client) starts a second worker over the same job's task queue.
rejectedBugs.impact: Two workers draining the same job's pending tasks concurrently can double-fetch the same partitions, inflating fetch volume, duplicating captures, doubling dedup work, and corrupting per-job task counters (tasks_completed can exceed tasks_total, breaking the progress bar math `100*tasks_completed/tasks_total`).
rejectedBugs.repro: POST /backfill/{id}/run twice in quick succession for a job with many pending tasks; observe two concurrent run loops and inflated/duplicated capture counts.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Guard on job state: before spawning, check the job's status (and/or a per-job-id in-flight registry) and return early (or 409) if a run is already active for that job_id. Track running jobs by job_id rather than by anonymous Task.

verdict.reasoning:
The literal observation is correct — run_backfill (server.py:175-190) creates a fresh WorkerEngine + asyncio.Task on every call and has no per-job_id in-flight guard. But the claimed IMPACT (double-fetched partitions, duplicated captures, doubled dedup work, tasks_completed > tasks_total) is REFUTED by the task-claiming design.

WHY IT'S NOT REAL:
1. Atomic task claiming. StateDB.claim_pending_tasks (state.py:420-436) selects PENDING rows, flips them to RUNNING, and commits in ONE fully synchronous SQLAlchemy block with no `await` inside. In the worker loop (engine.py:209) this is called as a plain synchronous call, not via to_thread/run_in_executor (those only wrap _flush's JSONL/Iceberg/GDrive writes at engine.py:445/459/491/519). Two POST /run calls in the same API process run their run_job loops on the same event loop; a synchronous function runs to completion before the loop can switch coroutines. So worker A flips tasks t1..tN to RUNNING and commits before worker B's claim runs; B then only sees the remaining PENDING rows. Each task is claimed by exactly one worker, and the two workers process DISJOINT task sets.
2. No double-fetch / no duplicate captures: a partition's task is executed once, so adapter.run_partition runs once for it.
3. No counter corruption: each task is completed once -> complete_task + increment_job_counters(completed=1) once. tasks_completed cannot exceed tasks_total from concurrent runs. The claim's specific "100*tasks_completed/tasks_total breaks" mechanism is false.
4. SPA reachability is overstated. app.js has exactly ONE /run call, auto-fired once after submit (line 590); the submit button is disabled during the request (line 572). There is no Run button, retry, or command palette that calls /run. A second concurrent /run requires a deliberate second/external client.

GENUINE-BUT-MINOR RESIDUAL (why low, not zero): If a second concurrent /run IS forced, (a) a redundant second WorkerEngine/JsonlStagingWriter is created — harmless because chunk filenames embed millisecond timestamp + uuid4 hex (jsonl.py _open_new), so no file clobbering; and (b) whichever worker drains its share and hits 3 empty polls first will, in its finally block (engine.py:223-229), set the job to COMPLETED slightly early while the other worker finishes an in-flight task. That is a cosmetic status/timestamp-timing nit; counts still reconcile because the in-flight task still completes and increments normally. This is a low-severity robustness gap, not the medium-severity data-corruption bug described.
verdict.correction: FALSE as stated. The double-run guard is effectively provided by atomic task claiming in StateDB.claim_pending_tasks (state.py:420-436), which runs synchronously on the single event loop and flips PENDING->RUNNING+commit before yielding — so two concurrent workers claim disjoint tasks. Therefore there is no double-fetch, no duplicate captures, and tasks_completed cannot exceed tasks_total. The cited harm/repro is not reproducible. The only real residual is a low-severity cosmetic robustness gap: with no guard, a forced second concurrent /run can flip the job to COMPLETED slightly early (engine.py:223-229) and spawn a redundant WorkerEngine (no data loss; JSONL chunk names are timestamp+uuid-unique). Severity should be downgraded from medium to low and the impact section rewritten — the suggested 409/in-flight guard is a reasonable hardening but fixes only the cosmetic early-COMPLETED/redundant-engine effects, not any data corruption.

rejectedBugs.title: FTS index reuse keyed on row COUNT can serve a stale index when count is unchanged
rejectedBugs.description: _ensure_fts decides whether to rebuild the FTS index using two short-circuits: (1) if _fts_built_signature == _views_signature it returns True without checking count; (2) otherwise it computes COUNT(*) and, if count == _fts_built_for_count, it adopts the current signature and returns True WITHOUT rebuilding. Two different corpora with the same row count (e.g. one chunk replaced/rotated by another of equal length, or rows added and others removed) keep the old materialized captures_idx and old FTS index, so newly-written documents are not in the searchable index even though the view 'captures' sees them.
rejectedBugs.impact: FTS (the default 'auto' ranked path) can return results from a stale index after the corpus changes without a net row-count change, yielding too-few or wrong-ranked results. This compounds the 'search is janky / bitcoin returns 2 results' symptom: the prefix fallback only runs when FTS returns 0, so a stale FTS index that returns a couple of old hits suppresses the more complete fallback.
rejectedBugs.repro: Build the FTS index, then rotate/replace JSONL chunks such that total row count is unchanged but content differs. Search a term present only in the new content: FTS misses it because captures_idx was never rebuilt (count matched).
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Key the FTS rebuild decision on the source-file signature (the same _views_signature used elsewhere), not on COUNT(*). Rebuild whenever the signature changed; drop the count-equality short-circuit or combine it with a content fingerprint.

verdict.reasoning:
The code description is accurate: `_ensure_fts` (src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py:330-332) does adopt the current `_views_signature` and return True WITHOUT rebuilding `captures_idx`/the FTS index whenever `count == _fts_built_for_count`, even if the source-file signature changed. Equating "row count unchanged" with "corpus unchanged" is logically weak. However, I cannot demonstrate this as a user-affecting bug in any real path, so the claim is refuted:

1. For the count short-circuit at line 330 to fire on a CHANGED corpus, the same in-memory `DuckDbIndex` object must survive across the corpus change (so `_fts_built_for_count` persists). But every actual search entrypoint constructs a FRESH `DuckDbIndex` per call:
   - API `/search` (api/server.py:435) builds a new `DuckDbIndex` per request. On a fresh instance `_fts_built_for_count = -1` and `_fts_built_signature = None`, so line 318 fails and line 330 (`count == -1`) can never match -> it ALWAYS rebuilds. The count short-circuit is effectively dead for the API path.
   - CLI `search` (cli/main.py:2616) builds a new `DuckDbIndex` per process invocation -> same, always rebuilds.

2. The bug is filed under "Workers / Tail / Planner (concurrency)", but grep confirms none of src/awareness/workers, /planner, or /tail use `DuckDbIndex` or `.search()` at all. The concurrency framing is inapplicable.

3. The only long-lived `DuckDbIndex` reuse is the TUI dashboard (cli/main.py:_make_tui_layout, refreshing every ~2s), but it calls only `idx.execute(...)`, never `idx.search()`, so it never reaches `_ensure_fts`. `execute()` uses `_refresh_views_if_stale`, which is correctly signature-keyed with no count short-circuit. The interactive CLI search loop (cli/main.py:2670) reuses one instance but only pages a single fixed query; it does not straddle a corpus mutation in practice.

4. The "constant count, changed content" precondition is itself hard to hit organically: JSONL staging is append-only and atomic (storage/jsonl.py; the live chunk is a `.jsonl.tmp` excluded by the `*.jsonl` glob). `capture_id` is hashed from `observed_ts` (util/hashing.py:161-164), so re-fetches produce NEW capture_ids and ADD rows (count goes UP -> rebuild triggers via line 330 inequality) rather than replacing at constant count. The dedup `captures` view (PARTITION BY capture_id) therefore doesn't yield a same-count content swap from normal ingestion. Committed chunks are never rewritten in place; the only deletion (workers/engine.py:512) is a whole-chunk unlink gated on `enable_jsonl_staging` being disabled (a count change, not an equal-count swap). The repro itself requires out-of-band file manipulation ("rotate/replace JSONL chunks such that total row count is unchanged"), which the running system never does to itself.

Net: a latent fragility/code-smell (count is a poor proxy for content; the correct content-aware key `_views_signature` is already computed and used everywhere else), but not an active, user-affecting bug. The claimed linkage to the 'bitcoin returns 2 results' symptom is unsubstantiated.
verdict.correction: Real-as-a-code-smell, false-as-a-bug. The count-equality short-circuit (duckdb_index.py:330-332) is dead/unreachable in the two actual search entrypoints because both the API server (per-request) and the CLI (per-process) create a FRESH DuckDbIndex whose `_fts_built_for_count` starts at -1, forcing a full FTS rebuild on the first/only `_ensure_fts` call. No code path reuses a single DuckDbIndex object for `.search()` across a corpus change at constant dedup'd row count; the TUI dashboard reuses an index but only calls `idx.execute` (no `_ensure_fts`). The 'Workers/Tail/Planner (concurrency)' subsystem doesn't use search at all. The suggested fix (key the FTS rebuild on `_views_signature` and drop the count short-circuit) is nonetheless the correct hardening to remove the latent fragility, and is cheap/low-risk to apply.

rejectedBugs.title: Reseed loop sleeps a full tail_poll_seconds BEFORE the first feed re-arm; only GDELT is seeded immediately
rejectedBugs.description: The module docstring promises start() 'seeds initial discovery partitions' and the reseed loop re-arms feeds every tail_poll_seconds. The initial feed/sitemap tasks ARE seeded once via planner.submit_tail() (only on the job_id=None path). But the reseed_loop calls `await asyncio.sleep(settings.tail_poll_seconds)` (line 136) at the TOP of the loop, before adding any tasks. So the SECOND batch of feed discovery does not happen until a full poll interval has elapsed, and on the resume/--job-id path (where submit_tail is not called) there is NO initial feed seeding at all — the first feeds are only fetched after a full tail_poll_seconds (default 60s) delay. GDELT, by contrast, is seeded immediately at lines 114-121. This asymmetry means feed-based capture has a cold-start gap and, on the resume path, depends entirely on the delayed reseed.
rejectedBugs.impact: On `tail start`, RSS/Atom/sitemap feeds only re-poll after the first 60s (default). On resume (--job-id), no feeds are fetched until the delayed reseed fires, so the user sees a long period of apparent inactivity ('I ran tail start and nothing happened'). Combined with the JobStatus NameError, the resume path captures nothing.
rejectedBugs.repro: Start tail and observe that feed reseed log 'tail_reseeded' only appears after tail_poll_seconds, while 'tail_gdelt_seeded' logs immediately. On the --job-id path, no feed tasks exist until the delayed reseed.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Emit the initial feed/atom/sitemap discovery tasks immediately in start() for ALL paths (extract the per-seed task-building into a helper and call it once before the loop, or move the sleep to the END of the loop body). Ensure the resume (--job-id) branch also enqueues the initial seed tasks.

verdict.reasoning:
The claim's PRIMARY thesis (its title, impact, and repro) is that the reseed loop's top-of-loop sleep causes a full tail_poll_seconds (60s default) cold-start delay before feeds are first fetched. This is FALSE / mis-framed:

(1) Fresh `tail start` (job_id=None) path: `planner.submit_tail(seeds)` (planner.py:106, body at lines 108-127) immediately enqueues the initial RSS/atom/sitemap tasks into the DB. The worker `run_tail` loop (workers/engine.py:231-292) calls `claim_pending_tasks` every `min(poll_seconds, 1.0)` seconds — at most ~1s — and `claim_pending_tasks` (storage/state.py:420-436) has NO time/schedule gate: any PENDING task is picked up and processed immediately. So the FIRST feed fetch happens within ~1s, not after 60s. The claim itself concedes "the initial feed/sitemap tasks ARE seeded once via planner.submit_tail()". The reseed loop's `await asyncio.sleep(settings.tail_poll_seconds)` at engine.py:136 only governs the RE-POLL cadence (re-emitting discovery to catch newly published items). Polling a feed every 60s is the intended, correct behavior — not a bug. So there is no cold-start gap on the fresh-start path, and the "delays first poll by full interval" framing is incorrect.

(2) Resume `--job-id` path: It is TRUE that this path captures no feeds, but NOT for the reason the claim gives ("depends entirely on the delayed reseed"). The actual cause is that the `else` branch at engine.py:107-109 executes `self._state.set_job_status(job_id, JobStatus.RUNNING)` while `JobStatus` is never imported in engine.py (only `TaskState` is imported from awareness.schemas.jobs at line 29; AST analysis confirms no `JobStatus` import and no star import). This raises `NameError: name 'JobStatus' is not defined`, crashing `start()` at line 108 — BEFORE the reseed loop (defined at 123, scheduled at 198) or worker loop (207) are ever created. So the resume path is broken by a NameError, and the reseed timing is irrelevant to it.
