This NameError is a genuine high-severity bug, but the claim only mentions it in passing as a secondary "Combined with" note and attributes the resume-path failure to the wrong root cause.

Verdict: As written, the claimed bug (reseed-loop timing causing a delayed-first-poll cold-start) is not a real defect — the first fetch is immediate via submit_tail, and the 60s sleep is the intended polling interval. The only genuinely broken behavior (resume path) has a different root cause (the JobStatus NameError) that this claim does not correctly identify.
verdict.correction: FALSE as framed. (a) The "delayed first poll / 60s cold-start" thesis is refuted: fresh `tail start` seeds initial feed tasks immediately via planner.submit_tail (planner.py:106-127) and the worker claims them within ~1s (workers/engine.py:288-291 + storage/state.py:420-436 has no time gate). The top-of-loop sleep at engine.py:136 is just the intended re-poll interval, not a bug. (b) The resume `--job-id` path IS broken, but the root cause is NOT the reseed timing — it is a NameError at engine.py:108 (`JobStatus` used but never imported; only TaskState is imported at line 29), which crashes start() before any loop is created. That separate NameError is the real high-severity defect; this ticket mis-attributes the symptom and over-states the timing issue.

rejectedBugs.title: detect_language swallows ALL exceptions via `except (ImportError, Exception)`, masking real langdetect errors
rejectedBugs.description: detect_language wraps the import+detect in `except (ImportError, Exception)` and returns None. `Exception` already subsumes `ImportError`, so the tuple is redundant, but more importantly it catches every error (including programming errors / unexpected runtime failures) and silently returns None, so a genuinely broken language-detection path is indistinguishable from 'language unknown'. langdetect is a hard dependency in pyproject.toml (langdetect>=1.0.9), yet in the current environment importing it fails — meaning EVERY capture gets language=None with no log line, no metric, and no signal that language detection is non-functional. This silently degrades the 'language' field across the whole corpus.
rejectedBugs.impact: All captures may carry language=None even when content is detectable, with zero observability. Downstream language filters/labels and the per-doc 'lang' shown in the terminal are wrong/empty, and operators cannot tell the feature is dead. Contributes to the general 'janky / silently dropped data' impression.
rejectedBugs.repro: In an env where langdetect import fails (current .venv), `detect_language('a'*200)` returns None with no log. The redundant except masks the ImportError entirely.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Catch the specific exceptions: `except ImportError: return None` and a separate `except Exception: logger.debug('langdetect_failed', ...); return None`, and emit a one-time warning/metric when langdetect is unavailable so the silent disablement is observable. Remove the redundant `(ImportError, Exception)` tuple.

verdict.reasoning:
The claim's central premise is factually false. I verified that langdetect-1.0.9 is installed in /Users/nazmi/Desktop/awareness/.venv and imports successfully. Running detect_language end-to-end (PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python) returns correct results: 'en' for English text, 'fr' for French, and None only for short (<80 char) or genuinely undetectable input (e.g. numeric-only). (b) The `except Exception` arm is intentional and load-bearing: langdetect.detect() raises LangDetectException, which I confirmed is a subclass of Exception (MRO checked), on undetectable input. So the only true parts are a cosmetic redundant-except and a missing debug log on a rarely-hit, by-design path — style/observability nits, not a behavioral or correctness bug. Not user-affecting.
verdict.correction: FALSE as a bug. The load-bearing assertion ("langdetect import fails in the current environment, so every capture gets language=None") is wrong: langdetect-1.0.9 is installed and detect_language returns correct codes (verified: 'en'/'fr'/None). The redundant `except (ImportError, Exception)` tuple is a genuine but cosmetic lint nit (B014) — behavior is identical to `except Exception`, which is intentionally needed because langdetect.detect() raises LangDetectException (an Exception subclass) on undetectable text, and the function's contract is explicitly best-effort returning None. None is the designed fallback at all call sites (`hint or detect_language(...)`). At most this warrants a trivial cleanup (drop the redundant ImportError, optionally add a one-time debug log) — not a correctness fix and not user-affecting.

rejectedBugs.title: iso() re-runs to_utc on an already-validated datetime with a dead-branch ternary
rejectedBugs.description: iso() returns `to_utc(dt).isoformat() if dt else None`. The `if dt else None` guard is dead because the function already returned None for dt is None at line 57; here dt is always a non-None datetime, so the ternary's else branch is unreachable. More notably, to_utc is invoked again to convert an already-tz-aware datetime, which for a naive datetime silently stamps UTC (potentially wrong if the caller intended a different zone) and for an aware datetime is an extra astimezone. This is a minor correctness/clarity smell rather than a hard failure, but the redundant guard suggests the author was unsure of the invariants, and naive datetimes are coerced to UTC without warning.
rejectedBugs.impact: Naive datetimes passed to iso() are silently assumed UTC (consistent with the rest of the module, but can mislabel timestamps if a naive local time ever reaches it). The dead branch is confusing for maintainers. Low real-world impact since most timestamps are already UTC-aware via the DocCapture validator.
rejectedBugs.repro: `iso(datetime(2024,1,1,12,0))` -> '2024-01-01T12:00:00+00:00' (naive treated as UTC). The ternary else is never taken.
rejectedBugs.suggested_fix: Simplify to `return to_utc(dt).isoformat()` (dt is guaranteed non-None here), or assert tz-awareness and call dt.astimezone(UTC).isoformat() directly to avoid silently stamping UTC onto naive inputs.

The claim's headline ("redundant double-utc-conversion", "re-runs to_utc on an already-validated datetime") is FALSE/misleading. `iso()` receives a raw `datetime` parameter that has NOT been previously validated or passed through `to_utc`. `to_utc` is called exactly ONCE — there is no double conversion. Most decisive refutation: `iso()` has ZERO callers anywhere — grep across src/ and tests/ finds no import or invocation, no __all__ export, no dynamic reference. It is dead/unused code, so no user can be affected. The single real defect (the dead `else None` branch) is an unreachable style smell inside an unused function.

This is a style/clarity nit, not a behavioral or correctness bug. The claim even self-rates as "low / minor smell rather than a hard failure." Per the skeptical bar (real ONLY if it actually breaks behavior or correctness, not a style nit), this does not qualify.

(1) The function's behavior is correct and verified: naive->UTC and aware->UTC conversions both produce the right result, consistent with the module's documented invariant ("All public timestamps are UTC tz-aware datetimes"). (2) The claim's central premise of a "double / redundant to_utc conversion" is wrong — iso() receives a raw datetime parameter that was never previously normalized, and to_utc is invoked exactly once; there is no prior validation to make it redundant. (3) The only genuine defect is the dead `else None` branch on line 58 (line 57 already handles dt is None), which is a pure cosmetic clarity nit with no behavioral effect. (4) Decisively, iso() has no callers anywhere in src/ or tests/ — it is unused/dead code, so it cannot affect any user. Suggested cleanup (still cosmetic-only): simplify line 58 to `return to_utc(dt).isoformat()`.

improvements.title: Discover real Common Crawl crawl IDs from collinfo.json instead of fabricating them by ISO week
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py (crawl_ids_for_range, _iso_year_weeks); src/awareness/sources/cc_index.py; src/awareness/sources/fineweb.py (all import crawl_ids_for_range)
improvements.current_state: crawl_ids_for_range() maps [start,end] to CC-MAIN-YYYY-WW by walking ISO weeks and snapping to odd weeks (~26 IDs/year). Common Crawl actually publishes ~12-17 crawls/year at irregular weeks, lags real time by 1-2 months, and uses non-uniform week numbers. For a default 'last 30 days' window in 2026 it emits e.g. CC-MAIN-2026-19/21/23 — none of which exist. Every wet.paths.gz GET 404s and _run_discovery silently returns, so backfills emit ~0 docs. This is the dominant cause of the 'no idea how to scrape' symptom. Verified empirically.
improvements.proposed: Fetch the authoritative crawl list once (https://index.commoncrawl.org/collinfo.json, a JSON array of {id, name, 'cdx-api', 'from', 'to'}) and cache it (TTL e.g. 12h on disk under data/cache). Implement crawl_ids_for_range(start,end) = [c['id'] for c in collinfo if intervals overlap [start,end]], parsing each crawl's actual from/to timestamps. If the window is empty (too recent), fall back to the N most-recent published crawls so a backfill is never silently empty. Keep a small hardcoded seed list as an offline fallback. Add a metric cc.crawls_resolved and WARN-log when 0 crawls overlap the requested window.
improvements.rationale: The crawl cadence is data, not a formula; deriving it analytically is fundamentally unsound because CC's schedule is irregular and lags. collinfo.json is the canonical source CC itself documents for this.
improvements.expected_impact: Backfill goes from ~0 documents to fetching real corpus shards. Directly fixes the primary scraping symptom. Also fixes FineWeb 'dump' alignment (same fabricated IDs are passed as the HF config name, currently guaranteeing load failures).

improvements.title: Surface empty/404 discovery instead of swallowing it (silent no-op guard)
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py (_run_discovery), cc_index.py (run_partition), gdelt.py, feeds.py, fineweb.py; src/awareness/workers/engine.py
improvements.current_state: Every adapter returns silently on HTTP non-200 or empty results (logger.warning then `return`). A task that discovers 0 URLs / fetches 0 shards still completes 'successfully' with docs_emitted=0. The job status shows tasks_completed rising while docs_emitted stays 0, so an operator sees green tasks and no data and concludes the app 'has no idea how to scrape'. Errors are logged at warning level but not aggregated into a user-visible signal.
improvements.proposed: Add a per-job health rollup: count discovery tasks that produced zero sub-partitions and fetch tasks that produced zero captures. When a job completes with docs_emitted==0 but tasks_total>0, set job notes/status to a distinct 'completed_empty' state and emit a metric ingest.empty_discovery{source_type}. In the CLI status/search 'no results' path, if the corpus row count is 0, print an actionable hint ('no documents ingested yet — run `awareness backfill` / check crawl availability'). Promote repeated 404s on wet.paths.gz/gkg to a single ERROR with the resolved URL.
improvements.rationale: Silent success on zero output is the worst failure mode for an ingestion engine; it is indistinguishable from working. Making emptiness loud converts a mysterious symptom into a diagnosable one.
improvements.expected_impact: Operator immediately sees why search returns nothing (empty corpus vs query issue). Cuts debugging time and prevents the 'broken everywhere' perception.

improvements.title: Fix BM25 search recall: drop the implicit 30-day window and always union the stem-prefix recall path
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py (search, auto path); src/awareness/cli/main.py (search defaults start='30 days ago')
improvements.current_state: Two compounding recall bugs. (1) The CLI search defaults to --start '30 days ago' and that fetch_ts filter is ANDed into the FTS query, so 'bitcoin' only matches docs captured in the last 30 days — for a mostly-backfilled corpus this silently hides almost everything, plausibly explaining 'bitcoin returned only 2 results'. (2) In `auto` mode, FTS runs first and if total>0 the stem-prefix fallback is NEVER taken, so morphological/compound variants the Snowball stemmer over-stems (e.g. possessives, 'bitcoins' vs 'bitcoin') are dropped whenever FTS finds even one hit. DuckDB match_bm25 is disjunctive by default (verified), so multi-word queries are not the issue — the window and the all-or-nothing fallback are.
improvements.proposed: (a) Default the CLI/API time window to None (all time) for search; keep --start/--end as opt-in filters. (b) In `auto` mode, compute FTS results AND the stem-prefix result set, then UNION by capture_id, ranking FTS hits by BM25 score first and appending prefix-only hits below (score NULL) — i.e. recall-complete with rank preservation, instead of FTS-or-prefix. Cap the union at max_results. (c) Expose match_bm25's `fields` and optional `conjunctive` args so a user can require all terms when desired.
improvements.rationale: Recall should never silently depend on a default date window, and a ranked engine should add the lexical-variant recall path, not gate it behind 'FTS found zero'. These are the concrete mechanics behind 'search is broken/janky'.
improvements.expected_impact: 'bitcoin' returns the full set of matching docs across the corpus rather than 2. Eliminates the most common 'janky search' surprises (date-window truncation + over-stemming).

improvements.title: Add field-boosted BM25F-style scoring (title weight) and length-aware ranking
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py (_ensure_fts, search FTS path)
improvements.current_state: FTS indexes title+text as one undifferentiated blob with default k1/b and no field weighting. A query term in the title ranks identically to one buried in a 50k-char body, and very long documents are not properly normalized relative to short ones beyond BM25's default b. There is no IDF-aware term boosting or title prior.
improvements.proposed: Move to a BM25F-style score: score = w_title*BM25(title-only index) + w_text*BM25(text index), with w_title≈3.0, w_text≈1.0, by building two FTS indexes (or scoring title and text separately via two match_bm25 calls) and summing. Tune DuckDB's create_fts_index parameters k1 (~1.2) and b (~0.75) explicitly, and optionally pass per-call b for the long WET bodies. Add a light recency prior on ties: final = bm25 * (1 + lambda * exp(-age_days/tau)), lambda~0.1, tau~30. Validate on a small labelled query set with nDCG@10.
improvements.rationale: BM25F (Robertson et al.) is the standard fix for multi-field documents; a title hit is far more indicative of relevance than a body hit. Explicit k1/b tuning matters because web bodies have extreme length variance.
improvements.expected_impact: Substantially better top-k ordering (title-matching docs surface first); typical nDCG@10 gains of 0.05-0.15 over single-blob default-param BM25.

improvements.title: Make SimHash banding satisfy the pigeonhole guarantee for the actual Hamming threshold (recall-exact retrieval)
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/state.py (NEAR_DUP_SEGMENTS/SEG_BITS, add_near_dup_index, find_near_dup_candidates); src/awareness/dedup/engine.py (near_threshold)
improvements.current_state: 128-bit signatures are split into 16 bands of 8 bits, but the dedup threshold is Hamming<=24. The Manku/Jain pigeonhole guarantee (two sigs within distance d share an exact band) only holds when bands b > d, i.e. here only for d<16. Between 16 and 24 bits of difference, candidate retrieval is purely probabilistic — true near-dups are silently missed before the Hamming check ever runs. The benchmark even labels this an 'engine retrieval gap' vs MinHashLSH. So recall at the shipped threshold is capped by the band scheme, not the fingerprint.
improvements.proposed: Choose bands from the threshold via the pigeonhole identity: to guarantee a shared exact sub-band for all pairs within Hamming<=T over a B-bit signature, split into r bands and probe all C(r, r-ceil) band-combinations such that r > T at the chosen granularity; concretely for B=128, T=24 use the standard Manku scheme of r=25 bands (or 8 bands of 16 bits with multi-index probing over (r choose r-1) combos) so any pair with <=24 differing bits collides in at least one probed key. Practically: increase NEAR_DUP_SEGMENTS so segments > threshold, or implement multi-probe (enumerate band subsets) so the guarantee holds. Add a benchmark assertion that engine recall == all-pairs-oracle recall at the shipped threshold.
improvements.rationale: The whole point of banding is an exactness guarantee; with b<=d it degrades to a heuristic and the documented 'retrieval gap' is self-inflicted. Aligning band count to the threshold restores guaranteed recall.
improvements.expected_impact: Closes the engine-vs-oracle F1 gap shown in benchmarks/bench_simhash.py (end-to-end near-dup recall rises toward the fingerprint ceiling, ~F1 0.86->0.99 at the same precision).

improvements.title: Replace the hand-picked Hamming threshold (24) with a data-driven, false-positive-controlled cutoff
improvements.area: src/awareness/dedup/engine.py (near_threshold default/derivation); benchmarks/bench_simhash.py
improvements.current_state: near_threshold=24 is a hardcoded magic constant justified by prose ('unrelated docs sit at ~45+', 'precision erodes near 36'). There is no calibration to the actual corpus, no false-positive rate target, and the 64-bit provenance simhash uses a separate threshold=3. The right cutoff depends on signature width and corpus token statistics, which the constant ignores.
improvements.proposed: Derive the threshold from the bit-error model. For B-bit SimHash, P(bit flip) p ≈ (1/pi)*arccos(Jaccard-ish similarity); the per-pair Hamming distance for unrelated docs is ~Binomial(B, 0.5), mean B/2. Pick T as the largest integer with P(Binomial(128,0.5) <= T) <= target_FPR (e.g. 1e-6 -> T around 35), then cap by the empirically measured similarity of the corpus. Provide a `awareness dedup calibrate` command that samples the live corpus, fits the unrelated-pair distance histogram, and reports the FPR-controlled T (and the precision/recall curve). Default T to the calibrated value, falling back to 24 only when uncalibrated.
improvements.rationale: A threshold should be set by a target false-merge rate against the real distance distribution, not a narrative. The Binomial(B,1/2) null gives a principled, width-aware cutoff.
improvements.expected_impact: Predictable, documented false-merge rate; typically recovers recall headroom (T can safely rise from 24 toward ~32-35 at controlled FPR) without false merges.

improvements.title: Weight SimHash shingles by IDF (corpus rarity), not just local 1+ln(count)
improvements.area: src/awareness/util/hashing.py (simhash128 weighted path)
improvements.current_state: simhash128 down-weights frequent shingles only within a single document via 1+ln(1+count). This dampens intra-doc repetition but does nothing about corpus-level boilerplate: a shingle like 'all rights reserved' appears once per doc, gets weight ~1, and dominates the signature of otherwise-distinct pages sharing the same template. Charikar's original formulation weights each feature by its informativeness (IDF), which this omits.
improvements.proposed: Maintain a streaming document-frequency table (count of docs containing each shingle hash, e.g. a Count-Min sketch keyed by the 64-bit shingle hash to bound memory). Weight each shingle by tf-idf: w = (1+ln(1+tf)) * ln((N+1)/(df+1)). High-df boilerplate shingles get near-zero weight and stop polluting signatures. Hashes are already computed, so the only added cost is a sketch lookup/update per shingle. Keep the current local weighting as the cold-start fallback before df stats accrue.
improvements.rationale: IDF weighting is the standard, theoretically-grounded way to make SimHash robust to shared boilerplate; it is exactly what separates template-identical-but-content-different pages.
improvements.expected_impact: Fewer false near-dup merges across pages sharing a CMS template, and tighter signatures for genuinely-similar content — measurable precision gain on boilerplate-heavy corpora (web/news).

improvements.title: Harden language detection: fastText/CLD3 with confidence, length gating, and FineWeb metadata trust
improvements.area: src/awareness/normalize/text.py (detect_language); used by commoncrawl_wet.py, fineweb.py
improvements.current_state: detect_language uses langdetect (a port of an old Naive-Bayes detector) on text[:5000] with seed=0, returns only a top-1 label and no confidence, and silently returns None for <80 chars. langdetect is known to be unstable on short/code-switched/markup-heavy text and has no probability output, so the languages_filter in the WET/FineWeb adapters can wrongly drop or keep documents. except (ImportError, Exception) also swallows all errors.
improvements.proposed: Switch to fasttext lid.176 (or pycld3) which returns calibrated probabilities over 176 languages. Gate on confidence: accept the label only if p>=0.65 AND len>=120 chars, else mark language='und' (undetermined) rather than None so downstream filters can choose to keep it. Sample the longest ~2-3k chars rather than a fixed prefix (avoids nav/boilerplate-language bias). For FineWeb, trust the dataset's own 'language' field (already populated) and only run detection when it is absent. Narrow the except to the detector's specific exception and log a counted metric on detector failure.
improvements.rationale: A confidence-aware, modern LID is materially more accurate on web text, and trusting upstream metadata avoids redundant, lower-quality re-detection. 'und' instead of None prevents silent over-filtering.
improvements.expected_impact: Fewer wrongly-dropped non-English docs and fewer mislabeled rows; language filters become trustworthy. Typical LID accuracy on web text rises from ~0.90 (langdetect) to ~0.98 (fastText lid.176).

improvements.title: Add a content-quality / boilerplate filter to WET extraction (length+symbol+stopword heuristics)
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py (_parse_wet_to_captures); src/awareness/normalize/text.py
improvements.current_state: WET parsing accepts any 'conversion' record whose normalized text passes only a min_chars>=200 gate. WET text already includes nav menus, cookie banners, link farms, and SEO spam; none are filtered. This pollutes search (low-quality hits) and dedup (boilerplate-dominated signatures), contributing to 'janky' results.
improvements.proposed: Apply lightweight quality heuristics shared by FineWeb/C4 (Gopher/RefinedWeb rules): reject if mean line length < 10 or > 1000 chars; if fraction of lines ending in '.' is too low; if symbol-to-word ratio (#,…,/) exceeds ~0.1; if the top-2 most-common lines exceed ~30% of lines (duplicate-line boilerplate); if stopword coverage (the/and/of/to) is below ~0.06 (signals non-prose/menus). Compute a single quality_score in NormalizedText and drop below a tunable threshold; record discarded_reason for observability. Keep thresholds in config.
improvements.rationale: These are the documented, cheap C4/Gopher quality signals; they are O(n) over the text and dramatically reduce junk in both search and dedup.
improvements.expected_impact: Higher-precision search results and cleaner near-dup signatures; fewer 'why is this garbage in my results' moments. Removes a large fraction of low-value rows at negligible CPU cost.

improvements.title: Raise default crawl breadth (shards/results per crawl) and make it configurable
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/base.py (_register_defaults instantiates cls() with defaults); commoncrawl_wet.py (max_shards_per_crawl=1); cc_index.py (max_results_per_crawl=200)
improvements.current_state: Adapters are registered via bare cls(), so CommonCrawlWetAdapter defaults to max_shards_per_crawl=1 (one ~100-500MB WET shard out of tens of thousands per crawl) and CommonCrawlIndexAdapter caps at 200 CDX results. Even after the crawl-id fix, a backfill samples a vanishingly small, non-representative slice — reinforcing the 'doesn't really scrape' impression. The '1 shard' default is described as a smoke-test value but is what ships.
improvements.proposed: Plumb max_shards_per_crawl, max_results_per_crawl, and rows_per_partition from config (e.g. cc_wet_shards_per_crawl default 8, cc_index_max_results default 5000, fineweb_rows_per_partition default 2000), and have _register_defaults read settings instead of using constructor defaults. For domain-narrowed backfills, prefer the CDX index path (precise) over blind WET shard sampling. Document the throughput/cost trade in config help. Add a sampling note: shards are an i.i.d. sample of the crawl, so N shards gives ~N*records_per_shard docs with bounded sampling error.
improvements.rationale: A research ingestion engine that pulls one shard per crawl cannot represent the web; the breadth knobs exist but default to smoke-test values and aren't wired to config.
improvements.expected_impact: Backfills produce a meaningful, tunable corpus volume; search has enough data that 'bitcoin' (and everything else) returns substantive results.

improvements.title: Fix histogram sampling bias and add real percentiles (reservoir sampling + p50/p95/p99)
improvements.area: src/awareness/obs/metrics.py (_Histogram)
improvements.current_state: _Histogram keeps only the FIRST 256 observations (`if len(self.samples) < self.max_samples`) and as_dict() never uses samples at all — it reports only count/sum/min/max/avg. Any latency/size distribution is therefore biased toward the earliest samples and exposes no tail percentiles, so benchmark/runtime latency claims (p95/p99) cannot be computed correctly.
improvements.proposed: Replace the truncating buffer with Vitter's Algorithm R reservoir sampling (uniform over the full stream at fixed memory): keep index i; for the k-th observation with k>max_samples, replace samples[randint(0,k)] with prob max_samples/k. In as_dict(), compute p50/p90/p95/p99 via numpy.percentile (or a t-digest for unbounded accuracy). This makes the reported distribution unbiased and adds the tail stats that matter.
improvements.rationale: First-N truncation is a textbook sampling bias; reservoir sampling gives a provably uniform sample at O(1) memory, and percentiles are the meaningful latency statistic, not min/max/avg.
improvements.expected_impact: Trustworthy latency/size distributions and correct tail-percentile reporting in metrics and benchmarks; removes a silent statistical error.

improvements.title: Make near-dup benchmarks defensible: bootstrap CIs and a real-text validation corpus
improvements.area: benchmarks/bench_simhash.py, benchmarks/corpus.py
improvements.current_state: Accuracy F1 is reported as point estimates on a single seeded synthetic corpus whose vocabulary is template-generated; it has no confidence intervals and may not reflect real web boilerplate/Zipfian token distributions. The README/benchmark headline numbers (F1 ~0.99 vs MinHash) are single-run and could mislead. The 'best F1 over a sweep' for the tuned engine also risks threshold overfitting to the synthetic set.
improvements.proposed: (1) Report F1/precision/recall with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals: resample the pair set B=1000 times and report mean±CI. (2) Add a held-out real-text near-dup validation set (e.g. a small slice of a public news-copy / CORE-style dataset, or perturbed real WET records) and report numbers on it alongside the synthetic one. (3) Select the tuned threshold on a train split and report on a disjoint test split to avoid optimistic bias. (4) Keep the synthetic corpus but document it as a smoke/repro fixture, not the headline.
improvements.rationale: Single-seed point estimates on self-generated data overstate precision and hide variance; bootstrap CIs and a real-text holdout are the standard way to make dedup benchmarks credible and reproducible.
improvements.expected_impact: Honest, variance-aware benchmark claims that generalize to real corpora; prevents threshold/F1 overfitting to the synthetic generator.

improvements.title: Tighten exact-dup hashing and tune shingle size k for the corpus
improvements.area: src/awareness/util/hashing.py (content_hash uses xxh3_64; _shingles k=3)
improvements.current_state: Exact-dup detection keys on a 64-bit xxh3 content hash. At web scale (10^8+ docs) the birthday bound gives a non-negligible collision probability (~50% at ~5e9 docs, and ~1e-3 at ~10^7 docs), and a single collision silently merges two distinct documents into one dup-group with no verification. Separately, the shingle size k=3 is fixed with no justification; optimal k trades recall (small k) vs precision (large k) and depends on average doc length.
improvements.proposed: (a) Use the existing xxh3_128 (already used for doc_id) for content_hash, dropping collision probability to negligible (~1e-21 at 10^9 docs), OR keep 64-bit but verify exact-dup candidates with a length+prefix check before merging. (b) Make shingle k configurable and benchmark k in {2,3,4,5} on the near-dup F1 curve; for typical article-length web text k=4 or 5 usually maximizes F1 (fewer accidental shingle collisions between unrelated docs). Document the chosen k with its F1 evidence.
improvements.rationale: A 64-bit exact-content hash is under-provisioned for web scale and merges silently on collision; 128-bit removes the risk for free. Shingle size is a real tunable that is currently an unexplained constant.
improvements.expected_impact: Eliminates silent exact-dup false merges at scale; data-driven k selection yields a measurable near-dup F1 improvement.

improvements.title: Remove the silent 30-day default window on CLI search (root cause of 'bitcoin returned 2 results')
improvements.area: src/awareness/cli/main.py (search cmd, lines 2595-2596, and the dashboard search at 2460-2461)
improvements.current_state: The CLI `search` command defaults `--start` to the literal string "30 days ago" and `--end` to "now". These are passed straight into `DuckDbIndex.search(start=, end=)`, which appends `fetch_ts >= $start AND fetch_ts <= $end`. For every bulk source the corpus is dominated by Common Crawl WET / FineWeb, where `fetch_ts` is the ORIGINAL WARC capture date (months-to-years old) — see commoncrawl_wet.py:326-327 (`WARC-Date`) and fineweb.py:145 (row date). So the default query silently excludes essentially the entire historical corpus; only the handful of live tail/GDELT captures from the last 30 days survive. By contrast the FastAPI `/search` endpoint (api/server.py:429-430) defaults start/end to None (no window). The two surfaces disagree, which is exactly the 'broken/janky in many places' symptom.
improvements.proposed: Make the CLI match the API: default `--start`/`--end` to no time filter (None) unless the user explicitly passes them. Concretely change the Typer options to `start: str = typer.Option("", ...)`, `end: str = typer.Option("", ...)`, and only compute `start_dt = to_utc(start) if start else None`, `end_dt = coerce_relative_end(end) if end else None`. Apply the same to the dashboard search (lines 2460-2461). Additionally, in `DuckDbIndex.search`, when a window is supplied also OR against `published_ts`/`observed_ts` so that a doc with an old `fetch_ts` but recent discovery is not dropped. Add a one-line result footer when a window is active and `total>rows`: 'N older results hidden by --start/--end; pass --start "" to search all time.'
improvements.rationale: The single highest-impact correctness bug. The data model deliberately stores the historical capture date in fetch_ts, but the default UI applies a recency filter as if this were a live news index. Users searching a corpus built from Common Crawl will see almost nothing and conclude search is broken.
improvements.expected_impact: Search recall on a populated corpus jumps from ~0-2 hits to the true match count. Eliminates the most visible 'janky search' symptom. CLI and API become consistent.

improvements.title: Add retries with exponential backoff + Retry-After handling to all fetchers (root cause of 'no idea how to scrape')
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py, feeds.py, gdelt.py, tail_recrawl.py; new src/awareness/util/http.py; config/settings.py (max_retries, backoff_base_sec already exist)
improvements.current_state: `Settings.max_retries=4` and `backoff_base_sec=1.5` are defined (settings.py:80-81) and surfaced in the config schema, but grep shows they are NEVER referenced by any source or fetch helper. Every adapter does a single `httpx` GET and on ANY error (`except httpx.HTTPError: ... return`) or non-200 it logs a warning and returns an empty result. Common Crawl's CDN (data.commoncrawl.org) and GDELT routinely return 403/429/503/slow-loris under load; a single transient failure silently yields zero documents for that shard/slot with no retry and no DLQ entry. There is no 429/503 Retry-After honoring and no jitter. This is the mechanical reason the engine 'has no idea how to scrape': the first hiccup ends the fetch as a silent no-op.
improvements.proposed: Create `util/http.py` with `async def fetch(client, url, *, headers, settings, stream=False) -> httpx.Response` implementing: attempts = settings.max_retries; retry on httpx.TransportError/TimeoutException and on status in {408,425,429,500,502,503,504}; sleep = min(cap=60, backoff_base_sec * 2**attempt) + random.uniform(0, 0.5*backoff_base_sec) (full jitter, decorrelated). On 429/503 honor `Retry-After` (seconds or HTTP-date) if present, taking max(header, computed). Emit metrics `http.retries`, `http.giveups` labeled by host+status. Route all four adapters' GETs through it. On final give-up in a planner-emitted task, raise so the worker's existing retry/DLQ path (engine.py:383-389) records it instead of silently returning. Add a hard per-request timeout already present; add a connect timeout split via httpx.Timeout(connect=10, read=settings.request_timeout_sec).
improvements.rationale: Public-web bulk hosts are flaky and rate-limited by design; a crawler with zero retry/backoff cannot make forward progress. The config knobs already promise this behavior but it was never wired in, so operators believe it works when it does not.
improvements.expected_impact: Fetch success rate on CC/GDELT under real conditions rises from best-effort-single-shot to robust; transient 429/503 storms no longer translate into empty corpora. Failed fetches become visible (DLQ + metrics) instead of silent. Directly addresses symptom #2.

improvements.title: Expose max-shards-per-crawl so a backfill fetches more than 1 WET file per 2-week crawl
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py (__init__ default=1, plan()), src/awareness/sources/base.py:114-125 (registry instantiates with default), schemas/jobs.py (BackfillRequest), cli/main.py backfill_submit (~1079)
improvements.current_state: `CommonCrawlWetAdapter.__init__(max_shards_per_crawl=1)` hardcodes 1 shard. The registry builds it with the default (base.py: `reg.register(cls())`) and nothing ever overrides it: `plan()` reads `self._max_shards_per_crawl`, and discovery picks `shards[:max_shards]` (commoncrawl_wet.py:174). Each CC-MAIN crawl publishes ~90,000 WET shards (~100-500MB each, ~30k docs each); fetching exactly 1 means a backfill ingests ~1/90,000th of a crawl. There is no CLI/BackfillRequest field to raise it. Combined with the comment 'Default to 1 shard per crawl for sanity in smoke tests', the production default is a smoke-test default. This is why even a 'successful' backfill produces almost no searchable content.
improvements.proposed: Add `max_shards_per_crawl: int | None = None` to `BackfillRequest`. In `plan()` read `request.max_shards_per_crawl or self._max_shards_per_crawl`. Add `--shards-per-crawl` (default e.g. 4, documented as 'per ~2-week crawl') to `backfill_submit`. In discovery, when `domains`/`languages` are requested, prefer using the CC URL index (cc_index adapter) to select shards likely to contain those domains instead of `shards[:N]` head-truncation (which always grabs the same alphabetical-first shards). Keep a global safety cap via `max_tasks`.
improvements.rationale: The corpus size a user gets is governed by an un-overridable smoke-test constant. Even with search and retries fixed, there is nothing to find because ingestion volume is capped at 1 shard. Head-truncating shards also biases the sample to the same files every run.
improvements.expected_impact: Backfill volume scales with an operator-controlled knob; a default of 4 shards/crawl over a 1-month window yields ~hundreds of thousands of docs instead of ~30k from a single shard. Makes search results non-trivial. Addresses symptom #2 and indirectly #1.

improvements.title: Stream WET parsing as an async generator instead of buffering the whole shard in a Python list
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py:245-267 (_run_shard) and 274-368 (_parse_wet_to_captures)
improvements.current_state: `_parse_wet_to_captures` parses an entire WET shard and returns `list[DocCapture]` (one Python object per record, ~30k DocCapture pydantic models holding the full normalized text of every doc). `_run_shard` calls it via `run_in_executor` and only then iterates. So peak memory per in-flight shard is the whole shard's decompressed text materialized as objects (hundreds of MB), multiplied by `worker_concurrency` (default 8). With several WET tasks concurrent this is multi-GB and risks OOM; it also delays first-yield until the entire shard is parsed (latency + no early backpressure).
improvements.proposed: Convert the parser into a producer that streams records over a bounded `asyncio.Queue` (size = settings.bounded_queue_size, which is currently defined-but-unused). Run `ArchiveIterator` in a worker thread that pushes one DocCapture at a time via `loop.call_soon_threadsafe(queue.put_nowait, cap)` (or `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(queue.put(cap))` to get backpressure when the consumer is slow), and have `_run_shard` async-iterate the queue, honoring `context.is_stopping()`. This caps resident captures to the queue depth, makes the flush path apply real backpressure to the parser, and lets dedup/storage start while the shard is still being read.
improvements.rationale: Single-process engine must bound memory; the current design's footprint grows with shard size x concurrency with no ceiling. Streaming also turns the existing bounded_queue_size knob into a real backpressure mechanism.
improvements.expected_impact: Peak RSS per shard drops from O(shard size) to O(queue_depth x avg doc). Enables higher worker_concurrency without OOM; reduces time-to-first-document per shard.

improvements.title: Fix the per-domain rate limiter so inter-fetch delay is actually enforced under concurrency
improvements.area: src/awareness/util/ratelimit.py:36-53
improvements.current_state: `PerDomainLimiter.acquire` reads `slot.last_release` to compute the wait, but `last_release` is only updated in `release()` (when a request finishes), and the per-domain semaphore allows `concurrency` (default 2) holders at once. With concurrency>1 the spacing computed from `last_release` is meaningless: two coroutines can acquire simultaneously, both read the same stale `last_release`, both compute wait<=0, and fire back-to-back — so `min_delay_sec`/crawl-delay is not honored. There is also no global fetch cap (settings.global_fetch_concurrency=32 is defined but unused), so per-host politeness is the only throttle and it is broken.
improvements.proposed: Track a per-domain `next_allowed_at` monotonic timestamp guarded by an asyncio.Lock. In acquire: `async with slot.lock: now=loop.time(); wait=max(0, slot.next_allowed_at-now); slot.next_allowed_at=max(now,slot.next_allowed_at)+delay` then `await asyncio.sleep(wait)` OUTSIDE the lock. This serializes the slot assignment so N concurrent fetchers to the same host are spaced by `delay` regardless of concurrency. Keep the semaphore for max in-flight. Separately, add a process-wide `asyncio.Semaphore(settings.global_fetch_concurrency)` acquired in tail_recrawl/WET/GDELT fetches to bound total open sockets. Use `loop.time()` (monotonic) instead of `time.time()`.
improvements.rationale: Politeness is a correctness/abuse requirement; the current limiter can hammer a host at full concurrency, risking IP bans (which then manifests as 'scraping doesn't work'). The unused global cap means raising worker_concurrency opens unbounded connections.
improvements.expected_impact: Crawl-delay and min-delay are enforced deterministically; fewer 429/ban events; bounded socket usage. Improves sustained scrape success.

improvements.title: Add attempt-bounded, backoff-delayed task retries instead of immediate re-PENDING busy-retry
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/state.py (fail_task:460-477, claim_pending_tasks:420-436, TaskRow), src/awareness/workers/engine.py:383-390
improvements.current_state: On a non-dead failure, `fail_task` immediately sets status back to PENDING (state.py:476). The worker loop's `claim_pending_tasks` will re-claim it on the very next poll (every 0.5s) with no delay, incrementing `attempts` each time. So a task that fails fast (e.g. an immediate 403) spins through all `max_retries` attempts in ~2 seconds with no backoff, then dead-letters — defeating the purpose of retry and hammering the failing host. There is also no `next_attempt_at` column, so retries cannot be time-scheduled.
improvements.proposed: Add `next_attempt_at: datetime` and `attempts` semantics: in `fail_task`, when not dead, set `next_attempt_at = utcnow() + timedelta(seconds=min(cap, backoff_base_sec * 2**attempts) + jitter)`. In `claim_pending_tasks`, filter `WHERE status='pending' AND (next_attempt_at IS NULL OR next_attempt_at <= now)`. Decide dead-lettering on `attempts >= max_retries` (the engine already computes `dead = task.attempts >= max(1, settings.max_retries)`; align the off-by-one so a task gets exactly max_retries tries). Surface `tasks.retry_scheduled` metric.
improvements.rationale: Retry without backoff is just a fast path to the DLQ and an accidental DoS on the upstream. Time-scheduled retries give transient failures (rate limits, brief 5xx) a real chance to succeed on a later attempt.
improvements.expected_impact: Transient failures recover instead of exhausting attempts in 2s; upstream pressure reduced; DLQ contains only genuinely dead work. More documents successfully ingested per run.

improvements.title: Re-partition Iceberg by month(fetch_ts)+source_type and add a compaction job to stop tiny-file explosion
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/iceberg_schema.py:61-63 (ICEBERG_PARTITION_SPEC), src/awareness/storage/iceberg.py (append), src/awareness/storage/state.py (manifests/compaction), a new compaction command
improvements.current_state: Partition spec is `day(fetch_ts)` + identity `source_type` (iceberg_schema.py:62-63). For Common Crawl WET / FineWeb, `fetch_ts` spans MANY years and is spread across millions of distinct days, so a single backfill writes one tiny Parquet data file per (day, source) per append batch. With flush batches of 500 records (settings.storage_flush_records) and append-per-flush (iceberg.py:154-164), the table fragments into thousands of sub-MB files — pathological for Iceberg scan planning and DuckDB iceberg_scan. The `manifests`/`compacted_at` machinery and `list_pending_manifests`/`mark_manifest_compacted` exist in state.py but no code ever compacts; nothing calls them.
improvements.proposed: (1) Change partitioning to `month(fetch_ts)` + `source_type` (MonthTransform) to cut partition cardinality ~30x. (2) Buffer Iceberg appends to a larger target (e.g. accumulate >=storage_flush_records*N or 128MB before `append`) rather than appending every 500-row flush. (3) Implement a real `awareness storage compact` command that reads `list_pending_manifests`, rewrites small files via PyIceberg's rewrite_data_files / or reads JSONL chunks and bulk-appends, then calls `mark_manifest_compacted`. Schedule it after a backfill completes. (4) For DuckDB, after compaction call ANALYZE and rely on Parquet row-group stats for fetch_ts/domain predicate pushdown.
improvements.rationale: day() over a multi-year corpus is the wrong pivot and the per-flush append amplifies it into a tiny-file storm, which is the dominant query-latency cost on a populated warehouse. The compaction primitives were stubbed but never connected.
improvements.expected_impact: Order-of-magnitude fewer Parquet files; faster scan planning and faster range/domain queries; lower metadata bloat. Makes search/inspect responsive at scale.

improvements.title: Persist and incrementally update the DuckDB FTS index instead of full rebuild on any corpus change
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py:307-358 (_ensure_fts), 142-296 (view refresh)
improvements.current_state: `_ensure_fts` materializes the ENTIRE captures view into `captures_idx` and rebuilds the BM25 index (`PRAGMA create_fts_index(..., overwrite=1)`) whenever the row COUNT changes (it keys off `_fts_built_for_count`). On an append-heavy corpus this means a full re-materialize + full FTS rebuild on essentially every search after ingestion — O(corpus) per query. Worse, `captures` is a view over `read_json_auto([...all jsonl files...])` UNION iceberg_scan, so each rebuild re-reads and re-parses every JSONL chunk from disk. At even modest scale, search latency degrades to seconds and feels 'janky'.
improvements.proposed: Materialize `captures_idx` as a persistent DuckDB table inside the same database file (not a view-backed rebuild), and append only NEW rows on refresh: track the max `observed_ts`/a monotonically increasing chunk watermark, and on refresh `INSERT INTO captures_idx SELECT ... FROM captures WHERE observed_ts > $watermark`. DuckDB FTS cannot incrementally update, so either (a) rebuild the FTS index only when N new rows since last build exceeds a threshold (amortize), or (b) keep a small 'hot' delta table searched with ILIKE/prefix and the big cold table searched with BM25, UNION the results. Cache the built table across the process and only refresh on the existing `_source_signature()` change. Add `search.latency_ms` and `fts.rebuilds` metrics.
improvements.rationale: Re-reading all JSONL and rebuilding BM25 per query is the search-side performance cliff. Incremental/amortized indexing keeps steady-state search bound by the query, not by corpus size.
improvements.expected_impact: Search latency goes from O(corpus) per call to O(matches); large-corpus search becomes interactive. Removes a major 'search is janky' contributor.

improvements.title: Export the in-process metrics registry and add per-fetch structured outcome logs/tracing
improvements.area: src/awareness/obs/metrics.py (in-process only), src/awareness/api/server.py (add /metrics), all sources (fetch outcome logging)
improvements.current_state: `MetricsRegistry` is a module-global created per process (metrics.py:101-108). CLI commands are short-lived processes, so counters die at exit and are never scraped; there is no `/metrics` endpoint and no Prometheus exposition. Fetch failures are logged at WARNING with terse keys (e.g. `gdelt_slot_missing`, `cc_wet_paths_fetch_failed`) but there is no consistent per-fetch record of {url, host, status, attempt, latency_ms, bytes, outcome}, no trace/span correlation across plan->fetch->dedup->store, and no counter for 'shards that yielded 0 docs'. An operator cannot answer 'why did this backfill ingest nothing' without reading code.
improvements.proposed: (1) Add a Prometheus exposition: `pip install prometheus_client`, mirror counters/histograms, and expose `GET /metrics` in the FastAPI app; for CLI runs, optionally push to a Pushgateway or write a `snapshot()` JSON to data/metrics/ on exit. (2) Standardize a `fetch_result` structured log + histogram `http.latency_ms{host,status}` and counters `fetch.ok/fetch.err/fetch.empty{source,host}` emitted from the new util/http.py. (3) Add a lightweight trace_id (uuid per task) bound via structlog contextvars (already imported in logging.py) so all logs for a task correlate. (4) Add a `backfill report` line: 'shards fetched / shards empty / docs/shard' so silent no-ops are visible.
improvements.rationale: Both user symptoms are partly invisibility problems: the engine fails silently. Real metrics + per-fetch outcome logs make 'scraping does nothing' diagnosable in seconds and provide SLOs (fetch success rate, docs/shard).
improvements.expected_impact: Operators can see fetch success rate, empty-shard rate, retry/giveup counts, and search latency live; silent no-ops become alertable. Strong multiplier on every other fix's debuggability.

improvements.title: Reuse a shared httpx client + connection pool and enforce global fetch concurrency
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py, feeds.py, gdelt.py, tail_recrawl.py; config/settings.py (global_fetch_concurrency unused)
improvements.current_state: Every fetch constructs a fresh `httpx.AsyncClient(...)` inside the function (`async with httpx.AsyncClient(...)` in each adapter), so there is no connection pooling/keep-alive reuse across thousands of fetches — each request pays TLS+connect setup, and there is no cap on total concurrent clients/sockets. `settings.global_fetch_concurrency=32` and `extract_concurrency=4` are defined and shown in the config wizard but referenced nowhere in src (confirmed by grep). So the only concurrency control is per-domain (which is itself buggy) and worker_concurrency; a multi-domain tail run can open unbounded simultaneous connections.
improvements.proposed: Introduce a process-singleton `httpx.AsyncClient` with `limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=settings.global_fetch_concurrency, max_keepalive_connections=...)` and `http2=True`, created once and injected via AdapterContext.extras (the context already carries extras['limiter']/extras['robots']). All adapters use it instead of per-call clients. Wrap actual sends in a global `asyncio.Semaphore(settings.global_fetch_concurrency)`. Wire `extract_concurrency` to bound the number of concurrent trafilatura/warcio executor parses (a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor of that size passed to run_in_executor) so CPU-bound extraction doesn't starve the default executor.
improvements.rationale: Per-call client creation defeats keep-alive and pooling (slower, more TLS churn) and leaves total concurrency unbounded; the knobs meant to control this are dead config. Sharing a pooled client is both faster and safer.
improvements.expected_impact: Higher fetch throughput via keep-alive/HTTP2 reuse, bounded sockets/FDs, and CPU-bound extraction no longer saturating the event loop's default thread pool. Makes the documented config knobs real.

improvements.title: Make CLI and API share one config-driven search-default resolver (mode/fields/window/limit)
improvements.area: src/awareness/cli/main.py (search ~2592, dashboard ~2458), src/awareness/api/server.py:422-456, config/settings.py search_* fields
improvements.current_state: Search defaults are resolved independently in three places with divergent behavior: CLI search hardcodes a 30-day window and reads search_default_mode/fields/limit; the dashboard search (cli/main.py ~2458) has its own copy; the API /search defaults window to None and reads the same settings. The duplicated logic is how the surfaces drifted (the 30-day bug exists only on CLI). There is no single function that maps (user overrides + settings) -> normalized search kwargs.
improvements.proposed: Add `resolve_search_params(query, *, start, end, mode, fields, limit, max_results, settings)` (e.g. in storage/duckdb_index.py or a new search module) returning the normalized kwargs dict, with the agreed default being NO time window unless explicitly provided. Call it from CLI search, dashboard search, and API /search so all three behave identically. Add a regression test asserting CLI and API return the same `total` for a known corpus and query (would have caught the 'bitcoin -> 2' divergence).
improvements.rationale: The janky-in-many-places symptom is partly the absence of one source of truth for search behavior; centralizing prevents future drift and makes the 30-day fix permanent.
improvements.expected_impact: Consistent results across CLI, dashboard, and API; a test guards against re-introducing windowing/mode divergences.

improvements.title: Make the storage flush crash-safe and Iceberg appends idempotent (no dup/loss on mid-flush crash)
improvements.area: src/awareness/workers/engine.py:417-523 (_flush), src/awareness/storage/iceberg.py:154-164 (append), src/awareness/storage/jsonl.py
improvements.current_state: In `_flush`, the buffer is cleared (engine.py:428) under the lock BEFORE the rows are durably written to JSONL/Iceberg. If the process crashes after clearing but before/while `self._jsonl.write` or `self._iceberg.append` runs, those captures are lost (they were already removed from the buffer and the task may later be marked complete). Conversely, JSONL write and Iceberg append are not transactional with respect to each other or to task completion: a crash between JSONL append and Iceberg append leaves the two stores inconsistent, and on task re-run the same captures can be appended to Iceberg again (no capture_id-level idempotency on append). The combined `captures` view dedups by capture_id at read time (duckdb_index.py:255-264), which masks Iceberg dup rows but bloats storage.
improvements.proposed: (1) Reorder so rows are written durably (fsync the JSONL chunk) and the manifest row committed BEFORE the buffer is considered flushed; only on success advance state. Treat JSONL+manifest as the source of truth and make Iceberg a derived, replayable copy fed from committed manifests (so a crash just leaves uncompacted manifests, never lost data). (2) Make task completion + 'captures durably staged' atomic from the resume point of view: store the batch_id/last chunk in the task checkpoint so a re-run skips already-staged batches. (3) For Iceberg, dedup on append by checking capture_id against the latest snapshot (or rely solely on compaction-from-manifests which is naturally idempotent because it rewrites whole partitions). Add a startup reconciliation that re-stages any manifest not yet compacted.
improvements.rationale: A single-process engine that clears its in-memory buffer before durable write has a real data-loss window, and non-idempotent Iceberg appends cause silent duplication that only the read-time view hides. Checkpoint/resume must be exactly-once-effective.
improvements.expected_impact: No capture loss on crash mid-flush; resume is idempotent; Iceberg stops accumulating duplicate rows; storage size and dedup stats become accurate.

improvements.title: Stop silently restricting search to the last 30 days (primary cause of 'bitcoin → 2 results')
improvements.area: src/awareness/cli/main.py (search command, lines 2592-2667); contrast with src/awareness/api/server.py /search (lines 422-456)
improvements.current_state: The CLI `search` command declares `start: str = typer.Option("30 days ago", "--start")` and `end="now"`, then passes `start_dt/end_dt` into `idx.search(...)`, which appends `fetch_ts >= $start AND fetch_ts <= $end` to BOTH the FTS and prefix paths (duckdb_index.py base_filters, lines 430-445). Crucially, `fetch_ts` for Common Crawl WET and FineWeb is the ORIGINAL crawl/publish date taken from the WARC-Date header (commoncrawl_wet.py line 326-327) or the dataset `date` field (fineweb.py line 145) — typically months-to-years in the past. So a corpus full of 2023/2024 Bitcoin pages is invisible to a search whose default window is `[now-30d, now]`. The HTTP API `/search` endpoint has NO default window (start/end default to None), so the SPA and the CLI disagree — the exact 'janky in many places' inconsistency the user reports.
improvements.proposed: Default the CLI `--start` to None (search the whole corpus) exactly like the API. Implement: change the option to `start: str = typer.Option("", "--start", help="Restrict by capture date; empty = all time")` and only build `start_dt = to_utc(start) if start else None` / `end_dt = coerce_relative_end(end) if end else None`. Pass `start=start_dt, end=end_dt` (which `idx.search` already treats as 'no filter' when None). Add a one-line result footer when a window IS applied: `f"(filtered to {start_dt:%Y-%m-%d}..{end_dt:%Y-%m-%d}; pass --start '' for all time)"` so the restriction is never silent. Keep `inspect`/`counts` requiring an explicit `--start` (those are range tools), but search should default to unbounded.
improvements.rationale: This is the single highest-probability explanation for '2 results'. The date predicate is ANDed into the WHERE for every match mode, so even a perfectly-built BM25 index returns almost nothing once 99% of rows fall outside the 30-day window. Aligning CLI with API also removes a whole class of 'works in the browser, broken in the terminal' surprises.
improvements.expected_impact: Searching 'bitcoin' returns the full ranked set instead of the 2 rows that happened to be captured in the last 30 days. Eliminates the CLI/SPA inconsistency. No data migration needed.

improvements.title: Make the FTS index rebuild on real content change, not just net row-count delta
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py `_ensure_fts` (lines 307-358), `_fts_built_for_count` and `_fts_built_signature`
improvements.current_state: `_ensure_fts` decides whether to rebuild the materialized `captures_idx` + FTS index using two gates: (1) `if self._fts_built_signature == self._views_signature: return True` (skip), else (2) `count = COUNT(*) FROM captures; if count == self._fts_built_for_count: ... return True` (skip rebuild). The `_views_signature` is a (path,size,mtime) fingerprint of JSONL files + Iceberg metadata json. Two failure modes: (a) COUNT-based gate — if a compaction deletes N staging rows and Iceberg gains the same N rows, the net `COUNT(*)` is unchanged, so the FTS index is NOT rebuilt and silently serves stale doc IDs (or misses brand-new content that replaced old). (b) The signature only covers mtime/size; an in-place rewrite that preserves size (rare but possible with fixed-width compaction) won't trip it. The index can therefore lag the corpus, so a freshly-ingested 'bitcoin' doc is unsearchable until something else changes the row count.
improvements.proposed: Replace the count-equality gate with a content fingerprint that cannot collide on edit-in-place: rebuild when `self._views_signature` changed (already computed and cheap) OR when a lightweight corpus digest changed. Concretely: after building, store `self._fts_built_signature = self._views_signature` (keep) AND drop the `count == self._fts_built_for_count` early-return entirely — rely solely on the file-signature, which already changes on every JSONL chunk add/rotate and every new Iceberg metadata json (the only ways rows enter). If you want defense-in-depth against same-size rewrites, fold a `MAX(fetch_ts)` and `COUNT(*)` pair into the signature: `sig2 = conn.execute('SELECT COUNT(*), max(observed_ts) FROM captures').fetchone()` and compare the tuple. Rebuild if either the file-signature OR sig2 differs. This is O(1) extra per query in the cached/fast path because you only run the probe when the file signature already moved.
improvements.rationale: Row-count equality is not a valid 'unchanged' test under a compaction model where staging rows migrate into Iceberg (delete-here-insert-there). Keying freshness on the actual on-disk file signature plus a (count, max-timestamp) pair makes 'is the index current?' a function of the data, not an accident of arithmetic.
improvements.expected_impact: New documents become searchable deterministically after the next query (or refresh()), eliminating 'I ingested it but search can't find it' — a concrete contributor to the 'broken/janky' perception.

improvements.title: Fix corpus starvation: WET fetches only 1 shard/crawl by default (registry uses bare cls())
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/commoncrawl_wet.py (`__init__ max_shards_per_crawl=1`, line 100-104; `plan` line 107-124); src/awareness/sources/base.py `_register_defaults` (lines 104-126, `reg.register(cls())`)
improvements.current_state: Adapters are registered as `reg.register(cls())` with NO constructor args, so `CommonCrawlWetAdapter()` runs with `max_shards_per_crawl=1` and `FineWebAdapter()` with `rows_per_partition=500`. A default backfill (`backfill submit --start ...`) with no `--domain` therefore fetches exactly ONE ~150MB WET shard per ISO-week crawl. After `normalize_text` min-200-char filtering and language detection, a single shard yields a small, topically-random slice of the web. There is no config knob: `max_shards_per_crawl` is a hard-coded constructor default unreachable from settings/CLI. The empty `data/jsonl` and zero-row state DB on disk confirm the engine currently produces a near-empty corpus, which is why ANY query (not just bitcoin) returns a handful of rows.
improvements.proposed: (1) Add settings: `cc_wet_max_shards_per_crawl: int = 8`, `fineweb_rows_per_partition: int = 5000` in config/settings.py. (2) In base.py `_register_defaults`, construct adapters from settings instead of bare `cls()`: `reg.register(CommonCrawlWetAdapter(max_shards_per_crawl=s.cc_wet_max_shards_per_crawl))`, `reg.register(FineWebAdapter(rows_per_partition=s.fineweb_rows_per_partition))`, `reg.register(GdeltAdapter())`. (3) Add CLI flags on `backfill submit`: `--cc-shards`, `--fineweb-rows` that thread onto BackfillRequest and into the partition payload (the runner already reads `payload['max_shards']` per-partition, so honoring a per-request override is a 2-line change in `plan`). (4) Make shard selection deterministic-but-spread: instead of `shards[:max_shards]` (always the first N, line 174), stride-sample `shards[:: max(1, len(shards)//max_shards)][:max_shards]` so you cover the crawl's hash-space rather than one corner of it.
improvements.rationale: 1 shard/crawl is a smoke-test default that shipped as the production default. The math: a crawl has ~90k WET shards; sampling 1 is ~0.001% of the crawl. Striding 8 spread shards multiplies recall ~8x AND de-biases topic coverage, directly increasing the odds that 'bitcoin' (and everything else) has documents to rank.
improvements.expected_impact: Orders-of-magnitude more documents per backfill, drawn from across the crawl rather than one shard prefix. Turns 'the app has no idea how to scrape' into a corpus large enough for search to be meaningful. Operator can still cap for smoke tests via the new flags.

improvements.title: FineWeb is a silent no-op because `datasets` isn't installed — make the failure loud and the dep installed
improvements.area: src/awareness/sources/fineweb.py (`plan` lines 56-61, `run_partition` lines 94-98); pyproject.toml; planner default source set (planner.py lines 56-66)
improvements.current_state: `FineWebAdapter.plan()` does `try: import datasets except ImportError: logger.info('fineweb_skipped_missing_datasets_lib'); return []`. I confirmed `datasets` is NOT installed in the project venv (`.venv/bin/python -c 'import datasets'` → ModuleNotFoundError). So one of the THREE default BODY sources (planner.py adds COMMON_CRAWL_WET, FINEWEB, GDELT when no --source given) contributes exactly zero documents, and it does so at log level INFO with no surfaced warning in `backfill status` or the CLI. The user sees 'submitted, ran, tiny corpus' with no signal that a third of their ingestion path is dead.
improvements.proposed: (1) Either add `datasets` to the core deps in pyproject.toml, or move FineWeb behind an explicit `[fineweb]` extra and STOP listing FINEWEB in the planner's default source set unless the extra is importable. (2) Promote the missing-dep log to `logger.warning` and record a structured job-level note: when `plan()` returns [] due to ImportError, append to the job notes / a `degraded_sources` field so `backfill status` and the status table show 'FineWeb: SKIPPED (datasets not installed)'. (3) In the CLI `backfill submit` output, after planning, print the per-source task counts (planner already logs `planner_emitted_tasks` with count) so a user immediately sees `CC-WET: 4 tasks, FineWeb: 0 tasks (skipped), GDELT: 8 tasks`.
improvements.rationale: Silent no-ops are the worst failure mode for 'it has no idea how to scrape'. A source that contributes nothing should be impossible to miss. Either ship the dependency or stop advertising the source as a default.
improvements.expected_impact: Either FineWeb actually ingests (large, clean text corpus → far better search recall) or the user is told plainly it's off. Removes a silent 33% loss of default ingestion capacity.

improvements.title: Upgrade ranking: BM25 with title field-boost + recency prior instead of raw single-blob BM25
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py `_ensure_fts` (lines 348-350) and FTS query (lines 467-487)
improvements.current_state: `create_fts_index('captures_idx','capture_id','title','text', stemmer='english', stopwords='english')` indexes title and text into ONE bag of words, and the query scores with a bare `match_bm25(capture_id, $q)` ordered by score DESC. Consequences: (a) a query term appearing in the TITLE is weighted identically to one buried in a 50k-char body — so a page literally titled 'Bitcoin' can rank below a long unrelated article that happens to say 'bitcoin' 30 times; (b) no recency signal, so a 2013 page outranks today's news on score alone; (c) DuckDB BM25 params k1/b are defaults, untuned for web text whose lengths vary by 1000x.
improvements.proposed: Compute a composite score in SQL on top of match_bm25. Step 1: index title and text but exploit DuckDB FTS per-field scoring is limited, so instead synthesize a title boost by ALSO matching the title directly: `score = match_bm25(capture_id,$q) * 1.0 + (CASE WHEN title ILIKE '%'||$q||'%' THEN 2.0 ELSE 0 END) + recency_bonus`. Step 2: recency prior with exponential decay — `recency_bonus = $w_rec * exp(-greatest(0, date_diff('day', fetch_ts, now())) / $halflife_days)` with `$halflife_days≈180`, `$w_rec≈0.5*avg_bm25`. Step 3: expose `k1` (default 1.2) and `b` (default 0.75) as tunables on `create_fts_index` (it accepts them) and set `b=0.6` to penalize long web pages less aggressively. Final ORDER BY the composite. Keep it a single SQL expression so it stays one pass over the candidate set.
improvements.rationale: Classic BM25 = IDF · (tf·(k1+1))/(tf + k1·(1−b+b·|d|/avgdl)). Web bodies have enormous |d|/avgdl variance, so untuned b over-penalizes long authoritative pages; lowering b and adding an explicit title boost restores the intuition that a title hit is a strong relevance signal. A bounded exponential recency term (mathematically a multiplicative log-linear prior) breaks ties toward fresh content the way users expect from a 'live web awareness' engine.
improvements.expected_impact: Dramatically better top-10 ordering: title-matching and recent pages surface first. Directly addresses 'search feels broken' even once recall is fixed.

improvements.title: Add phrase, prefix, and fuzzy (trigram) matching so quoted/typo/partial queries work
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py `search` modes (SEARCH_MODES line 40, FTS path 458-491, prefix path 493-535), `_tokenize_query` (576-579)
improvements.current_state: I verified DuckDB FTS `match_bm25` silently returns NOTHING for `bit-coin`, `"exact phrase"`, `C++`, and `foo OR bar` — it strips punctuation/operators and never errors, so in explicit `--mode fts` those queries yield zero rows. There is no phrase search (token order/adjacency is ignored), no prefix search beyond a stem-root ILIKE, and no fuzzy/typo tolerance — a query 'bitcon' (typo) returns nothing because the stem 'bitcon' ILIKE '%bitcon%' matches no document. Modes today are auto/fts/prefix/substring only.
improvements.proposed: (1) PHRASE: detect a quoted query `"..."`; for it, after FTS narrows candidates, post-filter with a regex/ILIKE adjacency check `text ILIKE '%'||replace(phrase,' ','%')||'%'` AND verify token order with a Python `re.search(r'\bword1\W+word2\b')` on the snippet candidate set, or use DuckDB's `regexp_matches`. (2) PREFIX (true): support a trailing `*` (e.g. `bitco*`) by matching `term%` at a word boundary: `regexp_matches(lower(text), '\m'||$prefix)` (DuckDB supports `\m` word-start). (3) FUZZY: add a `fuzzy` mode backed by DuckDB's `jaccard`/`levenshtein`/trigram: build a trigram set per token and rank by `1 - levenshtein(token, candidate_word)/len`. Cheapest implementation: enable the `fts` extension's stemming PLUS a fallback that, when auto-mode FTS+prefix both return 0, runs `WHERE levenshtein(lower(title||' '||text-window), $q) <= ceil(0.2*len($q))` over a LIMIT-capped scan, or precompute a `qgram` column. (4) Sanitize the FTS input: strip characters DuckDB FTS drops and, for hyphenated tokens like 'bit-coin', also try the joined form 'bitcoin' so the user isn't penalized for punctuation.
improvements.rationale: Users type quotes, partial words, and typos; a 'search that actually works' must degrade gracefully instead of returning empty. levenshtein/trigram give bounded-edit-distance recall (the standard fuzzy-search formulation) and DuckDB ships these scalar functions, so no new dependency is needed.
improvements.expected_impact: Quoted phrases, `term*` prefixes, hyphenated tokens, and single-typo queries all return sensible results. Removes a large slice of the 'janky' surface area.

improvements.title: Make pagination stable and stop recomputing COUNT(*) on every page
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py `search` (COUNT at 472-473 and 517-521, LIMIT/OFFSET at 485 and 533); CLI search loop (main.py 2669-2742)
improvements.current_state: Every page turn in the interactive CLI calls `idx.search(...)` afresh, which re-runs `SELECT COUNT(*) ...` over the candidate set AND a new LIMIT/OFFSET query. Two problems: (1) cost — COUNT over the FTS/ILIKE predicate is recomputed for page 2, 3, 4… even though `total` never changes within a session; for a substring/prefix query that COUNT is a full scan of `captures`. (2) correctness — OFFSET-based paging over `ORDER BY score DESC` (FTS) or `ORDER BY fetch_ts DESC` (prefix) is unstable if the index refreshes mid-session (a new ingest shifts rows, so page 2 can repeat or skip rows). Also the `max_results` clamp logic (lines 413-416) silently rewrites the caller's offset, which can make the CLI's `n`/`p` navigation land on a different page than the user asked for.
improvements.proposed: (1) Return `total` once and have the CLI cache it across page turns (only re-fetch rows on n/p, reuse the cached total). (2) For ranked FTS, add a deterministic tiebreaker to the ORDER BY (`ORDER BY score DESC, capture_id ASC`) so OFFSET paging is stable. (3) Offer keyset pagination for the recency-sorted prefix path: accept an optional `after_fetch_ts`/`after_capture_id` cursor and translate to `WHERE (fetch_ts, capture_id) < ($cursor_ts, $cursor_id) ORDER BY fetch_ts DESC, capture_id DESC LIMIT n` — O(limit) regardless of page depth, and immune to mid-session inserts. (4) Compute COUNT only on page 0 and pass it back; when the clamp rewrites offset, return the effective offset in the payload (it already returns `offset`) and have the CLI read `res['offset']` instead of its local variable so display and state stay consistent.
improvements.rationale: Deep OFFSET pagination is O(offset+limit) per page and unstable under writes; keyset pagination is the standard fix and DuckDB executes the tuple comparison efficiently. Caching total removes a redundant full scan per keystroke in the CLI loop.
improvements.expected_impact: Snappy page turns even on large result sets, no duplicated/skipped rows when ingestion runs concurrently, and CLI navigation that lands exactly where the user asked.

improvements.title: Add facet counts (by source, domain, language, time bucket) to search results
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py `search` (returns total/rows only); src/awareness/api/server.py /search (lines 422-456); CLI search render (main.py 2700-2728)
improvements.current_state: `search` returns `{total, rows, ranked, mode, fields, query}` with no aggregate breakdown. A user who searches 'bitcoin' and gets few results has no way to see WHERE the matches live (which source, which domains, which time range) — so they can't tell whether the corpus is thin, mis-filtered, or just date-skewed. The standalone `counts` command exists but requires an explicit date range and ignores the query, so it can't explain a given search.
improvements.proposed: Add an optional `facets: bool=False` (or `facets='source,domain,language'`) parameter to `idx.search`. When set, after computing the candidate WHERE (reuse the exact same predicate string + params already built for the FTS/prefix path), run grouped aggregates against that predicate: `SELECT source_type, COUNT(*) n FROM <candidates> GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 20` and likewise for `domain`, `language`, and a `date_trunc('month', fetch_ts)` histogram. Return them under `res['facets']`. Wire `?facets=...` into the API endpoint and render a compact facet panel in the CLI/SPA (e.g. 'Sources: cc-wet 812 · rss 140 · gdelt 33 | Top domains: …'). Implementation detail: factor the candidate predicate into a CTE `WITH hits AS (<select capture_id FROM ... WHERE predicate>)` so total, rows, and every facet share one predicate and stay consistent.
improvements.rationale: Faceting both improves UX and is a diagnostic: if 'bitcoin' shows '2 results, all from 2014, all cc-wet', the user instantly understands it's a corpus/date issue, not a search bug. Sharing one predicate CTE keeps facet counts exactly consistent with the result set.
improvements.expected_impact: Users can drill into and reason about result sets; operators get instant insight into why a query is thin. Turns search from a black box into an explorable surface.

improvements.title: Fix highlighting/snippets to match what FTS actually matched (stems, not raw query)
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py `_snippet_for` + `_tokenize_query` (lines 494-625); src/awareness/cli/main.py `highlight_query` (lines 2404-2450)
improvements.current_state: Two layers highlight differently. The FTS path matches STEMMED tokens (e.g. 'running' matches 'run'), but `_snippet_for` and the CLI `highlight_query` highlight the RAW query terms with `\b(term)\w*` word-boundary regex. So when BM25 ranks a doc because its stem matched, the snippet may contain the match but NOT highlight it (query 'mining' won't visually highlight a doc that matched on stem 'mine'/'mined'), making correct results look irrelevant. Also `_snippet_for` centers on the FIRST raw-term occurrence; for a multi-term query it doesn't prefer the densest window, so the snippet often misses the most relevant passage. `_tokenize_query` drops 1-char tokens (`len>=2`), so a query like 'Q' or 'X' (or CJK single chars) is un-highlightable.
improvements.proposed: (1) Thread the actual matched roots into highlighting: `search` already computes `snippet_terms = roots or terms` for the prefix path; do the SAME for the FTS path by stemming the query tokens (`_stem_roots`) and passing those roots as `snippet_terms`, and have the CLI highlight on roots with a `root\w*` pattern (so 'mine' highlights 'mining'). (2) Best-window snippet: instead of first-occurrence, score each candidate window by number of DISTINCT query roots present (a simple sliding window over match positions) and pick the densest — standard 'best passage' selection. (3) For CJK/short tokens, fall back to substring highlighting when `\b` word boundaries don't apply (CJK has no word boundaries) by detecting non-ASCII and using plain `re.escape(term)` without `\b`. (4) Unify the two implementations: have the CLI call a shared highlight helper that takes the server-provided `terms`/roots, so server and client never disagree.
improvements.rationale: Highlighting that doesn't match the ranking logic makes correct results look broken — a direct driver of 'search is janky'. Densest-window snippets and stem-aware highlighting are the standard fixes and reuse data the search already computes.
improvements.expected_impact: Snippets reliably show and highlight why each result matched, including stemmed and partial matches; short/CJK queries highlight too. Restores user trust that results are relevant.

improvements.title: Warn loudly when a backfill plans zero tasks (e.g. CC-index needs --domain, all sources empty)
improvements.area: src/awareness/planner/planner.py `submit_backfill` (lines 42-91); src/awareness/sources/cc_index.py `plan` (returns [] without domains, lines 38-40); CLI backfill_submit (main.py 1078-1127)
improvements.current_state: `CommonCrawlIndexAdapter.plan` returns [] unless `request.domains` is set; `FeedsAdapter.plan` always returns []; FineWeb returns [] when `datasets` is missing. `submit_backfill` sums `total` tasks but never checks whether `total == 0` — it logs `planner_backfill_submitted total_tasks=0` at INFO and returns a job_id as if successful. The CLI then prints '[green]Submitted backfill[/green]' with no indication that the job will do nothing. A user who runs `backfill submit --start 2024-01-01 --domain example.com` expecting CC-index, but mistypes the source filter, gets a cheerful green success and an empty corpus — then blames search.
improvements.proposed: In `submit_backfill`, after the planning loop, if `total == 0` raise or return a structured warning: set the job status to a terminal `EMPTY`/`COMPLETED` with a note `'no tasks planned: <reasons>'` where reasons enumerate why each in-scope adapter produced nothing (e.g. 'CC-INDEX: requires --domain', 'FINEWEB: datasets not installed', 'GDELT: range produced 0 slots'). Surface this in the CLI: if `status['tasks_total'] == 0`, print a yellow warning block instead of green success, listing the reasons and the fix. Optionally make the planner return per-source `(source, planned, reason)` tuples so both CLI and API can render the breakdown.
improvements.rationale: A job that plans zero work should never look like a success. Telling the user precisely why each source was empty turns a baffling empty corpus into an actionable message ('install datasets', 'pass --domain').
improvements.expected_impact: Eliminates the 'I ran a backfill and nothing happened' class of confusion that feeds the 'no idea how to scrape' perception; users self-correct misconfigurations immediately.

improvements.title: Harden auto-mode fallback so punctuation/operator queries never return empty
improvements.area: src/awareness/storage/duckdb_index.py `search` auto/fts branch (lines 455-491)
improvements.current_state: In `auto` mode, the code runs FTS first; if `total > 0` it returns ranked rows, else it falls through to prefix. BUT `fts_eligible` is only true when `fields == DEFAULT_SEARCH_FIELDS`; and for an explicit `--mode fts`, when `match_bm25` strips the entire query to nothing (I verified 'bit-coin', '"phrase"', 'C++' all yield 0 and do NOT error), the function returns `total=0` with NO fallback — the user gets an empty result set despite obvious matching documents.
